articles.title: DISIRESS IN LANCASHIRE.
articles.text:
DISIRESS IN LANCASHIRE.

THE RELIEF COMMITTEES AND
WORKING CLASS SUBSCRIPTIONS.

"Lives there a man with soul so dead,
Who never to himse,if hath said,
This is my own, my native land!

COLD and callous must be the heart of that
man,which does not throb with sympathy far
the sufferings and privations now being ex-
perienced by the operatives in the cotton dis-
tricts. Even that of an Hyde Park bludgeon
man—who is only a few removes from the
brute creation—must feel some sympathetic
pulsation on hearing of the misery and starva-
tion now stalking through those populous ,
districts. All benevolent and right-hearted
men feel sympathy for, and a desire to alle-
viate, the misfortunes even of those who have
brought their misery upon themselves by their
own imprudence; how much deeper and wide
spread, then; should be that sympathy for the
thousands of men, women, and children,
rendered destitute by no fault of their own,
but who are the victims of bad legislation and
" cottonocracy" selfishness. cabinet ministers,

Peers members of parliament, bishops,
bankers, men of all classes, members of relief

committees, even poor law guardians—aye
start not, reader, even poor law guardians—
have one and all, in the press and on the plat-
form, borne high and ample testimony to the
fortitude and patience with which the' cotton
operatives, and those connected with them,
have borne themselves under their unmerited

-
privations. One Cabinet minister, the Chan-
cellor of the Exch€ quer, went so far as to say,
"that the conduct of the working classes had
been so noble under their sufferings that in
any future consideration of the extension of
the franchise in Parliament it would be re-
collected by the Government." But while this
public testimony is given to the operatives,
what is the treatment they are privately re-
_ .

c-eiy-ing from many of these relief committees,
poor law guardians, and others of the cotton-
ocracy ? Wholesale disfranchisement; a total
refusal of relief to those holding any shares in

_
a co-operative or building society; persecu-
tion, by giving partial relief only, to those who
have at any time made themselves obnoxious

to the manufacturers by taking an active
part in trades' union matters; and the ap-
plication of the labour test to those who
have been hard workers all their lives
until the present period of forced idleness. This
is no idle statement, but a positive fact, openly
stated in the local papers, and vouched for by
parties of respectability. The subject was
recently alluded to by the Rev. Mr. Verity, the
rector of Habergham, near Padiham, in a let-
ter which appeared in the columns of this
paper. Why is this? The answer is plain.
Working men are carefully and systematically
excluded from acting on these relief committees,
(with one exception, I believe, that of the Sal-
ford Working Men's Association), and hence
the fa.ntastic tricks, short sighted policy, and
f.alse humanity, indulged in by men "dressed
in a little brief authority." At Ashton-under-

Lyne, and other places: the working class elec-
tors who hare been compelled to accept tem-
porary relief from the poor rates, have been
struck of the parliamentary roll as paupers;
according to the strict letter of the law; thus,
having been reduced to a state of pauperism by
no fault of their own, they are then coolly
robbed of their manhood rights by the pro-
fessing humanitarians and charity mongers on
relief committees. Again, these committees
have come to the determination of refusing
relief to any persons holding a share or shares in
a co-operative, manufacturing, or building com-
pany. What is this but a premium to future
improvidence? Under the present circum-
stances the holder of this scrip is as destitute
as any of his fellows; he is the holder of a bit
of paper valueless and unsaleable, as the
parties to whom he might in other times dis-
pose of it, are now equally destitute with him-
self. lo consider a man in this position as
possessed of "property," and to refuse him
relief on that account, is a mockery, and a
piece of Jesuitism disgraceful to those who
practise it. It looks very like a bit of manu-
facturing and shopkeeping spite to those who,
in a humble but honourable way, were be-
coming manufacturers and shopkeepers for
themselves. Common decency, if not
humanity, should have prevented such
a scandal. It is more difficult to prove
the refusal of relief to those who have been
active in trade society matters, inasmuch as
this is very rarely the assigned reason, but the
fact is patent all over the relieved districts.
The application of the labour test to men who
have all their lives laboured bard for their
living, and who are now
is
from causes be-
yond their own control, s cruel and heartless;
the enforcement of this test, only intended for
the vagabond and lazy pauper, on the honest
and. industrious operative, is condemned by all
but those concerned in enforcing it as a bad
policy, likely to bring forth bitter fruit. It
will be evidently not the fault of these Lanca-
shire poor law guardians, if the now peaceable
and wed-conducted though famishing opera-
tive, is not speedily transformed into the dis-
contented and disaffected agitator.
Bearing the above facts in mind, what should
be the replf of the Trades' Unions, and other
bodies,of working men, to the many and con-
tinued appeals th them for pecuniary aid?
i
Not to relax n their, subscriptions, but to take
care to whom those subscriptions are entrus-
ted, and to ascertain how they are applied. I
hope, for the credit and honour of my fellow
workmen, they will withhold their support
from the present relief committees, who are in
almost every instance acting as I have above
stated. Day after day may be seen in the pub-
lished Mansion House lists the subscriptions
of working men, individually and Collectively;
and I regret thiS, knowing the funds are not
applied in the way that working men would
themselves apply them if they had the distri-
bution. It will be said that hitherto there
has been no properly constituted body to
Whom subscriptions could be sent. Pro-
bably not; but this deficiency no longer
?lists. The working men of Paaiham, Burn-
and other places in East Lancashire,
deeply sensible of the present bad and partial
system under which the relief money has
been distributed, and resenting the systematic
exclusion
of their class from the relief commit._
tees, held- a meeting last Saturday in the Odd-
fellowsa, Padiham, and having heard an
-hll
address from the Rev. Mr. Verity, the rector
of Habergham, resolved on establishing the
" East Lancashire Central Operatives Relief
Committee," with branch committees all over
the county. The object is not to supplant or op-
pose any of the middle class relief committees,
c.
ignorance, which are now,
now in existence, but to supplement them; to
relieve those deserving
ases
either wilfully or from wholly or
partially passed over. The relief committees
connected with this fund are not confined to
working men, but comprise all classes, and all
shades of political and religious opinion. The
Central Committee meet daily at the Committee
Rooms, Speak Buildings, Burnley Road,

No, 53

Padiham, Lancashire; Mr. Wilkinson being
the treasurer, Mr. Peacock, the secretary, and
the Rev. Mr. Verity, the chairman. Let, then,
the subscriptions .of my fellow workmen,
instead of going to swell the funds of those
relief committees who treat working men as
I have described, be sent either direct to the
treasurer of the " East Lancashire Relief
Fund," at the above address, or to the office of
the BEE-1117E newspaper, where a subscrip-
tion list is opened, and all monies received are
forwarded weekly to the treasurer, with whom
the manager of the paper is in daily communi-
cation.

Trades' Unionists! do not send your money
to those committees who punish trades'
unionists by wholly or partially refusing :them
relief from their funds.
Co-operators! withhold your monies from
those committees who declare that those who
hold shares in your societies are "possessors
of property," and not entitled to relief.
Reformers! keep back your subscriptions
from those who rob your fellow workmen of
their franchise, because they have become tem-
porary recipients of poor law relief.
Working. Men ! do not contribute to those
committees, the members of which enforce the
cruel pauper labour test upon your hard work-
ing and industrious brethren.
Trades' Unionists! Co-operators! Re-
formers! Working men of all classes! sub-
scribe liberally in your societies and shops,
contribute individually to the extent of your
means, in behalf of your distressed brethren in
the cotton districts, and having done your duty
in this respect, then perform another, namely,
take care that your subscriptions do not go
into the hands of committees entirely compo-
sed of that class who despise you, insult you,
and degrade you; who reduce your wages
whenever they have the opportunity; who re-
ply to your just demand for a reduction of the
hours of labour by a lock-out; who deny your
right or fitness for the franchise; but who are
always ready to flatter and cajole you in
their time of need. Support the East Lan-
cashire Relief Committee, and you will have a,
guarantee that your subscriptions will be ap-
plied as you would yourselves distribute them.
Do this, and you will receive the gratitude of
your Lancashire brethren, the approbation of
your own conscience, and give much satisfac-
tion to your friend SCOURGE.
Oct 17.

FATAL OCCURRENCE ON THE THAMES —Oll Saturday
an inquiry was instituted at the George, Great
George-street, Bermondsey, relative to the deaths of
Joseph Anderson, aged 67, and George J9hnson Hare,
aged 38, labourers employed at Fountain Dock, Ber-
mondsey-wall. Charlea Brady, a labourer, deposed
that on Wednesday, about five o'clock in the after-
noon, he was employed with Anderson, Hare, and a
number of other men, in constructing a gridiron' at
Fountain Dock. They hld two barges about 25 feet
apart, and to get from one to another there was a rat't,
consisting of three logs of timber. The whole of the
men got upon the raft, and Anderson, in endeavouring
to push it from the barge, overreached himself and fell
backwards into the water. The deceased, Hare, with-
out hesitation jumped into the water and swam
Inwards Anderson, but both suddenly disappeared.
He could not say whether Anderson caught hold of
Hare. From the evidence of the witnesses it appeared
that the bodies were recovered about half an hour
after the accident, and that the deceased, Hare, had
frequently beet Om means of saving people from
drowning by jumping into the river, The coroner
having remarked on the painful nature of the case,
the jury returned a verdict in accordance with the
evidence.

MELANCHOLY ACCIDENT AND Loss or FIVE LIVES
most melancholy accident, resulting in the loss of
five lives, took place on Sunday, near Bristol. It
appears that on the morning of that day five men,
named George Davey, John Bromley, John Gunstone,
John Pocock, and Charles Copp, all carpenters in the
employ of Mr. Rowland. Brotherhood, and engaged at
work on the bridge ot the Bristol and South Wales
Union Railway, had promised some fellow, workmen on
the other side of the Severn to meet them at Chepstow,
and having procured a boat, they proceeded on the
voyage. On their way they obtained the assistance of
a man named Price, a seaman on board a vessel lying
at anchor at the bridge, to steer them across the Severn,
which he did in safety. Finding that their companions
had left and gone across the Severn by way of Aust
Ferry, Old Passage, the six men then partook of some
refreshment, and, having Set sail for the return voyage,
all proceeded well until they came to the mouth of the
Chepstow river, when the wind had increased to a gale.
Price, the steersmen, reefed sail and put back again into
Chepstow river, persuading them to remain until Mon-
day unrning, or until the storm had abated ; but
Davey would not assent to this proposal, and, having
insisted on taking the helm from Price, turned the
boat's head, at the same time unreefing the sail. They
had made the passage about half way across the
Severn, when they were caught in a tremendous squall,
between two and three o'clock in the afternoon, and the
boat.immediately cap 4zed with its living freight, when
five out ot the six on board met a watery grave. Price
was the only man saved; having clung by his little
finger to the stern of the boat, he was washed on to the
sands. After the storm had passed away, the wife of
one of the workmen saw a figure on the sands, and
having raised an alarm, Mr. Parnall, of the Passage
Hotel, proceeded to the beach, and having a powerful
telescope at once recognised the object as the man
Price. Mr. Curthoys, with the help of Mr. Ada, im-
mediately put off in a boat to his assistance, and suc-
ceeded in rescuing him from a watery grave, after be-
ing in the water tor nearly two hours.

articles.title: LONDON, 6AYUADAY, OCTOBER, 18, 1862.
articles.text:
LONDON, 6AYUADAY, OCTOBER, 18, 1862.

SURREY HACKNEY CARRIAGE
.3IASTER.s' ASSOCIATIOY.

The first anniversary meeting of this society was
held oa Tuesday evening last, at Anderton's
Hotel, Fleet-street, and was very numerously attended,
not only by members of the society, but by many of
the proprietors belonging to the Westminster and

Central- Associations. Amongst the company were

Mr. Bury Hutchinson, barrister, Dr. Price, Mr. Gower,
of the Repository, Barbican, Mr. Lowe, of the White
Bear Tavern, Kennington, Mr. Beadle, &c., &c.

Mr. Ayers the president of the Surrey Association,
was in the chair, and Mr. Wellbeloved, of the Central
Association, fiaed the vice-chair. Having done justice
to a substantial dinner the cloth was removed, and the
more im eediate busineSs of the evening commenced.
the Chairman having given the usual loyal Oasts,
which were duly honoured, then proposed, Success to
the Surrey Hackney Carriage Masters' Association,
and all other associii•ions connected therewith.'
Mr. Piokering, till. Secretary of the Surrey Society,
responded to the toast. He said he felt proud at beiug
placed in his present position, and seeing so many
friends from all parts. The Association with which
he was connected was formed on the 15th Sept, 1861,
by himself and .15 other proprietor,. The first object
was to protect themselves against bad drivers, and
for this purpose they made, a rule that any driver
who left the employ of two masters improperly
should have his licence endorsed by them, which
would prevent him serving a third in the same
why. This only affected the badly cohlucted
drivers, and the good men, who formed the
great majority of drivers, had no occasion
to fear it. (Rear.) As the society progressed, they
felt themselves strong enough to grapple with the
many grievances under which the trade laboured,
owing to the defects in the present Hackney Carriage
Act, and having placed themselves in communication
with, and obtained the co-operation of the other asso-
ciations, they resolved to send a letter to Sir R. Mayne,
the Police Commissioner, soliciting him to receive a
deputation of proprietors. They complained, firstly,
that there was a deficiency of room for cabs on the
Val bus stands; secondly, an insufficient supply of
water at those stands for the horses; thirdly, of their
liability to be summoned for any defects in their cabs
and horses without any previous notice; and, fourthly,
requiring an alteraeion in the time of inspections. Mr.
Pickering then read from the minute book a long corre-
spondence between the Pollee Cornmiisioner and him-
self upon the subject, but up to the present time they had
been unable to obtain the desired interview, or any satis-
factory reply to the letter. To obtain any redress for
their present grievances they must have a revision of
the present Act, but that could only be obtained by
union amongst themselves. He, therefore, hoped that
associations would at once be formed in every district
of the metropolis, that they might go to Parliament for
a Select Committee of Inquiry with a view to an
amendment of the Hackney Carriage Act, many of the
provisions of which now bore so hardly both on pro-
prietors and drivers. The drivers were moving in the
matter, and were earnestly at work, and let not the
proprietors lag behind. He condemned the present
system of licensing, by which proprietors were pre-
vented from hiring drivers whom they wished, but
were compelled to employ any that Sir R. Mayne
chose to licence. (Cheers.)
Mr. Townsend replied on behalf of the Westminster,
and Mr. Balding on behalf of the Central Association,
the latter strongly advocating free trade in hackney
carriages, or at least that they should be placed on the
same footing as omnibuses.
Mr. Case said he thought the cause of their griev-
ances to be over legislation. He complained of their
having to run for 61. per mile, no matter what the
price of corn or horseflesh; however enhanced in price
these might be, their tariff of charges was arbitrarily
fixed. (Hear.) A great outcry had been made by the
public and by some portion of the press at their raising
the amounts to he paid them by their drivers. But
what were the facts? The average price they had
been charging the drivers previous to the Exhibition
was trom 15s. to 18s. per day, working with two
horses; but the demands of the public during the
Exhibition time had been so great that they were
compelled to employ three horses, and surely for this
; addition to their expenses they were entitled to charge
2s. or 3s. additional. (Hear.) The extra charge did
not meet the extra expenses, and this clamour against
them had been made in ignorance of facts. Omnibus
proprietors, railway and steamboat proprietors, hotel
proprietors, and other classes, had raised their prices,
and why was not the cab proprietor allowed to do
the same without abuse being heaped upon his head ?
Their only hope lay in their union. Without it,
nothing could be done; with it, they would accomplish
all they wanted. (Cheers.)
The Vice-Chairman, in very flattering terms, pro-
posed Tne Press, with three times three.'
Messrs. Byrne, Barrow, Corfield, Hartwell, and
Dyer, severally returned thanks.
Mr. Palmer proposed Success to the Cabmen's
Clubs.' He thought these clubs deserving of the sup-
port of the masters generally.
• Mr. Smith, Secretary of the South London Club,
responded. He said these clubs were well deserving
support. If proprietors when they wanted men, would
only send to these clubs they would always find good
men at their command. The delegates of the drivers
had for some time past been engaged in drawing up a
scheme for the amendment of the Hackney Carriage
Act, which was now complete. District meetings
of the men were about to beheld, to which the masters
would be invited, and they would thus be able to
judge for themselves what the men had been doing.
Let the masters and men cordially co-operate together;
their interests ought to be one, and they would soon
find the position of both parties improved. Re thanked
them on behalf of the men for the cordial manner in
which they had received the toast. (Cheers.)
Mr. M'Gwillim proposed the health of Mr. Pickering,
which was received with much applause, and duly re-
sponded to by that gentleman.
Mr. Phillips proposed the health of Mr. Jonathan I
Emmett, to which that gentleman replied. He ex-
pressed himself a convert to free trade.
Mr. Bury Hutchinson proposed the health of the
chairman, and in doing so entered at some length into
the way he thought the association should proceed to
attain its object. Hie services were always at their
command. (Rear.)
The Chairman, in acknowledging the toast, expressed
the pleasure he felt at seeing himself surrounded by so
many good men and true. He had always endeavoured
and would still continue to do everything in his power
to advance the interests of the trade. Re was for free
trade in cabs. (Hear.)
Tne Vice-Chairman's health having been proposed,
he concluded his acknowledgment of the toast by pro-
posing the health of Messrs. Gower and Beadle, who
had always proved themselves good friends to the

trade. -
Messrs. Gower and Beadle having replied, the pro-
ceedings, which had given the greatest satisfaction to
all present, about 120 in number, were brought to a
close. During the evening a largo number of proprie-
tors were enrolled as members ot the association.
The members of the press attending on the occasion
deemed it their duty to acknowledge the kindness and
attention a Mr. Pickering,, thD secretary,.

articles.title: AT BATIL
articles.text:
AT BATIL

GARIBALDI SYJIPATITY .21EETIIVG

A crowded meeting was held at the Guildhall, Bath,
on Monday evening, for the purpose of expressing
sympathy with Garibaldi.'
The mayor, Mr. Thomas Faller, presided'; and,
after a general review of the course of -Italian affairs,
and the part taken by Garibaldi therein, read letters
of apology—from inability to attend—from Dr. Tun-
stall, Mt. Tite, 11'LP., and other gentlemen.
The Rev. Mr. Penistan moved the first resolution,
declaring that the meeting, deeply impressed with
admiration of the sublime devotion of Garibalai to his
country's cause, and of the purity and simplicity of
his character, most cordially sympathise with him in
his recent misfortune. _ _ _ _

Mr. Whiting, in a speech of some length, seconded
the msolution. and went on to say :—Garibaldi woun-
ded! Garibaldi and liberty! Garibaldi! Why that name
seemed to strike the note of freedom in the ears of
the oppressed. It was a name that Italy rejoiced in,
and it was a name that would be handed down to
posterity. They had been in the habit, as a nation, of
holding in respect those men, those heroes, who had
achieved mighty deeds; those men who had fought
their battles and gained their noble victories. They
were taught from their earliest childhood to lisp the
names of those men who had fought for civil and
religious liberty. And that was perfectly right; but
he thought if they honoured those men whose bones
lay mouldering in the dust,' they were much more
called upon to respect and honour those men who were
living in their own day, who had achieved such great
and good things for their country. They therefore
looked to Garibaldi. He had done wondrous things
for Italy. He had made a noble sacrifice, and, regard-
less of all personal aggrandisement, had gone forth in
order to emancipate the people that were bound. Gari-
baldi had endeavoured to bring Rome to the nittion—to
Italy; but in his attempt be had fallen by the hands of the
It ,lian soldiers. In that noble attempt of his he had been
wounded and taken to the fortress of Spezzia—(cries of
'Shame ')—and it was in that condition that they
sympathised with the noble patriot. Some men would
tell them that Garibaldi had no right to endeavour to

take possession of Rome, and that—he had no business
there. But he contended that Garibaldi had business
there, which he had made known some years ago,
when he spice to the people of Newcastle in words
which would never be forgotten, and in which he
prophesied what had taken place. What did he. say
when he was presented with a sword and telescope by
the Newcastle citiz,-ns? He said: The future alone
will show how soon I must unsheath this noble gift

and again fight on behalf of that which is nearest --iny
heart—the freedom of my' native land; but be sure of
this, Italy one day will te free.' (Loud cheers.) They
saw, then that the great object ot Garibaldi was the
freedom Of his native land. Fur that he had unsheathed
the swerd ; for that the had gone forth; for that, be-
lieving he was doing right, Garibaldi had fallen into
the hands of Italian soldiers. The resolution was car-
ried by acclamation.
The second resolution was moved by the Rev. H.
Dyer. It stated that the meeting regarded with great
apprebens;on the prolonged occupation of Rome by a
foreign army, and trusted that army would be speedily
withdrawn. The people of England, he said, had
already expressed their cordial sympathy with Gari-
baldi, and their high admiration for him • and those
expressions would doubtless go across the continent
until they reached him, and again stimulate that
emotion which he had in vain tried to express in the
address which had been published, full of stirring,
glowing, and grateful admiration of England and of
England's sympathy for him, and for Italy in her
time of sorrow. _ _ _ _

sir. Alderman Hunt seconded the resolution, which
was carried amid loud cheering; after which another
resolution was passed, declaring that the moralinfluence
of England ought to be exerted, with a view to the
withdrawal of the army of occupation from Rome.
It was agreed that copies of the resolutions should
be forwarded to her Majesty's Minister for Foreign
Affairs, and also to General Garibaldi.
The meeting was subsequently addressed by Dr. C.
A. Sandoy, a Hungarian exile, and concluded with a
vote of thanks to the chairman.

articles.title: GARIBALDI RIOTS AT BIRKENHEAD.
articles.text:
GARIBALDI RIOTS AT BIRKENHEAD.

The Garibaldian excitement in Birkenhead, which
was so suddenly aroused last week by an attack of an
Irish mob upon the building in which the Parliamen-
tary Debating Society had met for the purpose of dis-
cussing the subject of 'Sympathy with Garibaldi and
Italy,' and increased by their cowardly assault upon Holy
Trinity Church. reached its heighton Wednesday, when
the Debating Society held their adjourned meeting.
ing. As anticipated, large crowds of people,
chiefly from the low Irish quarter of Birken-
head, assembled in Price-street and the streets ad-
joining Holy Trinity Church, and the schools
where the Parliamentary Debating Society met.
The discussion on the Garibaldi question went on. The
approaches to the room were strongly guarded by police,
from four to six hundred special constables, including
many volunteers (out of uniform), who assisted
the police to check the violence of the mob; but, in
spite of these efforts, several persons were severely in-
jured, many of the mob being armed with bludgeons,
old sabres, knives, &c. Women took an active part in
the affray; and one armed with a hatchet attacked a
policeman. In order to distract the police and darken
the air, the chimneys of most houses in the Irish
quarter were set on fire. This filled the streets with
dense smoke, under cover of which many acts of vio-
lence, both on persons and property, were committed.
The windows of a leather-shop and bread-shop in
Watson-street were smashed, and goods thrown into
the street. Some of these outrages were carried on by
women and girls. Three police officers, seriously in-
jured, have been taken to the hospital.
The meeting of the Debating Society took place,
and was throughout of an enthusiastic character, a
resolution expressing admiration of Garibaldi being
unanimously adopted.

BIRKENHEAD (Friday Evening.)—There have been
no further rioting since Wednesuay. Eleven men and
women (Irish) have been arrested as ringleaders, and
committed to Chester for trial. A detachment of the
49th Regiment, and a strong body of the Liverpool
police are now at the disposal of the magistrates. To
show the feeling existing in the town on Wednesday
night a squad of policemen, while passing some of the
mob, cheered lustily for Garibaldi, while last night
the Volunteers under Lieut.-Colonel King gave three
cheers for Garibaldi, as many for each of the magis•
ti ates, followed by three deep groans for the Pope, and
three still deeper for the Emperor of the French.

A WORKING MAN'S COLLEGE AT IPSWICII.—A pub-
lic meeting was held at the Town-hall, Ipswich on the
7th inst., for the purpose of inaugurating a Working

making. The chair was occupied by Allan Ransome,
Esq., and the meeting was addressed by Mr. Thomas
Shorter, semetary to the London Working Men's
College, and by the Rev. Henry Solly, secrßtary to. the
Working Men's Club and Institute Union, who came
from London in consequence of an application for
assistame to the London Working Nees College.

PRICE Two PENCE.

THE LADY,' THE STRANGER,' AND

THE RING.

On Tuesday, at Lambeth Police Court, Elizabeth
Wilson, a young woman dressed in deep mourning,
who was said to be living under the protection of a
'gentleman' at 6-1, Walnut-tree-walk, Lambeth, was
placed at the bar before Mr. Elliot, and charged on
suspicion with being concerned with a Frenchman,
not in custody, in stealing a diamond ring of the value
of £65, the property of Mr. Richard Attenborough,
pawnbroker, of Knightsbridge.
Charles Palmer, assistant to Mr. Attenborough,
deposed that on Saturday afternoon, between the hours
of four and five, a middle-aged foreigner called at the
shop of his master and requested to he shown a diamond
ring which was exhibited -for sale in the window, and
which was marked at 75 guineas. Mr. Basset, the
foreman of the shop, took the ring from the INindow,
and placing it on the counter the man took it up,
examined the number of stones which formed the clus-
ter, and, taking out his pooket-book, appeared to calcu-
late their value separately, and ultimately purchased
the ring for £65. He then requested that a per-
son might be sent with him to his residence,
61, Walnut-tree-walk, Lambeth, where he would
pay for it. Witness accordingly accompanied
the man to the house mentioned, the door of
which was opened by a female, then present, and the
man, on meeting the prisoner in the passage, addressed
her in the most endearing terms—calling her his dar-
ling, and said ho had intended to he home much
sooner. They then entered the parlour, and he (wit-
ness) went in there also, when the man wrote one or
two notes, which he handed to the prisoner, and she
left the apartment. The foreigner then said he kept
his money upstairs, and asked witness to let him have
the ring to show it to his friends upstairs, and he
left the parlour, closing the door after him. In about
five minutes after the prisoner returned to the parlour
with a dog in her arms, asked him if he were a judge
of dogs, and began to speak of the qualities of the
animal, for the purpose, as he believed, of engaging
his attention while the man made his escape. He at
length asked her if the man was not her husband.
The prisoner replied that he was not, and that she
knew no more about him than havinc, met him in the
street on the night before. Witness finding that the
man was gone away with the ring went to the station-
house, and having obtained the assistance of Sergeant
Shephard, a detective, he gave the prisoner into cus-
tody.
sergeant Shephard said that on going to the house,
61, Walnut-tree- walk, with the last witness, the pri-
soner informed him that all she knew of the French-
man who had stolen the ring was her merely meeting
. him for the first time on Friday night in the Kenning-
ton-road, and his sleeping with her for that night
only. The prisoner also said that on leaving her on
Saturday morning the man said he was going to call
on the French Ambassador to get some money, and
should be back in the course of the day. He (witness)
had ascertained that the prisoner had occupied the two
parlours of the house for some months, that she was
under the protection of a gentleman, but saw other
visitors. _ -

The defence set up was, that the foreigner who
stole the property was a perfect stranger to her beyond
one night's acqu dntance, and that she had no partici-
pation whatever in the robbery.
For the prosecution a remand was requested, and
Mr. Elliott granted it, but consented that the prisoner
might be allowed to go at large on good bail.

articles.title: EXTRAORDIN_4RY SUICIDE FROlf BLACKFRIARS-BRIDGE.
articles.text:
THE EXTRAORDIN_4RY SUICIDE
FROlf BLACKFRIARS-BRIDGE.

On Tuesday afternoon Mr. William Payne, the
city coroner, resumed at the Ship Tavern, Little
Bridge-street, Blackfriars, the inquiry touching the
death of a female unknown, who, it was alleged, com-
mitted suicide a short time since by jumping off Black-
friars-bridge into the river under very singular circum-
stances. it will be recollected that on the previous
occasion it was stated that on last Wednesday week a
large crowd assembled on Blackfriars-bridge in conse-
quence of a rumour that a young womon had been seen
to wrap a child up in her crinoline and leap into the
water. The next morning a young woman was found
under the pier, but no trace of a child was discovered.
Upon the 'resumption of the inquiry on Tuesday,
Mrs. Harriet Jones, Rundle-street, Haymarket,
recognised the clothes of deceased as those
of her sister, Rosalia Sarah Mady, aged 18.
Deceased had been in service with Mrs. Ba-
riere, Inkerman-row, Kentish Town. She left her
situation on the Saturday previous to her death, and
remained with witness until the Tuesday, when
, witness's husband ,I said she should either go to her
brother at Crayford or get a place. She then left, but
did not say where she was going to, and witness saw
her no more. She had only a shilling in her purse.
She told witness that at Mrs. Bariere's she had made 1
the acquaintance of the son of a master painter who '
was decorating the house, that she had walked
out with him on three or four occasions, and
that they had appointed to meet on the Sunday.
She went out accordingly, as she said, to meet him
on that day, but witness knew nothing further
of the matter. H. C. Mady, Great Ponton, Licoln-
shire, said that he made inquiries, and found that his
sister left her place on the Saturday. A portion of her
wages were stopped because she had set fire to a chair
and great coat. She appeared to have been lately un-
happy, and wrote to witness that she had no friends in
the world. The coroner, in summing up, said it was
most singular that amongst the crowd on the bridge
no one appeared to have actually seen the deceased
jump into the water. There was little doubt that
through some cause deceased had precipitated herself
into the water, but there was no evidence of the fact.
The jury returned a verdict ‘ That the deceased was
found dead in the waters of the Thames, but how she
came into the said waters there was no evidence to
show.'

SUICIDE OF A YOUNG WOMAN AND ATTEMPT AT
RESCUE —On Monday morning a young woman named
Brooks was walking with a young man down the
gangway leading to St. Paul's Steamboat Wharf;

after ejaculating something which could not be cor-

river. Tier male companion jumped in wilh the hopes
of saving the poor creature, but without effect. The
man himself had a narrow escape, and at first it was
doubtful whether he could recover from the effects of
the submersion.

articles.text:
LATEST TELEGRAMS.

THIRD ED ITION.-SATURDAY EVENING.

AMERICA.

NEW YORK, Oct. 6 (Evening.)—The Confederates,
under Generals Price and Van Dorn, supposed to num-
ber 40,000, attacked the Federal General Rosencranz
on the 3rd at Corinth, Mississippi. The fighting lasted
two days. General Rosencranz reported officially on
the sth that the rebels were repulsed with great
slaughter. He says The enemy is in full retreat,
leaving his dead and wounded. The loss is serious on
the Federal side, particularly in officers, but bears no
comparison with that of the enemy. Seven hundred
Confederate prisoners captured.'
I\TENV YORK, Oct. 7 (Evening).—The latest official
reports from Corinth state that the rebels have been
driven back five miles across the Hatchie river to-
wards Corinth. The Federals captured two batteries
and 300 prisoners. The Federal General Rosencranz
reports that the enemy is totally routed, throwing
everything away, and that the Federals are in sharp
pursuit. The Confederate General Martin is reported
killed. The Confederates have evacuated Frankfort,
Kentucky. The Federals are advancing on Frank-
fort. A small engagement has occurred at Newtonia,
Missouri. After two hours' fight the Confederates
broke and fled. They are said to be concentrating
beyond Newtonia, and the Federals are advancing to
renew the engagement. The majority of the Com-
mittee in the Confederate Senate has reported resolu-
tions that, after January next, Federal commissioned
or non-commissioned officers, when captured, shall be
kept at hard labour until the termination of the war, or
the repeal of President Lincoln's emancipation procla-
mation. Federal white officers training or command-
ing negroes on military enterprises against the Con-
federate States, or inciting slaves to rebellion, or pre-
tending to free them under Lincoln's proclamation,
shall, if captured, suffer death. President Davis
is authorised to adopt ouch other retaliatory measures •
best calculated to repress the atrocities of the enemy.
The Confederate Governor of North Carolina has
called a council to consider President Lincoln's eman-
cipation proclamation. General M'Clellan has issued
stringent orders against lawless depredations by the
troops. The operation of the draught in New York is
postponed until the 10th.

articles.title: PRUSSIA.
articles.text:
PRUSSIA.

BERLIN, Oct. 11.

In the Upper House to-day the vote upon the
proposition of the committee upon the budget was
taken by calling over names. The proposition was
rejected by 127 to 39. The bu iget as amended
by the Chamber of Deputies was also rejected by
150 to 17, the ministers voting with the majority.

-BERLIN, OCT. 13.

The Committee on the Budget passed a resolu-
tion, declaring that the vote of the Upper House
regarding the acceptance of the budget brought
forward by the government was opposed to the plain
sense and words of the constitution, and upon that
account null and void. _ _

In an evening sitting the President of the
Ministry read a decree of the King, dissolving the
Chamber.

articles.text:
THE ACCIDENT ON THE EDINBURGH
.AND GLASGOW RAILWAY.

LATEST PARTICULARS.
The total number of deaths which have resulted from
the collision on the Edinbergh and Glasgow Railway
on Monday evening, up to Wednesday morning, is
seventeen. The number of persons seriously injured
and under medical treatment is about fifty; and at the
lowest calculation about a hundred more have been
assisted home in a more or less injured state. The
persons killed all belong to Edinburgh and its neigh-
bourhood, excepting Mr. E. S Bolton, commercilia
traveller, ot Birmingham, who died shortly after his
extlication. George Newton, pointsman, has. been
I apprehended. Several of the wounded are
still in
danger. The engines and tenders of both trains were
smashed to pieces, and the driver and stoker killed.
All the bodies are not yet identified. Besides killed
and wounded removed to Edinburgh, 15 injured people
have been taken to Linlithgow. The cause of the accident,
it. is said, was owing to some misunderstanding as to the
signals at the single line, but it is not yet known who
was in fault.
As the result of the investigation made throughout
on Thursday, Sheriff Home issued a warrant for the
apprehension of William Davidson, the driver of the
pilot-engine last Monday; and he was brought to
Linlithgow on Thursday night in the custody of
Sergeant Buglass, and, after a lengthened examination
before the Sheriff, committed to prison for further ex-
amination.

As IT OUGHT TO BE.-A. wholesome correction was
administered to three young men at the Marlborough

them as gentlemanly young men,' but they had
been indulging on the previous night in the not very
gentlemanly amusement of breaking windows, creat-
ing a row, and assaulting policemen. For this they
were sentenced by Mr. Eleox to seven days imprison-

merit each.

The following telegram had been received at New
York:—

WASHINGTON, Sept. 30.
The following report of the victory of Antietam has
been forwarded to the head-quartets of the army by
General Iti'Clellan

Near Sharpshurg, Sept. 30, 1 30 p.m.
To Major-General H. W. Halleek, General-in-Chief o:
the "United States' Army.

General,—l have the honour to report the following
as some of the results of the battles of South Mountain
and Antietam. At South Mountain our loss was
443 dead, 1,806 wounded, and 76 missing. Total,
2,325. At Antietam our loss was 2,010 killed, 9,416
wounded, and 1,043 missing. Total, 12,469. Total loss in
the two battles, 14,794. The loss of the rebels in the two
battles as near as can be ascertained from the number of
their dead found upon the field and from other data, will
not fall short of the following estimate :—Major Davis,
Assistant Inspector-General, who superintends the burial
of the dead, reports about 3,000 rebels buried upon
the field of Antietam by our troops. Previous to
this, however, the rebels had buried many of their own
dead upon a distant portion of the battlefield which they
occupied after Ve battle, probably at least 500. The
loss of the rebels at South Mountain cannot be ascer-
tained with accuracy, but as our troops continually
drove them from the commencement of the action, and
as, a much greater number of their dead were seen on
the field than of our own men, it is not unreasonable
to suppose that their loss was greater than ours.
Fetimating their killed who were buried by them-
selves at 500, the total number of rebels killed in the
two battles would be 4,000. According to the rates
of our own killed and wounded, this would make their
loss in wounded 18,748. As nearly as can be deter-
mined at this time, the number of prisoners taken by our
troops in the battles will at the lowest estimate amount
-to 6,000. The full returns will, no doubt, show a
larger number. Of these about 1,200 are wounded. This
gives a rebel loss in killed, wounded, and prisoners of
26,552. It will be observed that this does not include
their stragglers, the number of whom is said by citizens
here to be large. It may be safely concluded, there-
fore, that the rebel army lost at least 30,000 of their
best troops.
From the time our troops first encountered the
enemy in Maryland until he was driven back into Vir-
ginia, we capt,ired 13 guns, 7 caissons, 9 limbers, 2 field
forges, 2 caisson bodies, 39 colours, and 1 signal flag.
We have not lost a single gun or a colour. On the battle-
field of Antietam 14,000 small arms were collected, besides
the large numbers carried off by citizens and those dis-
tributed on the ground to recruits and other unarmed
men, arriving immediately after the battle. At South
Mountain no collection of small arms was made, but
owing to the hasty pursuit from that point 400 were
taken on the opposite side of the Potomac.
GEORGE B. M'CLELLAN, Major-General.
The following are the latest items of intelligence con-

'New York, Sept. 30.—A special dispatch to the
Post says it is believed here that General Lee is preparing
for a forward movement from Winchester. It is proba-
ble, however, that he will find enough defensive work
on his hands without crossing the Potomac again. A.
special despatch from Cincinnati to-night says 'intelli-
gence has just been received from General Morgan,
who has evacuated Cumberland Gap with his entire
force, and is now well on his way to the Ohio
river. On evacuating the Gap General Morgan sprung
the mines, closing the passage through the mountains
so completely as to make it entirely impassable. All
the stores, artillery, and munitions of war were either
brought away or. destroyed, not leaving the value of
5 dols. to the enemy. General Morgan's force is much
larger than is generally suppesed. He has not only the
-veterans of his command, but has been receiving daily
additions of hundreds of the loyal citizens of East Ten-

that Marshall's and a portion of Bixby Smith's troops have
marched to intercept them. General Morgan desires to
meet them. Important movements have been ordered
against the forces of Kirby Smith and Marshall, which
will seriously interfere with their plans. We expect
important news from that region hourly. At Louisville
General Buell's force is fully organised, and fully
adequate to meet all the force of the Confederates in
Kentucky. A large portion of our forces there are

NEW YORK, Oct. 2, Evening.
General Wadsworth, Republican nominee for the
post of Governor of the State of New York, made a
speech, declaring that the Republican party intend to
hold the country together at wh9tever cost of life-blood
and suffering, and to devastate the country if necessary.
but not to survive its dismemberment. Mr. Foote, in
the Confederate Congress, has declared that proposals
for peace could only come from the South. If they were
refused, the evils to the civilised world resulting from
the continuance of the war would rest upon the heads of
the Northern leaders. Intelligence from Vera Cruz to
the 9th of September announces that the steamer
Jormandie had arrived safely out. General
Weld's= has advanced his head-quartirs three
miles nearer to Harper's Ferry, the Confederate ,
General Lee making mysterious movements at '
some points above Harper's Ferry. It is not
known where he intends operating. Rumours are ,
current of the Confederate Peace Commissioners being

M. GLADSTONE'S SECESSION SPEECH.—We are
enabled to state (says the Manchester Commercial _Daily
List of Saturday) that in the highest political circles
there is no anticipation of an immediate recognition of
the Southern Confederacy by this country. The sub-
ject has recently again been very seriously discussed by
the French cabinet, but it is highly improbable that they
would take separate action and depart from the under-
standing which has hitherto existed between the re-
spective governments. Mr. Gladstone's remarks may
therefore only be regarded as an expression of the opi-
nion which he shares in common with the general pub-
lic, that the South must now be regarded as a nation,
but it wouldbe erroneous to infer that any official recog-
nition of that fact has yet been decided on.

articles.title: SIR WALTER CROFTON.
articles.text:
SIR WALTER CROFTON.

Sir Walter Crofton, by invitation of the Mayor, has
delivered an address on the Irish convict system, at the
Philosophic Institute of Birmingham. After glancing at
the evils arising in the country from the ticket-of-leave
system as here administered, he said
_

In turning to another pad of the United Kingdom—
Ireland—with which I have been officially connected,
we naturally inquire—What is done about " tickets-of-
leave " there? Are they given under the same statute?
and if so, are they or are they not protective to the
public ? It is my business this evening to answer these
questions. I reply that the " tiekets-of-leave " are
issued under the same statute as in England: but that
great precautions involving many intelligible tests of
character are taken before they are given. That when
given, the regulations for enforcing the conditions of the
licence are so stringent as to protect the public against
the misdeeds of the holder. I now read to you the
regulations, which clearly indicate the course of pro-
ceeding. —(The lecturer here illustrated his discourse by
documents which are too lengthy for insertion.) But
these regulations do more than protect the public—they
protect the criminal against himself They act as lead-
ing-strings to him on his first entrance into free life.
Crime is thus made a hazardous calling, and it becomes
the interest of the liberated convict to refrain from follow-
ing it. The registration of cot riots, and the means of
identifying old offenders by photography, and by other
appliantes,are becoming so perfect, and so very generally
lead to the criminals receiving lengthened sentences for
whatever crimes tcey again commit, that the commission
of crime is invariably accompanied by very great hazard.
It has been objected that "police supervision would
create espionage." I reply that it would only be under
very faulty arrangements that such a result could ensue.
Espionage is the consequence of the appearance of sus-
picious characters, of whom the police know but little,
and imagine very much. Authentic information, ac-
companied by systematised, and, responsible police - pro-
ceedings, preclude abuseo la the same time I wish to
make it very, clear that.l. hoe up sympathy with those
persons who apply the term "liberty of the subject" to
the cases of" habitual offenders against the law," whose
original sentences have not, be it remembered, as yet
expired. The liberty of the subject, so construed,
would soon become the bondage of the honest
man. The procedure advocated is a portion. of the
criminal's training within the period of his sentence, of
which he is made perfectly cognisant before his libera-
tion. If it is decided to carry out this principle in its
integrity in England, it is of course obvious that some
course must be pursued which will divest its execution
of any unnecessary hardship. The criminals must be
made to understead and feel the whole scope of the sys-
tem, and to realise that the interests of the well-disposed
and the public are identical. The labour market must
be opened to the liberated convict as much as is possible,
and in no better way can this be accomplished than by
obtaining for the convicts' training the confidence of the
public. The confidence may be slow in being obtained;
but if the course of proceeding is based on sound princi-
ples, it will be sure. Experience of more natural crim-
inal training; the exercise of greater discrimination
between desperadoes and those criminals who would
willingly reform their lives, will produce the best and
the most satisfactory results. The case of the well-
intentioned criminal is not so fettered by the proposed
restrictions as may at first appear. The avenues of
labour, as I propose to show, need not be so entirely
closed against him as to preclude his carrying out his
industrious intentions; for if the home market cannot
or will not employ him, he is not precluded from pro-
ceeding elsewhere. In every Government prison it has
been the practice for many years to give gratuities to
convicts, and the practice has been very generally con-
sidered a wise one. Within certain limits lam entirely
of this opinion. As then convicts, who have been well
conducted and industrious during their detention, receive
a tolerable amount of gratuity, they will be in a position,
with some privation and toil—brought on themselves,
be it remembered, by former misconduct—to reach other
countries in which labour is urgently required, and in
which they will not find equal temptation to relapse.
Colonial ground should become to them a most impor-
tant element of reformation • and few will, in my opinion,
be the eases in which it will fail to be so.'

articles.title: WILLS AND BEQUESTS'.
articles.text:
WILLS AND BEQUESTS'.

The will of his Grace the Most Reverend John Bird
Sumner, D.D., P.C., Archbishop of Canterbury, was
proved in her Majesty'e Court of Probate on the Ist
Inst. The trustees and executors nominated are his
son, the Rev. John H. R. Sumner, M.A. ; his son in
law, the Rev. John Thomas, D.C.L. ; and his nephew,
Charles Sumner, Esq., Barrister at Law. The per-
sonalty was sworn under £60,000. The will bears date
1858, signed J. B. Centaur, and witnessed by his
secretary, Felix Knyvett, Esq., solicitor, and W. H.
Withall, solicitor, Parliament-street. The will is
contained in a few brief sheets. Dr. Sumner's wife
died in 1829, the year after his elevation to the see
of Chester, leaving several children. The Archbishop
bequeaths all his copywright and MSS. to his son-
in-law, John/ Thomas, subject to the right of the
Society for Promoting Christian Jnowledge to pab-
fish any of his expositions of Scripture. To his
daughter Georgiana' who is already provided for, he
leaves one-tenth of his entire property, real and per-
sonal, for the benefit of her only child. The estates
in Cheshire, Lancashire, and Northumberland, and all
other his estates, real and personal, he directs to be
divided between his sons John and Robert, and his
daughters Maria and Louisa. On the decease of his
daughter, Louisa Sumner, a sum of £5,000 is left to be
divided amongst the children of his late daughter, Ann
Colpoys; and on the decease of his daughter Maria,
the interest of her share to be paid to her husband,
the Rev. John Thomas, and the principal to their
children on coming of age. His grace has left legacies
to all his servants proportioned to their length of ser-
vitude.

The will of John William Spicer, Esq., of Esher,
Surrey, was proved in London under £160,000, the
executors nominated in the will being the testator's
son, John W. G. Spicer, Esq. and Abraham G.
Robarts, E.g. The latter gentleman having since
died, the testator appointed by codicil his brother,
Henry Christopher Roburts, Lg., as an executor,
to whom a power was reserved. The testator died
possessed of a handsome fortune, consisting both of
realty and personalty. Mr. Spicer was a partner in
that long established and wealthy firm of Messrs.
Combe, Delafield, and Co., brewers. The will was
executed in 18.59, and a codicil in 1860, and contains
the following dispositions :—To his wife, in addition to
£l,OOO a-year under marriage settlement, he leaves a
further annuity of £BPO, with an injunction to his
executors and trustees that she is to possess during the
remainder of her days those comforts which she has
hitherto enjoyed. To his eldest son he has devised his
real estate, together with the residue of the personal
property. To each of his two younger sons legacies of
£5,000, and to his other children £2,000 each. There
is also a legacy of £5OO to a son of the late Major
Spicer, H.E.I.C. Legacies are left to his servants,
varying in amount according to the time they have
been in his establishment.

The will of Major-General John Chirl es Beckwith,
C.B. was proved in London by Captain John Halli-
burtOn Murray, R.N., the testator's brother-in-law.
The property in this country was sworn under £25,000.
The general died in July last at A la Tour ltement,
Italy, having executed his will in 1859 and a codicil in
1860. To his wife he bequeathed his plate, furniture,
money in England and at ids foreign banker's, together
with an immediate legacy of £l,OOO, and many other
bequests, as well as having settled upon her an annuity.
The General has bequeathed liberal annuities to his
sister and nieces, and made bequests to other members
of his family, appointing his brother-in-law, Captain
Murray, residuary legatee. Legacies are also bestowed
upon his servants.

NEW LICENCES TO BREWERS. ^ On the 10th, new
licences to brewers for the s,le of beer were granted,
under the Customs and Inland Revenue, or the 'Budget'
act of last session, and are to be yearly renewed on the
loth of October. Before a brewer can obtain a licence
(other than the first) a declaration must be made of the
quantity of malt and sugar brewed in the year. It is
provided that where a licence for the sale of beer exceeds

brewed for which the licence was granted is less, the
difference is to be repaid to the brewer, and, when

deemed brewers for the sale of beer. The new duty for
the sale of beer to any person who first becomes a brewer
is 12s. 6d.' and the duty, where the quantity does not
exceed 20 barrels, is to be the same. Where the quan-
tity is more than 20 barrels and does not exceed 50,

AN OLD DnovEn.—Mr. Christopher Macrae, cattle •
dealer and farmer, Glenmore, Lochcarron, sold several
lots of Skye cattle at the last Muir-of-Ord market. Mr.
Macrae has been on the road, as a cattle dealer, for the
last fifty-two years, and was present at the opening of
the first market at Muir. He has not missed a single
Portree market for the last fifty-two years. His grand-
father died at the extreme age of 108, and during his
long life never disgraced his shapely limbs by donning
the trews. Mr. Macrae's son, who was with him at the
resent Muir-of-Ord market, is a fine specimen of the
hardy Highlander, is about twenty-four years of age,
dressed in the Highland garb, and is determined to
follow his great grandfather's example by never wear-
ing trousers. Mr. Macrae is still hale and bear_y, and ,
bids fair to continue on the road fUr twenty years to '
conic—lnverness Courier.

articles.title: BEE-HIVE, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 18, 1862
articles.text:
THE BEE-HIVE, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 18, 1862

ALLEGED WIFE MURDAR.

An inquiry was held by Mr. H. Raffles Walthew,
deputy coroner for East Middlesex, at the Suffolk
Arms Tavern, Bcston-street, Hackney-road, on Tues-
day night, respecting the death of Mary Anne Jones,
aged 22 years. The case caused considerable excite-
ment in the neighbeurhood, in consequence of rumours
that the decca,ed lost her life through violence
inflicted by her husband, and crowds congregated in
the street where the inquiry was held. Mrs. Martha
Turner said deceased was her daughter, and resided
with her husband, a hawker, at No. 65, Boston-street.
She was a delicate young woman, and very jealous
and bad tempered. She died on Friday last. She had
a black eye, and she told witness on last Wednesday
week that she had had a quarrel with her husband
about a curtain, and that she fell against a door, and
blackened her eye. She had to go to the doctor. Mrs.
Mary Ann Dyer, 65, Boston-street, said that she heard
the deceased and her husband quarrelling some time
since. Deceased told witness that she received her
black-eye by being pushed against a door by her
husband. Deceased complained to witness of her head
and chest. Witness never saw her husband strike her.
He was a kind man. Mrs. Alice Frost, who resided
next door to the deceased, said that she was a very
nice young woman, and had not a had temper. On
the ntght of last Tuesday week witness was awoke by
loud screams, and cries of Murder.' The cries con-
tinued for a quarter of an hour. The next morning
she was informed that it was Mrs. Jones who had been
screaming. Mr. E. Pitt, M.R.C,S. llsckney -road,
said that deceased called en him complaining of suffer-
ing in her head and chest. She had a. blackeye. She
had inflammation of the membranes of the brain.
The post-mortem examination showed the immediate
cause of death to have been the inflammation
of the membranes of the brain, which might have
been produced by a blow, but there was no proof
that it had. Margaret Bell, boot machinist, caid that
she resided at 25, Bostonestreet On Tuesday week
she and her sister were awoke by a feaxful noise in the
street. There were screams of Polled' and Murder.'
Witness went to the window and. saw-Mrs. Jones out-
side her own door, and her husband on the threshold.
He struck deceased violently with his clenched fist
eight or nine times. She cried out, Oh, don't kill
me! You are murdering me! Don't strike my
head.' The husband went in and shut the door.
Deceased went to the door and called out to her ser-
vant girl, Mary, give me the baby. I will make
away with myself, and trouble you no more.' The
whole disturbance appeared to have lasted a
long time. The next morning witness saw that
Mrs. Jones's eye was very black and bruised.
Clara Bell said that she was alarmed by the
disturbunce described by last witness. She saw
Mr. Jones strike his wife a dozen times' with force
enough to kill a woman. He knocked her down.
The row was so great that several persons came to
their windows. It occurred between one and two
o'clock in the morning. Mr. Eaily, stepfather to the
accused, said that he could produce evidence to con-
tradict the last two witnesses' and called Mrs. Martha
Beaumont, who said that she heard a quarrel between
Mr. Jones and his wife about three weeks or a month
ago. He pulled her into the house by the sleeve but
did not strike her. It was about eleven o'clock at
night. A juror remarked that witness might be allud-
ing to a different occurrence. The court was then
cleared, and, after an hour and a half's deliberation,
an adjournment was decided upon by the jury for the
production of further evidence: The court accordingly
adjourned.

EXTRAORDINARY CONVICTION
USDER THE NEW POACHING ACT.

At the petty sessions held at Halesworth, on Wed-
nesday last, before the Rev. W. C. Edgell, (chairman),
H. A. S. Bence, Esq., and Rev. H. Owen; Frederick
Nesling, of Westleton, labourer, was charged with
having in his possession on a certain highway at Bul-
camp, a net used for the purpose of taking game, being
suspected of coming from certain lands belonging to
and in the occupation of the Earl of Straarroke,
where he had been unlawfully in search a game;
which net was then and there seized by Policeman
Elliott, of Wangford. And James Staff, of Darsham,
was charged with being then and there present, aiding
and abetting the said Frederick Nesling. From the
report in the Suffolk Chronicle the evidence against the
prisoners appears to have been that they were found
on the highway about four or five miles from their
homes with a game-net 29 or thirty yards long.
According to the statement of the police-constable,
there sere feathers in it, and the men were quite near
to the preserves of the Earl of Stradbroke, the polictman
shortly before meeting them having heard the gate go.
The prisoner Nesling admitted having made the net to
sell, but denied using it, or the intention of using it
himself; and the prisoner said he was not guilty in
knowing what the man had with him. Nesting also
affirmed that the feathers spoken of by the policeman
had been put in the net after the policeman had taken
possession of it. The remaining evidence against the
prisoners was, that Staff had been twice convicted of
poaching, and Nesling was believed to be a notorious
poacher—the police .constable giving these statements
as a reply to a question of the chairman of the bench,
whether the men were likely to be poaching. when they
were taken. The magistrates withdrew for about ten
minutes. On returning into the room, the, Chairman
said—Your case has had the greatest possible attention
given to it by the magistrates, and we have had every
wiuh to give you the full benefit of any doubt
existing in our minds; but we cannot allow -our•
selves to have any doubt on the subject in this case.
You are found a long way from your homes with
unlawful implements upon you, and the evidence is
amply sufficient to satisfy the bench of your having
been on land for the purpose of poaching. We have
tried to find out your habits, and we are sorry to find
that your characters in this respect are not good. We
are perfectly satisfied that the offence was committed,
and as your habits are those of poachers, and you are
not known to be industrious men, but, on the con-
trary, to be breakers of the law, we feel it quite a
case to enforce the full penalty of the law which it is
in our power to do. We, therefore, adjudge you to
pay each a fine of £5 besides costs, and your net is to
be burned by the police. In default of the fine you
will have two months' imprisonment in Ipswich Gaol,
with hard labour. The costs in each case are 7s. 6d.
Mr. Bence told Staff that he warned kim 12 months
ago to turn to an honest life.
Staff said he could get no work.
The men Were removed in custody.

THE LATE POACHING AFFRAY NEAR NOTTINGHAM.—
At the Notts Quarter Sessions, on Monday, three men,
named Edward Oldbury, William Lenten, and Joseph
Williamson were charged before Lord Belper awl a
full bench a magistrates with night poaching, accom-
panied with violence, in the preserves of Lord Middleton,
at Radford. It appeared from the evidence that about
three o'clock on the morning of the 13th of August two
keepers, named Keeling and Cross, were out watching,
and shortly afterwards they came in contact with the
poachers. Oldbury had a gun. The keepers asked
the men what they were doing, upon which Oldbury
replied that, If the keepers were not off he would
knock their brains out,' at the same time striking Cross
a severe blow on the face with the butt-end of his gun.
Cross and Oldbury then closed, and a struggle took
place for the possession of the gun, the former ulti-
mately obtaining it. The poachers then commenced
throwing stones, and a large boulder stricking Keeling,
he was knocked down and rendered insensible. All
the poachers kicked him while he was down, saying
that 'they would finish him.' The prisoners got away
but were afterwards apprehended by the police. The
jury found all the men guilty, and his lordship said it
was one of the worst cases he had ever heard ; it was a
mercy the men bad escaped with their lives. He should
sentence them to twelve months' imprisonment with
hard labour.

FITZ-R-OV-INETOTAL ASSOCIATION. —The twenty-third
anniversary meeting of the members of the Fitzroy
Teetotal Association was heldion Tuesday evening in
the Queen's Concert Room, Hanover-square. Mr.
Harper Twelvetrees occupied the chair, and on the
platform were Mr. J. A. Horner, Mr. Draper, the Rev.
J. Christien, the Rev. Mr. Serjeant, and 'several gen-
tlemen known for their attachment to the Temperance
movement. After a hymn had been sung, the report,
which gave an interesting and encouraging account of
the operations of the association during the year, was
read. In connection with the association there were
weekly lectures, a lending library, a band of hope, co.n-
certs, readings, &c., and through these various agencies
a great deal of good was being effected. The chair-
man said he was glad to hear that the association
was of so comprehensive a character, and that its
efforts had been crowned with so much success. Many
things indicated that the great temperance movement
was telling on the customs of society. No doubt a
great work was still before temperance reformers, but
they would succeed if they persevered. The heavy
taxation of the country was justly complained of, but
many of the complainers imposed on themselves the
still heavier tax resulting from the consumption of
intoxicating drinks. If the people would become sober
they would soon obtain political power. He consi-
dered that the traffic in intoxicating liquors produced
an enormous deal of mischief, and he hoped that the
Permissive Bill would soon be obtained. He con-
cluded a speech, which was much applauded, by advis-
ing those persons in the meeting who had not taken
the pledge to sign without delay. The report wasp
adopted; and Mr. Chnstien and other gentlemen
afterwards addressed the meeting, which was numer- I
ously attended.

articles.title: CONVICTION PASITIONABLE
articles.text:
CONVICTION PASITIONABLE

S IV; NDL ARS.

At the Bath quarter sessions on the 11th, before T.
W. Saunders, Esq., recorder, two swindlers, named James
Frale, 37, and Mary Ann Greenslade, 20, who have been
carrying on an extensive system of fraud in di-fferent
parts of the kingdom, were indicted for conspiring to
steal three gold watches and t roe gold chains, value.f.6o.,
the property of Edwin Routley, at Rath, on the 22nd of
August; also with conspiring to steal a silk dress and
other articles valae £l7, he property of Me-srs. Jolly
and son, of Milsom-street. It will be recollected that in
August last the prisonors took lodgings at 19, Royal-
circus, Bath, representing that they had just come from
Scotland. Whilst occupying this fashionable habitation
for a few days, they contrived to obtain goods from
several of the prineipil tradesmen of the city. Amongst
these was Mr. Routley, of Broad-street, upon Irhoin the
male prisoner called, and after representing that he
wished to make a present to his lady, he selected two
gold watches and chains to be sent to the circus for her
to choose from. He also selected a gold:watch and chafe
for himself. Mr. Routley took up the watches himself,
the same evening, when he saw the femaleprisoner, who,
after looking at them, expressed her approval of the one 1
the captain' had selected for himself, but, professed to
be doubtful as to his choice of the one to be presented to
herself. She therefore told Mr. Routley that, as the
captain' was out at dinner, if he would-call in the morn-
ing he could have the money for the watches which
might be selected. The articles were left, and the same
evening the female prisoner quitted the house with a
carpet bag, containing the watches and other articles,
which she procured the assistance of a workman, whom
she casually met, to carry for her, until they came up to
the male prisoner, who was leaning against the rails in
the park, and who then took the bag. The prisoners
walked to the railway station at Twerton, two rail es front ,
Bath, and started by train. Next day Mr. Routley, find-
ing the parties had leftthe,Circus without any intimation
of their intention to do so,,became alarmed. The pollee
were put upon the scent, and the day after their flight
from Bath, the male prisoner was found in the act of
pledging one of the watches at the shop of a pawn-
broker in Bristol, where the female prisoner had pre-
viously pledged one of the chains. The jury found
both guilty, and the Recorder sentenced the male pri-
soner to twelve month's imprisonment, with hard
labour; and the female to six months. Mr. Hughes,
the chief of police, was in possession of warrants to
apprehend the prisoners and take them to Edinburgh, on
charges of having obtained about £lBO worth of pro-
perty fraudulently in that city, had they been discharged
at Bath.

articles.title: PORTUGAL.
articles.text:
PORTUGAL.

Lisßox October 7.—Her Majesty Donna Maria Pia,
the youthful Queen-Consort of Don Luiz, King of
Portugal, arrived in the Tagus on Sunday, the 4th, at
noon, on board the Portuguese steam frigate Bartholomew
Dias, after a favourable voyage from Genoa, accom-
panied by two other Portuguese and five Italian steam
frigates. Yesterday the rest of the official programme
was so tediously carried out that it took the whole day
before Her Majesty could be duly landed, conveyed to
the church of St. Domingos for the nuptial blessing, and
thence to? the Palace of Ajuda, which their Majesties
did not reach until past seven at night, thoroughly
wearied by the ceremonial accompaniments of a Royal
marriage. The weather fortunately could not be more
favourable. The streets of Lisbon were literally crowded
with the inhabitants and thousands who had come from

the provinces to welcome their young Queen. Her
Majesty during the whole of the procession was received
with great enthusiasm, which she acknowledged with
graceful dignity, and made a most favourable impres-
sion upon her new subjects. The public demonstra-
tions of satisfaction with this Royal marriage have been
more hearty than usual; the illuminations and other
festive preparations were upon a larger scale, and
it is to be hoped that Providence will concede a
lengthened period of domestic happiness to their
Majesties, and of prosperity to the country, which
has been so seriously tried of late years in its material
interests by yellow fever, cholera, bad harvests, and
defective vintages, and in its dynasty by the sufferings
and losses of the Royal Family. Fortunately, Portugal
has had no revolutionary disturbances of any moment to
add to its afflictions during the late reign, and the recent
abortive attempts only tend to prove the country dis-
posed to that peace and tranquillity which may enable it
to derive full benefit from the new life it ought to receive
by the railroads, now fast approaching completion, if
the Government have the good sense to remove numer-
ous obstructions on commerce and to establish a reason-
ab.le tariff.

articles.title: WHEN WILL THE WAR END?
articles.text:
WHEN WILL THE WAR END?

Under the heading, 'When will the War End ?' the
_Richmond Divatch of the 27th ult. publishes, an article,
of which the following are extracts :
This is a question oftener asked than answered. We
have been asked the question repeatedly; but if any
one should ask us, When will the world end,' we
should be just as able to give an
.opinion
The only way that the war can end is by the exhsus-
tion of the North or the extermination of the South.
The North has determined to subjugate or annihilate
us. It gives us only this alternative, The Union 0:
death.' That,:in sum and substance, is all that its
most Conservative politicians propose. It is in vain
that some of them deny the cruel determination that
we have indicated. Is there one of them, Conservative
Republican or Conservative Democrat, who will pro-
claim that he prefers the sacrifice of the Union' to
extermination of the South? The Union is the god
of all parties alike, except the Ultra-Abolitionists,
who, strange to say, are the only men in the North wil-
ling to set it aside.' The war has been carried on
from the beginning by the Conservative classes, and
scarcely an Abolitionist is to be found its armies. If the
Union sentiments' which so pervade the Notth were
genuine patriotism, we might have. some hope of its
abatement, or, if it were mere fanaticism, the gust of
passion might howl itself out; but it is the practical,
substantial greed of gold which will never let go its
grip as long as life remains. The North is fighting, not
only for the Southern trade and commerce, but to make-
the Soath pay the enormous debt accumulated in this
war. Not only this, but it is fighting for its very being.
The idea is common that it is the South alone which is
contending for national existence. But if the North
ultimately fails in this war she will fall as fast and far
as Lucifer in his descent from Heaven. The brightest.
jewels of her crown wrested from her grasp, the
chief sources of her revenue withdrawn, and. a
national debt half as large as that of England piled
upon her shoulders, her cities solitary, her harbours de-
serted,- her Manufactories silent, her military capacities so
paralyzed that she can neither command respect abroad,
nor insure order in her own incongruous population,
composed of a seething mass of the ignorant, depraved
and fanatical of all nations, she will cling to the Union '
and to the war, by which only she hopes to preserve it,
as. the shipwrecked mariner clings to the last plank that
,lies between him and the fathomless depth of eternity.
We must bear these facts in mind when we are tempted
by the syren.songs of hope to look for a speedy peace,
and to relax the exertions which alone can save our
throats front the throttle of a powerful nation, engaged in
a fearful and final struggle for life or death. We wish
we could descry a brighter prospect, but we see no
reason for such predictions. The unmanly expectation
of foreign intervention which so long deluded our people
has long ago proved an idle dream. Europe nfst only
refuses to intervene, but rejoices in her heart over the
American troubles, because they are exhausting and
rendering impotent • for injury to despotic Governments
that continent whose free. institutions have always kept
her in a nightmare of alarm. England, the chief instru-
ment in the disruption of the old republic, preserves
rigid r.eutrality,—that is, she furnishes the North
material and the South moral aid; she permits the North
.to purchase materials and munitions of war which the
South, by reason of the blockade, is only. .partially able
to do, and she praises the South for its military prowess
and patriotic devotion. She puts weapons into the hands
of the Northern combatants, and she. pats the Southern
combatants on the head, and cries, Brave, boys, pitch
into him.' We are beginning to understand all this, and
to dismiss from our minds the monstrous delusion of
foreign intervention.

SINGULAR DEATH—EarIy on Saturday, the 11th
James Cane, mate .4' the North Star, now lying in the
London Docks, while walking from the ward-room to
the. cabin, for the purpose of cutting a candle, carrying
with him a pair of scissors, tripped and fell, when the

A sportsman in the neighbourhood of the wood of
Clairmarais (Somme), shot a few days ago an unusually
large raven, having round one of its legs a small iron
r-' g, on which were engraved the words, Born at Cour-
ti.-4y in 1772: This fact is a confirmation of the opinion
of certain naturalists that ravens live for a century and
upwards.

MunnEn AND MADNESS.—In 'a recent number we
stated that several persons had become insane by brood-
ing over the wrongs of Mrs. M`Lachlan, and had been
