articles.title: ABOLITIO-V OF SLAVARr PROCLAMATION..
articles.text:
ABOLITIO-V OF SLAVARr
PROCLAMATION..

The Government of the United States, still boastful,
but perfectly conscious of its precarious condition, at
this critical juncture, makes a desperate attempt to
frighten its antagonists, and win the sympathies of the
liberals of Europe, by issuing a Proclamation to the
effect, that on the Ist of January next, all persons
held as slaves within any State of which the people
shal be in rebellion shall be held free, and that
their freedom shall be reccc,”ised and maintained by
the civil and military power of the United States
Government. It seems a bold measvre ; but had it
been earlier it had been more effectual. Every one
must now regard it as a mere impulse of desperation
and despair. Besides, it is, after all, but a half measure.
It is not to be a total abolition of slavery. Loyal States
are to be allowed to buy and s-11 human flesh. It is
only rebels who are to be denied that privilege. No
one can pretend that the North love and pity their
enslaved black brethren. They are merely re-
garded as a valuable property), of which rebels are to
be deprived. It is a military manceuvre, or a political
dodge, or any thing but a moral movement. It is truly
un.ise, because if it hs any effect upon the Southerners
it will only be to make their hostility more deadly.
It will now be war to the knife. There is no hope of
compromise or conciliation unless the Nertli be thort,ughly
humiliated. Then, again, the partial abolition of
slavery, a.,,4 a means of revenge, will afford no pleasure to
extreme abolitionists, and give the greatest offence to the
large parties of Northerners who hate and despise the
blacks, and have no abstract detestation of slavery, and
who see in the liberation of Southern slaves most serious
commercial losses and inconveniences, not by any means
exclusively Southern. Perhaps Mr. LINCOLN anticipates
a seryile-rebellioia; but, though it is liaely.,enough that
some of the slaves will run away from their Southern
masters, and claim the offered liberty in the North,
they will not rise .against those who have been virtually
more kind to them than the Northerners, who have
taken so many opportunities to express publicly their
disgust for all people of colour. Mr. LINCOLN himself
has advised the blacks to emigrate, because he thought
it was impossible for them to associate on equal terms
with the white races, who have a natural antipathy to
them.

The proclamation is particularly ill-timed as a means
of intimidation, for it appears at the very moment
when, in spite of the late check, the South is stronger,
perhaps, and more full of hope than it h4s
ever been before— when it is conscious that
it has driven the North to extremities, and that a
measure of this nature could only have been resorted to
in an hour of perplexity and dread. Besides, it is
obviously a means of despairing spite, of idle malignity,
and nothing is so contemptible as such threats un-
supported by the power immediately to enforce them. The
negro slaves will by no means be assured at present that
the Northerners are surer of final victory than the
Southerners. Appearances are decidedly in the opposite
direction. Suppose the South subdued, after depriving
all America of so much cotton, rice, and tobacco, as are
procured by slave la•bour, what would Mr. LiNcoLN gain
from the South, and what would he do with four mil-
lions of unemployed freed slaves unaccustomed to act
for themselves, and who will be a living cloud upon
the land.—Court Circular.

articles.title: TOTAL LOSS OF THE LEOPATRA
articles.text:
TOTAL LOSS OF THE LEOPATRA

The following are the particulars of the loss of the
Royal Mail screw steamer Cleopatra
The above ship was totally lost on the bar (entrance
to the Sherboro' River), about 100 miles south of
Sierra Leone, on the night of the 19th of August,
about half-past nine o'clock. A few.minutes previous
to the hour mentioned land was reported on the star-
board bow, when the course of the steamer was at
once altered; but it proved of no avail, as she struck
almost immediately afterwards, and although every
available means were used to get the ship off she
could not be moved from the spot she had strum on.
Although the Cleopatra held fast all night—the
engines being kept going about half speed astern, to
prevent the ship verging ahead—still every one had
hopes that she would be got off in the morning by
kedging. Daybreak of the 20th revealed to us our
true position. About 6 a.m. the ship's gig was lowered
in charge of the second officer to take soundings, and
shortly afterwards the long boat was lowered to receive
an anchor and cable to kedge the ship off. The long
boat was very nearly being capsized by getting broad-
side on to the rollers, and was obliged to be pulled
into smooth water to bail her out. The gig now
returned, and with some difficulty the second officer
managed to get on board, but the boat was obliged
to leave the ship's side to save her from being stove
in. As both boats bad now left the ship, and
were some distance off, signals were made for their re-
turn, but apparently without being observed by those
in the boats. The ship had been bumping very
heavily all the morning, and it was desirable as a last
resource that the kedges should be got out. It was
therefore agreed that a third boat should be lowered, in
charge of the chief officer, to recal the other two boats.
This boat was lowered about 11 a.m. Shortly after-
wards we were obliged to cut away the fore and main
masts to ease the ship. By this time it was evident
that it would be impossible for any of the boats to re-
turn to the ship on account of the heavy breakers
alongside and the strong tide running, so that we were
now dependent on one boat. The engines had now
stopped of themselves, the boiler being nearly filled
with sand, while the surf broke constantly and with
tremendous force against the ship. The morning of
the 21st broke, but no signs of any of the ship's boats.
We still agreed to remain on board in the expectation
of some assistance from a man-of-war from Sierra
Leone. We discovered that during the night
we had been driven in towards the shore a con-
siderable distance, and now lay firmly embedded
in the sand. The ship was a total wreck.

It was determined that the last boat—a life-boat—
should be lowered next morning (22nd), containing no
one but the passengers and a picked crow; the captain
(Delamotte) and the remainder of the officers and
crew agreeing to take to rafts, which were immediately
begun to be constructed. During the night the stern
partly gave way, and it required every possible ex.
ertion, with the aid of sails hung over the stern, to
keep the saloon from being flooded. This was, indeed,
a most anxious night for all on board. About 6 a.m.
the next morning (22nd) the only remaining boat was
prepared for the passengers, and in about half an hour
afterwards the ladies and children were safely stowed
in the places allotted them, it being previously
arranged that the gentlemen should not enter the
boat until it was lowered into the water, life
lines being all ready for them to lower themselves
at a proper opportunity. Eventually the boat was
lowered, and every one got safely into her. Shortly
after leaving the ship's side she narrowly escaped being
swamped, the beat being completely filled with water.
However, she was kept afloat by being constantly
baled out, and as soon as she reached smooth water
was brought to anchor on account of the strong ebb
tide. At the commencement of the flood tide the boat
was again got under weigh, and shortly afterwards
met one of the traders' boats, into which the ladies and
children were put, the gentlemen proceeding in canoes
to Telabana Factory, a place about twenty-three miles
from the wreck, where they remained for the night.
To return to the wreck. Seeing that the boat had got
a. strong ebb tide, it would be dangerous to launch any
rafts; but about one p.m. we launched the first raft, and
with some difficulty part of the firemen and nearly all
the Kroomen got on to it, one Krooman losing his life
in the attempt; and it was afterwards ascertained on
landing that three others were drowned. This was the
only raft launched this day. About 3 p.m. the stern
was carried away, and the ship evidently broke in
two about the engine-room, and filled rapidly with
water, barely giving us time to get the mails and
specie removed. The ship was now full of water, with
the exception of the fore compartment, leaving us still
the fore cabin and forecastle for shelter, but, unfor-
tunately this only lasted until 10 p.m., when the water
began to make in the fore part of the vessel also, and
so rapidly that in less than an hour the water nearly
reached the main deck. The breakers were now so
y broke clear over the ship,
they
position all night,
leaving
fearfully avaym thosatt
Uncomfortable
August the 23rd. They then agreed to abandon the
wreck, and about 2 p.m. two rafts were launched, and
about eighteen persons got upon the largest. Unfor-
tunately it capsized before it left the side of the vessel,
and Mr. Webster, the chief engineer, was drowned.
This was not known, however, until the raft reached
the land, when the body of Mr. Webster was discovered
lashed to one of the timbers. The second raft reached
the shore in safety. The captain and eight men
remained on board to construct another, which they
made from the mizen-mast, and some hen coops. On
the 23rd a boat containing Mr. Hanson, Lloyd's agent,
and a crew of five men attempted to come off to the
ship, but the boat was swamped by the breakers and
all on board perished. The captain and the few who
remained with him were on the 2nd of September com-
pelled to abandon the ship, and after committing them-
selves to the raft arrived in about two hours safely on
the beach and proceeded up the river to the factories,
where they were most hospitably received. Most of
the crew and some of the passengers had previously
proceeded to Sierra Leone in a small steamer sent from
there for the purpose. In the remainder a small vessel
was chartered. After a tedious passage of five days
they arrived safely at Sierra Leone on the Bth of
September, the greater portion being laid up with
fever.

The captain of the Cleopatra is highly praised for

articles.title: MR. WHITWORTH'S GUNS.
articles.text:
MR. WHITWORTH'S GUNS.

Mr. Whitworth writes to the Time,' on the subject of
his guns, and their power of penetration :
My own experiments with penetration shell were
chiefly made with al-pounder gun (borel .3 in.), weighing
1 cwt. Its results were fully borne out by those of a 6.
pounder (bore 2.3 in.), and a 12-pounder (bore 3 in.),
and, though I had never tried the 70-pounder (5-4- in.
bore), and the 120-pounder (7 in. bore) with shell before
I went to Shoeburyness, the results of the smaller guns
enabled me to state beforehand with confidence what the
guns and shells would do.
_

' - They did what I expected and showed they had power
to spare.
Having felt my way thus far, I feel justified in saying
that both the 5f inch bore and 7 inch bore guns will
penetrate stronger defences at greater ranges than were
tried at Shoeburyness.
It should also be remembered that my 5f inch gun,.
which fired its shell effectively at 200 yards, is in weight
about a ton less than what was stated in your article to
be the maximum suitable for ships' guns. By adding to
its weight it is clear that a more powerful gun than the.
5i inch can be made still within that prescribed maxi-
mum; the Shoeburyness trials prove that the thickest
iron-plated ships would be shelled with such a gun at
fighting ranges.
My larger gun has a bore precisely that of the 110-
pounder rifled gun (7 inches), which, with the 68-
pounder smooth bore, was so often tried against the
Warrior and other targets. It is true that it is, and I
think ought to be, heavier than the 110-pounder; heavier
guns are being asked for for cupola ships, and as pivot guns
they may be used with great advantage. It should,.
perhaps, be explained that my 7 inch gun was made at
Woolwich, .in consequence of arrangements decided upon
after Lord Palmerston and Sir eornewall Lewis had
witnessed trials of my 70-pounder at Shoeburyness about
twelve months ago. Not having the means of construct-
ing ;so large a gun at Manchester, I requested to bo•
allowed to have it made at Woolwich. This was done,
ander the efficient superintendence of Mr. Anderson, ac-
cording to drawings supplied by myself. The gun differst
in construction from the rifle guns of the service; its
metal is differently distributed, its form is different, and
it has a fixed breech, being a muzzle-loader.
I Had the then- existing means permitted it, I should
have preferred making the gun throughout of homo-
geneous iron (as my 70-pounders are now able to be
made) which with an equal weight of metal would affprd
very much greater strength. As, however, the service
guns at Woolwich are made on the coiled system, I em-
ployed hoops of welded coiled iron, like those I used for
my first gun in 1855, and have used for the outer hoops,
of my large guns ever since.
It is a common error to suppose that the 'coiled
system' was first employed in the construction of the
service rifled guns, whereas the fact is that many years
before those guns were made the method of building up
guns with coiled hoops, welded together by end pressure,
was well known in this country. Without wishing for a
moment to detract from the merit of those who have
practically carried out the system, I claim to be entitled
none the less to use an old method known long ago, and
which I used for all large hoops until lately. Improve-
ments in the manufacture of homogeneous metal now
enable me to use hammered moulded hoops of that metal,
which have double the strength o welded coiled hoops
of wrought iron, and which I avo therefore always
preferred and used for the inner ft. es of my rifled guns.

articles.title: _RECRUITING FOR T.ffE AR3IY.
articles.text:
_RECRUITING FOR T.ffE AR3IY.

In .the report for 1860, issued by the Director-Gene-
ral of the Medical Department of the Army, of which
we have already given some details the system of
inspecting recruits is minutely described. The recruit
is not only examined by a medical officer at the out-
station or depot where he may be enlisted, but
he must ba brought to a staff-surgeon before being
finally approved of and sent to a regiment. Be-
tween the Ist of January and the 31st of December,
1860, 27,853 recruits were examined by the staff
surgeons, who rejected 7,128, or 256 per 1,000 of
those broight before them. In the fen years of
1832-41 the rejections were in the proportion of 298 per
1,000, and in the 10 years of 1842-51, 335 per I,oooil.
There have been some alterations in the system, there-
port adds, which prevent exact comparison, but there is no
doubt but that the percentage of rejections in 1860 is
much below the average of former years. Much varia-
tion is caused from year to year by the variation in the
demand for soldiers. When there is no pressure the
most eligible recruits only are taken, and whesx there is
a great demand many who are not quite fit, are passed.
An interesting comparison is made with the returns of
the French army, where, however, in consequence of
the balloting over the whole population, the rejections
give a better idea of the proportion of the whole popu-
lation fit for military service, the rejections in the
British army probably showing too high a proportion. In
1859, in France, 200,926 recruits underwent medical
inspection, and 63,820, or 317 per 1,000 werepronounced
unfit, being almost identical with the proportions tin the
primary inspections in the British army.
An interesting table is given of the causes of rejec-
tion, from which it appears that two-fifths were made
on account of bad health, a feeble constitution, indi-
cated by such defects as scrofula, phthisis' loss or decay
of many teeth, small or malforniied chest, &c.; one-fifth
was made on account of ailments affecting the soldier's
power of marching, such as diseases of the joints, of the
veins (varix), &c., while the proportion of rejections.
from defects of the upper extremities are small. On
comparing the causes of rejection in England, Scotland,
and Ireland, the most striking points of difference are
the high proportion in England from small and mal-
formed chest and curvature of the spine; in Scotland,.
from loss and decay of many teeth, deemed to be an in-
dication of unsound health, &e.; and in Ireland from
diseases of the eyes arid eyelids. The proportion of men
above five feet eight inches in considerably greater in
the Scotch recruiting districts than either in the Eng-
lish or Irish, while the proportion of men under five'
feet five inches is nearly one-fourth higher in Ireland
them in Great Britain.

I

As approximate evidence of the extent to which the '
population are protected from smallpox' it may be men-
tioned that of the recruits received in England 747 in •
1,000 bore marks of vaccination, 790 in Scotland, anat.*
816 in Ireland. The numbers marked with smallpox
were 151 in England, 102 in Scotland, 116 in Ireland,
leaving wholly unprotected 102 in 1,000 in Ragland,
108 in Scotland, and 68 in Ireland. 'llllet,
As to the state of education among recruits, the num-
bers unable to read or write are, in English, Scotch, and
Irish districts respectively 247, 163, and 321; able to
read only, 51;156, and 145; and able to read and write,
702, 681, and 534; showing that the proportion of
recruits wholly without education was highest in Ire-
land and lowest in Scotland, but that the proportion of
those who could write was higher in England than Scot-
land. In France, among the men liable to be drawn for
the army, the numbers were—unable to read and write,
303; able to read only, 32- able to read and write, 633 ;
not ascertained, 27 per 1,000; so that the proportion
wholly uneducated was larger than among the recruits
in England and Scotland, but rather less than in the -
Irish districts.

FALL OF A LARGE BUILDING AT TOTTENHAM.--FOF
the last two or three months several hundred men have
been daily employed in the construction of a large,
building, intended for an oil-cloth factory, at Green-
park, Tottenhsm, between Phillip-lane and Hanger-
lane, but whether it be that the side walls had been run
up to a height out of all proportion, as compared with
their width, or that the late heavy rains injuriously
affected the work, by washing away out of the joints
the binding portion of the cement, the whole thing, on
Sunday evening last, collapsed, and fell in-with a sound
resembling thunder, and causing no small sensation in
the neighbourhood.
ELECTRIC TELEGRAPH THROUGH
Journal de de St. Petersbourg of the 4th inst. contains an
important announcement with respect to telegraphic
communications between China and this country. An
order of the day of the Director-General of Ways and
Public Works states that the construction of the line of
Siberian telegraph, which has already reached Omsk,
and will, in the course of 1863, be extended, to Irkutsk,
has, with the assistance of the pest, allowed of a more
rapid interchange of communications between Europe
and China, and in consequence of this, and through the
medium of the Minister for Foreign Affairs, to open
communications thereupon, arrangements have been
carried out to enable the Western Powers to correspond
with China via Russia. Dispatches from the interior of
the empire, destined for ICiachta and Pekin, will be re-
ceived for transmission at the telegraph stations at
Petersburg, Moscow, and Nijni-Novgorod.
The marbles of Ireland are a valuable and unworked
treasure. For all kinds of marble, except pure white,
Ireland cannot be surpassed in any part of Europe.
in
There is a marble at Dunlewey, Donegal, which,
except for its approaching a dove colour, might compare
with the marbles of Carrara. It is a mere question of
taste, however, and one on which there ought to be room
for difference of opinion as to whether the colour, of the
Irish were not more chaste and elegant than that of the
Italian marble. But leaving this Point, to which I only
desire to glance, there can be no controversy about the
black marbles of Kilkenny Cork, Galway, &c., the
green and variegated of Connemara' and the several
ki Ids of so many shades to be found in Armagh, and
other parts of the country. Neither England nor Scot-
land can compete with Ireland for marbles. It is
probably one of the most cheering signs of the day for
Ireland that notice is being taken of her marbles, and it
augurs well for the future that a trade is springing up
between several parts of Great Britain and this country
for these valuable resources of industry.—Correspondent
of the Dublin Evening Hail.

articles.title: LATE GLASGOW MURDER.
articles.text:
THE LATE GLASGOW MURDER.

(From the Glasgow Examiner.)
This week a sort of post mortem examination has been
going on in the Chamber of our city Fiscals on the
Sandyford murder case. So far Mrs. APLachlan is legally
dead, and an inquiry is in preparation to see whether
she is worthy of death. The accounts given in the
<Efferent dailies differ considerably. The one says the
examination is conducted before the Sheriff (Alison),
and another says it is before the Fiscal only, and we
suspect the Fiscal who investigated the case before, and,
according to report, knew a little more than enough of
the Flemings to make his examination bear too hard
up, them. The object of this examination seems to be
to inquire whether there is not enough to show that
M'Lachlan was only a second party in the affair, and
whether, though worthy of death as eye-witness (accord-
ing to her own statement of the affair), and as the person
who carried off the plunder—all the plunder, for all the
-missing goods have been found. The Crown has
thrown a hard task on the agents for the doomed
woman. It demands to know what and how much of
leLachlan's last statement it can prove. Now, it is
pretty evident that they have given in already all the
evidence they had, and we fear they will be 'able to
make but sorry additions. Splendid rumours are afloat,
however, and of course the old gentleman' is the
doomed culprit in the public estimation, and any one
-who reads this last statement about to be proved, that he
is the alleged murderer, and just in proportion as he is
implicated will she be exonerated. The object of some
is to throw sufficient doubts on his innocence as to allow
her to escape as art and part' only in the foul deed.
The inquiry which was reported to have come off last
week is only in the course of preparation. Only on
Thursday last was leave granted to one of the prisoner's
agents to have free access to her alone, without any of
the prison officials. The agents show a pluck worthy of
a good cause, and so they ought, as human life ought
not to be slightly trifled with. Though we think they
made some blunders in the treatment of the case, we
must say they are clever practitioners, and will now do
their best; and if they succeed in proving the convict
only an accomplice they will earn laurels seldom reached
by persons in their position. If we understand their
position correctly, they wish to have enough against the
old gentleman' to remove the guilt of being sole, or
first actor, from Mrs. M‘Lachlan. We should think the
arraignment of Mr. Fleming not at all included in their
conimission, though facts may be elicited on which a
prosecution against him may be founded.

EFFECTS OF THE GLASGOW MURDER CASE.—We
have (stiys the Aberdeen Journal) a battle of principles
stirred up by this case. We have the action of a bene-
ficent jadicial system called in question. We have a
tumultuous attempt to concuss the authorities—a defi-
ance, by a Free Church clergyman, of the authorities to
'erect a gibbet in Glasgow, on which to hang the miser-
able woman, who has been found guilty of murder and
robbery, and confessed herself an accomplice in both.
We see the Press leading the mob, and accused of such
departures from its functions as Calls, according to some
of our contemporaries, for punishment and reprehension.
We see the Government yielding so far as to cause an
-additional inquiry, and we have to acknowledge that at
this moment the Glasgow populace have taken the ad-
ministration of justice into their own hands, and that
with all the public love for fair play, there
.is nothing
like fair play to be expected from the spint which at
present pervades them.

articles.text:
TEE METROPOLITAN RAILWAY.

The opening of thiscimportant line of railway will
not now be delayed for more than a few days, and but
for the small requirement of Colonel Yolland, the Go-
vernment inspector, it would have en opened for
th
traffic on Monday. An alteration e shape
flieistf
and size of the glass lan Ips of the ignals has
been considered necessary, and;:trtat:4l* exception,
everything has been approved. The permanent way,
the switokes and points, the bridges and stations--all, in
fact, that relates to the working of the line—has been
found satisfactory, and the contractors and officers of the
company have been complimented in the highest manner
by the Government Inspector for the admii-able manner
in which the works have been executed. The brick-
work of the tunnel and of the retaining wall has been
highly praised, as also the construction of the bridges,
and the station accommodation. The arrangements for
working the line are completed, and the engines and car-
riages are,all ready. Further trials have shown that the
plan of coSsuming the smoke and steam by the locomo-
tive engines has perfectly succeeded, and after a couple
of engines had been running backwards and forwards
during the whole day, no disagreeable effect arose from
any of the products of combustion in the tunnel. It
has been decided that he trains will start from Pad-
dington and Farringdon-street every ten minutes, from
eight in the morning till eight in the evening. From
six to eight o'clock in the morning, and from eight to
AweltialatNnight, the trains will run only every 20
minntee Txp'rtss trains will start every hour, running;
the whole distance from Paddington to Farringdon-
street in 10 minutes. 'With these exceptions all the
trains will stop at the intermediate stations, the time
occupied in the whole journey bein 15 minutes. The
lowest fare taken will be two-pence, Ad this will be
charged between any intermediate station, and the
lowest through fare will be threepence. There are
three classes of carriages, first, second, and third all,
however, equally well lighted by the gas earn( d with
the train. The second-class carriages are fitted with.
cushions, the third are light, spacious, and well venti-
lated, and the first are roomy, exceedingly comfortable,
and even luxurious in their general style and fitting.

THE FEDERAL G-OVERNMENT AND
THE SLAVE QUESTION.

-:The following circular, by Mr. Seward, addressed to
fathe diplomatic and consular agents of the United
tee, is published in the Paris papers :
•, Department of State, Washington, Sept. 22.
‘lll 'Gentlemen—You will receive by the mail which will
#tarry you this despatch evidence which will convince
llt• 1 you that the aggressive movement of the rebels against
tthe States remaining faithful to the Union is arrested,
• "i 4 and that the forces of the Union, strengthened and
frreanimated, are again ready to undertake a campaign on
4-k a vast scale. If you consult the newspapers you will
1. easily perceive that the financial resources of the insur-
,... rection.decline rapidly, and that the means of raising
troops hive been exhausted.
On the other side, you will see that the financial
isituation of the country is good, and that the call for
iesh troops, without which the material force of the
‘nation would be seriously crippled, is being promptly re-
sponded to. I have already naformed our representatives
abroad of the approach of a chancre in the social organisa-
tion of the rebel States. This change continues to make
itself each day more and more apparent. In the opinion
of the President the moment has come to place the great
fact more clearly before the people of the rebel States,
and to make them understand that if these States persist
in imposing upon the country the choice between the
dissolution of this Government, at once necessary and
beneficial, and the abolition of slavery, it is the Union,
and not slavery, that must be maintained and saved.
With this object the President is about to publish a pro-
clamation, in which he announces that slavery will no
longer be recognised in any of the States which shall be
in rebellion on the Ist of JanuarT next. While all the
good and wise men of all countries will recognise this
measure as a just and proper military act intended to
deliver the country from a terrible civil war, they will
recognise at the same time the moderation and
magnanimity with which the Government proceeds in a
matter so solemn and important.
'I am, gentlemen, your obedient servant,
WILLIAM H. SEWARD.'

articles.title: BEE-HIVE, SATURDAY, OCTOW R 18, 142
articles.text:
THE BEE-HIVE, SATURDAY, OCTOW R 18, 142

MR. GLADSIONE' S
_VISIT TO THE

AGRICULTURAL PROSPECTS.

The week opened with a brisk, bracing, fine day.
Wind N.B. to E. Monday, however, was dull and
threatening; occasionally clear, but very thick at 4 p.m.,
when some heavy drops of rain fell for a short period;
but it was finer at night. The barometer, though, was
falling. Some wheat was got in with a good prospect,
and that planted the previous week show ed signs of
vegetating two days after it had been put into the
ground. There will thus be no doubt of the grain
being in a prime state, and growing well this season.
The sorts here alluded to were the Pedigree wheat sown
in Huntingdonshire the previous year from the original
stock, and Kessinglancl, which much resembles the for-
mer in sample.
Some rain had fallen the previous night; but Tuesday
morning was fine, breezy, and bright—wind cold, from
the N.W. However, about noon it began to rain, and
proved a very wet afternoon, so that so wing was com-
pletely stopped for that day. Wheat and beans
were still reported to be out, in the West Riding of
Yorkshire.
Wednesday was a fine bracing day, wind north-north-
east, sunny and breezy, so that autumnal tillage would
proceed steadily, the light lands being rendered letter
for the wheat going into the ground, by the previous
moisture. _ .

On Thursday it was fine and bracing, wind east,
thei mometer 60 degs. ; barometer very high—up to 30.30
ir., but falling with the wind pointing to the south-east.
Wheat sowing was vigorously pushed on, and went into
the ground in a prime state.
Samples of all the choicest qualities are now being
selected, and amongst the red the Nursery is having the
greatest run. This sort obtained the prize at the agri-
cultural show of Worcester on Wednesday. It was
r:pened early, and a superior sample. We have heard
of some grown in Hampshire which touched 661bs.
per imperial bushel. In Essex and Caanbridgeshire
it runs from 63 to 64 lbs. 1 lb. over or under,
according to the condition in which it was harvested:
a dry and breezy day on being carted would
make this difference. Then there are the Spald-
Browick, Sire, and Golden Drop; amongst
the white the Chidham, Earl Dude, Taunton Dean,
and the Rough Chaff. These do not run of so fine a
quality as the reds, but some good and true stocks are
to be selected from the runs, which can be recommended
generally, but more particularly to the Scotch farmers,
who from having a poor quality of their own, must resort
to the south for a choice article. We fancy they are
turning their attention more to red than usual; and
although the nursery is spoken against in some localities
as not yielding so well as others, yet the fen farmers are
reported to have grown of it five quarters per acre, and
this for the season must be looked upon as a most excel-
lent crop, and a satisfactory result in every respect. It
is a great favourite with most millers, making a strong
sack of flour, and will command a comparatively high
price. The Donna Maria red wheat, from Essex, pro-
duced in Worcestershire 34i bushels (of 621b5.) per acre,
and white Essex seed wheat in the same county,
and on the same farm, 34 bushels of (621bs) per acre,
but with the quality of the latter not so good as the for-
mer. For the season this must be considered a good
yield. Nearly all the wheats in that country were
secured in poor condition, which is much against com-
manding good prices. All the small and poor farmers
thereabouts have a wretched yield of wheat and barley.
The weather remained fine throughout Friday; wind
east; quite like October, but the barometer gave signs
of a change. This being the third fine day in succes-
sion, a great quantity of wheat had been got into the
ground in the primest order possible. From Yorkshire
on that day it was stated, 'Since last Friday the weather
has been fine on the 'whole; and, except beans, the
crops are secured hereabouts, after a rather protracted
harvest, and the yield varies much.'
A change occurred in the weather on the last day of
the week. Early in the morning a thunderstorm was
experienced, and some heavy rain fell up to 9 a.m. ;
after which it was finer, the wind having gone round to
the south-west, the week closinc, with a somewhat un-
settled appearance. The markets are not cheering to
the growers, the soft condition of so much new wheat
preventing its sale, even at moderate prices, while the
superabundant imports of foreign give the millers an
opportunity of securing as much as they want from
almost every important port of the United Kingdom.
The consumer is getting the benefit at all points.—
Oct. 11.

articles.title: INDIA.
articles.text:
INDIA.

The following is from the overland summary of the
Times of Intik; (Bombay), of Sept 12 :
Mr. Mead, of the Ilurkaru, and Mr. Judge, of the
Assam Company, were drowned on the morning of the
6th September at Catcutta, by the upsetting of a boat.
The Nawab of Savanoor, a member of the Bombay
Legislative Council, died at Savanoor on the 30th
August. The Hon. W. E. Frere, who was nominated
a judge of the High Court of this Presidency, has re-
signed his office, and has been succeeded by Mr. New-
ton. The Apollo Cotton Press Company, at their last
annual meeting of the 29th August, declared a dividend
of 1,800 rs. per share. Cholera is decreasing amongst
the troops at Meerut. It is understood that the new
Court House will be built on a site on the esplanade,
near the Cooperage. The affairs of the Bombay Steam
Navigation Company are to be wound up. The meeting
of the 3rd inst. disclosed further misdeeds of the
directors, involving the company in great loss. The
Chuppatee ' mevement appears to be nothing
alarming. The natives fearing a famine have adopted,
it would appear, this plan of propitiating their deities.
The Dewan of Travancore has published a proclama-
tion increasing the dui es upon all imports and exports
to and from the Travancore territory :—The duty on
exports and imports at 5 per cent. will henceforth be
6 per cent.; ditto at 8 per cent. will henceforth be 10
per cent.; ditto at 10 per cent. will henceforth be 12
per cent. It is in contemplation to lower the tariff
again so soon as .the finances will permit of doing so.
A meeting of East Indians has been held at Madras,
with the view of transmitting a memorial to parlia-
ment praying for the removal of disabilities imposed
by the decision of the Secretary for War, that East
Indians cannot hold commissions as medical officers in
the royal army. The Commander-in-Chief of India
has applied to the supreme government to release all
officers appointed to the new line regiments from their
connection with the civil department, in order that
they may immediately join their respectiv.e corps. A
public meeting will be held in Bombay on the 17th, at
which it is rumoured that the governor will preside, to
take into consideration means for alleviating the great*
distress in Lancashire. The municipal commissioners
have stated that they have no objection to the Gas Com-
pany establishing their works in the vicinity of the By-
culla Club, or in a spot not far from the Byculla-bridge.
In the districts of Ahmednuggur and Sattara forage
is very scarce, cattle are dying of starvation, and the
cultivators and other poorer classes are reduced to ex-
treme distress. The preliminary inquiry into the charge
against Captain Smales, paymaster of the 6th Dragoons,
at the police-office, has ended, and the magistrate has
committed the case to the session. Lieut. Jackson,
who stands charged with flogging his servant to death,
is likely to be sent to Meehan to be tried by a general
court-martial. The native prisoners concerned in the
notorious Morrelgunge case have been sentenced by the
High Court, and eleven found guilty of riot attended
with murder and abduction. Dowlut Chowkeydar is
to suffer death, and ten others to be imprisoned for life.
The alleged leader of the affray, Mr. Denis 14,ealy, will
be tried for complicity. The Rajah of Ochin has
abolished the tobacco monopoly, which hitherto ex-
isted within his territory. The Barbara, bound from
Bombay to Liverpool, put into Port Louis on the 4th
August, leaky, she having experienced heavy weather.
The Ameer Dost Mahomed had suffered great loss at
Baylanbaug, but was advancing on Herat. It was ru-
moured that troops had been promised by the Shah of
Persia for the defence of Herat. A man named Thomas
John Ghee has been fined £2O for coming as a passen-
ger to Bombay in the Malta, from Suez, without a
passage ticket or other authority. The health of the
island is improving. A model farm is to be laid out
near Nassick, under the superintendence of Captain
Kerr, V.C., late of the Southern Mahratta Horse. The
Tropic Bird appears to have foundered on the 16th
August. The Sirius picked up six of the Lascars and
made them over to the Clifton, who brought them up
to Calcutta. The captain and some of the crew have
not, been heard of, while it is stated that the chief
officer and eleven of the crew were drowned in a boat
which was swamped.

articles.title: ASSASSINATIDXS LV
articles.text:
THE ASSASSINATIDXS LV

PALERMO.

The Official Journal of Palermo gives the following
details respecting the murders lately perpetrated or
attempted in that city :
It appears that, on the .evening of that day, and
nearly at the same hour, fourteen persons were stiiettoed
in different parts of the city ,by men dressed alike and of
the same stature, so as for a moment to lead to the belief
that the crimes were committed by the same man. The
wounds were all inflicted with weapons of the same di-
mensions, and nearly all the strokes were aimed at the
abdomen. Fortunately, at the moment when the last
victim fell, three officers-of the 51st Regiment, seeing
the assassin in the act of taking to flight, pursued him,
but would most probably have berm unable to catch him,
owing to his perfect knowledge of every lane, and
corner, had they not been joined by the commandant of
the police force and another man. At length the mis-
creant, finding himself hard pressed, ran into a shoe-
maker's shop, and attempted "to push one of the journey-
men off his stool in order to take his place, and thus de-
ceive his pursuers; but this device did not succeed, and
he was taken. The bloody knife and a piece of.paper
with which he had endeavoured to wipe it clean, were
found about his person, and, on being taken before the
magistrate, he was recognised as being one Angelo Dan-
gelo, once employed as a porter in the Custom House.
After some hesitation he revealed the names of seven of
his accomplices, who were immediately arrested, and on
the following- day another man was taken up on a similar
charge, besides two others who had committed murders
at another time.'

On the same subject we subjoin the following extracts
from the Corriere Sicilian° :

'lf we were seized with horror at the atrocious acts
committed here on the Ist instant, our horror is still
more intense after reading a proclamation from the men
styling themselves the committee, in which clandestine
publication they shamelessly accept the responsibility of
those crimes. On the 2nd instant this committee of
cannibals, addressing the people, their brethren, ex-
pressed itself as follows :—" Act by incediarism, by the
pistol, by the stiletto—you know your enemies ! "
And do you know who these enemies are? They are
honest citizens walking quietly in the streets, and
unable to conceive that in the name of Rome and
liberty they may get a stab in the abdomen! Yes,
it is indeed in the name of liberty, which the " com-
mittee " declares to be oppressed, it is in the name of
Rome, which it declares to be sold to the Pope, that
these massacres are enjoined, that fourteen families
have been thrown into mourning, and that a whole
country is thrown into consternation. The "com-
mittee" talks of devastations by the troops; of men
shot down by hundreds by order of the Government:; it
tells us so, as if it were ta king to people in China.
Where, where are these devastations, these wholesale
executions, when from every corner of the island we
hear but one cry, for troops to protect us from thiewes
and assassins? The " committee " has recourse to the
stiletto of the most infamous camorists who dishonour
the town; they enrol their assassins from among the
minions of Maniscalco (under the Bourbons), and it
dares to talk of liberty and rights! What is it you in-
tend ? Under the high-sounding names of Italy and
liberty we know how much infamy can be concealed.
You entrench yourselves behind the ranks of a party
which, although not ours, still comprises many of our
friends. That party has a name, but you have none,
, unless it be that of assassins. What can your appeal to
arms and insurrection mean? What will be your
banner, your war-cry? Ah, if public opinion points you
out as Bourbonists, it is not far wrong. We regret but
one thing, and that is that, thanks to you, the state of
siege which weighs upon Sicily,'and is deplored by all,
notwithstanding its mildness, is only what we deserve.
For a country where an association like yours can sub-
, sist can only be saved by exceptional laws.'

A CAT-AND-DOG LIFE.-4 What do they mean by a
cat-and-dog life ?' said a husband to his angry wife.
Look at Carlo and Kitty asleep on the rug together.
wish men lived half so peaceably with their wives.'
Stop,' said the lady, tie them together, and, see how

DEATH THROUGH CRINOLINE.—On the 10th Mr.
v e held an inquest at Guy's Hospital, touching the
.4 if William
.14(icas' aged 27 years, a miner, who
res • at Sydenitain. It appeared that the deceased
was travelling in a railway carriage from London-bridge
to Pimlico, when at Gipsy-hill a female's crinoline got
jammed in the carriage door. The deceased put his
-head out to unfasten the door, when he received a fright-
ful blow on the head from the corner of an arch. He
was conveyed to the before-mentioned hospital, where
he expired from the injuries. The jury returned a
verdict of Accidental death.'

NO BEER, TOO MUCH PUDDING.—Beer, then, is Mt-
tritious ; but does it depend for this quality on the alcohol,
or on the other matters which are mixed with it The
teetotallers say that the latter is the case; that this gly-
cose, the dextrine, and various other nourishing matters
which are present, account for the supporting qualitiesoi
beer. Clearly, however, they only do this in part, and
not a greatpart; for a litre of good beer (nearly two pints)
contains, according to the analysis of M. Payen, only
about the equivalent of an ounce and a half of bread, so
far as these extraneous matters are concerned. This will
not nearly account for the diminution which takes place
in the peasant's daily food without his suffering loss of
health. The fact which lam her!) referring to is a very
well known one, and there is nothing more common than
to hear the newly-made teetotal convert boast, as of %
great personal virtue, of the increased amount of pud-
dings and bread that he can eat since his deliveranne
from the slavery of alcohol.—Carnhill Magazine.

articles.title: NORTH.
articles.text:
NORTH.

The Chancellor of the Exchequer, who has visited
several places in the north of England, arrived at York
on the 11th, and in the afternoon was present at an
elegant luncheon given by the Lord Mayor, in the
State-room of the Mansion-house.
The Lord Mayor proposed the usual loyal toasts, and
then gave the health of Mr. 'Gladstone, whose name
was received with loud cheering.
Mr. Gladstone, in returning thanks, after some re-
marks chiefly of local interest, said the Lord Mayor had
been pleased to refer in complimentary terms to his
appearance in York. Upon no personal ground could he
claim their notice but he believed that the character of
public servants and public men were warmly appreciated
and liberally and properly estimated by the people of
this country, and that every member of that body, how-
ever little he might be distinguished, yet when he
moved about among his fellow countrymen received in
his own person a large share of reward, which was due,
not to his individual exertions, but rather to the general
fidelity and efficiency with which the great works of
government and legislation had been carried for ward
during his lifetime in the country. (Applause.) He con-
tended that the increase which had taken place in mann-
factures and trade oflate years was not a mere signification
of the accumulation of wealth in the hands of the wealthy,
but it was likewise a happy testimony to the fact that the
privations of human life had been diminished, the
comforts of human life increased, and a sense of self-
respect strengthened amongst all classes of the com-
munity, in consequence of the great fidelity with which
the duties of government and legislation had been per-
formed. (Applause.) He hoped that something had
been done towards redeeming the reproach of former
times, that in the eager pursuit of wealth we had for-
gotten that it was not wealth alone which humanised
and elevated mankind; and although in more recent
times England had abated nothing of her commercial and
manufacturing energy, but on the contrary had seemed
to increase it, yet along with that increase there had
happily spread a deeper moral sense and a stronger con-
sciousness of the obligations that capital owed to labour,
a constant developement of benevolent designs for
the benefit of the masses; and in this respect we
saw the crowning blessing of our lives, in the
increased and still increasing and the closer grow-
ing union of all classes of the community. (Cheers.)
Mr. Gladstone expressed a fervent hope that
the blessings we enjoyed might be spread to the
other nations of the world. The Lord Mayor
had referred to the case of our brethren in America and
he could hardly express the disappointment as well as
pain with which he witnessed what was now going on
upon that great continent. He had never been one of
those who believed that the New World was to be an
improvement upon the Old—(a laugh)—and that was
owing no doubt to our local and municipal and insular
ideas in England, binding us down to a certain extent to
that which was purely English. (Applause.) While he
rejoiced to think that America was a free country, he
had always felt that there was something in the freedom
of America that was not of that genuine ancestral kind
like the freedom and liberty of this country. It seemed
that we had now lived to a period when that freedom
appeared to be somewhat in danger. Nearly every
packet brought accounts of measures which showed that
in the desperate agonies of the conflict now raging civil
and political rights were necessarily being offered up a
sacrifice to the necessities of the time; and there arose
in the mind a question, if possible more painful—
how, after the tremendous conflict and the enthroning
of force and military power above the ruin of
laws and good order—how was America hereafter to
return to a state of things in which, at any rate, she did
afford personal and individual liberty both as to property
and life F ,His earnest hope was that this question might
be favourably annwered ; but they all must feel that
the longer this terrific struggle went on the more doubt-
ful and difficult would it be for America to esniblish
that orderly and lawful state 'of things now for a time at
least superseded and suspended, an which we saw and
were accustomed to witness with .delight, as the best
security for the extension of her material prosperity and

THE DEMAND FOR RECOGNITION.

(From the Spectator.)
We have not yet waited for America as we once
waited for Spain, and the recognition of Spain's lost
colonies by Canning—almost the only available prece-
dent—was considered a precipitate measure. The
battle is not over yet, and the death of Mr. Lincoln,

NEGRO COURAGE.—One of the most remarkable acts
of daring during the war was the piloting by the negro
Robert Small, of the vessel called the Planter, from
Charleston, passing the guns of Fort Sumter, and running
her direct to the blockading fleet. The men and women
engaged in that exploit had solemnly agreed in advance
that, if pursued and without hope of escape, the ship
should be scuttled and sunk ; and that if she did not go
down fast enough to prevent capture, they would all
take hands, husband and wife, brother and sister, jump
overboard, and perish together.—Chatniers's Journal',

articles.title: MR. COBDEN IN EAST LOTHIAN
articles.text:
MR. COBDEN IN EAST LOTHIAN

Mr. Cobden was 'present on the 11th at a trial of
steam-ploughs, which took place at the farm of Ferry-
gate, East Lothian.
After the trials the company was entertained to lun-
cheon by the Right Hon. R. C. Hamilton Nisbet, in a
marquee, at Dirleton Castle.
The 'Health of the &rangers' was proposed by Mr.
Nisbet.

Mr. Cobden, who was received wn loud cheers, re-
sponded ta the toast Ile said—Mr. Nisbet, ladies and
gentlemen,—When I left Edinburgh this morning., in
company with my friend Mr. M`Laren, to pay a visit to
Mr. Pope, and witness an exhibition of the steam-plough,
I told not the remote,t idea that I should have found
myself in presence of a large agricultural gathering
such as I find here. But I can assure you I feel myself
honoured by being permitted to associate with you on
this occasion, to t e witness of the triumph of agricul-
tural skill in this the head-quarters of advanced
agriculture. lam myself the son of a farmer, and
my sympathies have always been with that class,
though I think I see some faces here who would
be inclined to feel dubious on that subject.—
(Laughter and cheers.) My right hon.. friend, your
chairman' has alluded to some passages of arms which
we have had in the House of Commons together. We
took different :views of a great national question, sincerely
and conscientiously differing on that question; but I am
prepared to say for myself, what Jam sure he will be equally
prepared to admit in me, that we had one common in-
terest in view, and that was the welfare of this great
country. (Loud cheers.) In advocating that policy
which I have done since I have been known as a public
man, I have never been under the impression that I was
acting in a manner to be injurious to agriculture. I
have always held a different language. I held that
language in presence of the tenant farmers of this country
twenty years ago. Now, I must ask of my right hon.
friend at the head of the table, candidly to admit
that though he fought the battle as manfully- as
way one could have done in that most manly of all
assemblies, the House of Commons, yet I will ask
him freely and fairly to admit to me that, in advo-
eating, as I have done, an unprotected, free and
unrestricted competition in agriculture, I have not taken
a course which has proved inimical to that great inte-
rest. I think he will admit that I stand here to main-
tain my ground, and I now claim experience to justify
me in the course which I have taken. What is it that
constitutes the prosperity of agriculture or any other
pursuit? It is to have a flourishing, rich, and increasing
number of customers. Without that no business can
prosper. You, as agriculturists above all things, want
a constantly increasing number of, and constantly
increasing wealth in, your customers—the manufactar-
ing, mining, and, industrial population of this country.
(Cheers.) Above all things, you want a prosperous
community, who can purchase your cattle and your
stock, because I need not tell you who are so far advanced
in that science of agriculture, that that which lies at the
very foundation of all scientific agriculture is, the large
and constantly increasing production of the manure-
providing animals, the cattle and sheep which you
rear on your land. But you cannot find customers
for that stock which is so necessary to advanced
agriculture, unless you have a thriving manufac-
turing, mining, and industrial population. You cannot
send these articles abroad. I can understand that you
might grow some commodities such as hops and other
articles, that you might send abroad, but the cattle
and sheep—the animal life that exists on your farm—
must be sold to your near neighbours, the manufac-
turing and industrial population. The course I took,
and the policy I advocated, was to create a rich and
prosperous community at your door; which would be
customers for your commodities. I think we may now
say we have succeeded in that. You have had a
constantly increasing development of wealth, a constantly
increasing export of your manufactures, and a constantly
increasing demand for your cattle, your sheep, and your
wool. These have been the foundation of your pros-
perity. I have always thought that both the land-owners
and the farmers took a very unworthy and ignoble view
of their own interest when they measured the value
of the land only by the price at which they could sell
their wheat. Wheat, gentlemen, is a barbarous estimate
a barbarous measure of the value of land. Wheat was
the sole dependence of your grandfathers when living
here at one quarter of the rent you now pay, and not
enjoying half the 'prosperity you now enjoy with your
fourfold rents. Therefore I say, in advocating the policy
which has improved the condition of your customers, I
have been advocating your interests. I could not
improve their condition without improving yours, and
your prosperily will go on increasing so long as your
customers go on progressing in wealth, and your
prosperity will begin to decline when they begin to
decay. lam sorry that at the present moment we have,
for a time, a great depression in the manufacturing
interest with which I have been particularly connected.
I hope it will only be temporary—(Hear, hear.) I hope
it will not last so long as to be felt by you in your
parsuits. I hope it will not be sufficient to check
the onward progress of what we have seen—a
grrlnd manifestation in what we have witnessed to-day.
I hope you will go on increasing in the application
of steam to the cultivation of the land, for that is
the next step in the progress of improvement. You
must dispense as much as possible with the old horse, the
horse of muscle and flesh, and take to the horse that will
be less costly to you, for his coals will be .Jess .than the
oats, and he will be less liable to accident or derangement
than your live animals. I should therefore hope the
prosperity of your agriculture will enable you to go on
still increasing and multiplying your instruments of
steam power. lam exceedingly obliged for the honour
you have done me on this occasion. It is a pleasure I
never had before of addressing a body of agriculturists
met together to consult and to enjoy themselves in the
midst of their own peculiar pursuits; 'feel myself
highly honoured, and not out of my pace in any way,
by being with you to-day. (Hear, and cheers.) Mr.
Cobden concluded by proposing The health of Mr.
Hamilton Nisbet,' remarking that, while they had met
in the House of Commons on the opposition benches,
they now met in social intercourse, and he accepted and
reciprocated the kind expressions which had fallen from
him on that occasion. (Loud cheers.)

THE INCENDIARY CASE AT NOTTINGHAM.—OR SalllT- I
day last, atthe Shire Hall, Nottingham, Henry Davis was I
brought up on remand, charged with setting fire to some
stacks at West Bridgford, Nottingham, the property of
Mr. W. Birldn, farmer. From the additional evidence
offered, it appeared that the prisoner's wife went to the
police-station on Wednesday evening last to see him.
When she saw him the prisoner said (in the presence of
an officer), I have tell them that I was there on that
day.' The officer said, There is no doubt that you
were there, from what you father-in-law said. He says
that you were near to the stack, and while lighting your
pipe you dropped the match ,and set the stack on fire.
You were frightened, and ran away.' Prisoner then
replied-4 That's just what it was,' and repeated the
statement. The dog which was caught amongst the
stacks on the day of the fire, and which proved to be
the principal means of his apprehension, was produced
in court. Upon seeing his master in the dock it ran up
and recognised him. The prisoner now denied making
the confession above alluded to; and several witnesses
were called with. the View of proving an alibi. The
bench, after considering a short time, committed the
prisoner for trial at the next assizes.
A YANKEE'S POWERS OF ROMANCE.—The agents of
two rival iron safe manufacturers were recently present-
ing the claims of their respective articles. The one was
a Yankee—the other wasn't. 'lle that wasn't told his
story. -A game cock had been shut up in one of hie
safes, and then it was exposed three days to the most
intense heat. When the door was opened, the cock
stalked out, flapped his wings and crowed loudly, as if
nothing had happened. It was now the Yankee's turn.
A cock had also been shut up in one of his safes with a
pouid of fresh butter, and the safe was submitted to the
trial of a tremendous heat for more than a week. The
legs of the safe were melted off; and the-door itself so
far fused as to-require the use of a cold chisel to get it
open. When it was opened, the cock was found frozen
dead, and the butter so solid, that a man who knocked
off a piece of it with a hammer had his eye put out by a
frozen butter splinter.

A TICKET-OF- LEAVE VoTER.-The Dover Chronicle
states that at the recent revision of the registration for
that borough the revising barrister admitted a ticket-of-
leave man to the elective 'rights of freemen, nOtwith-
standing that the man's father admitted he was under
penal servitude. Whatever, says the Chronicle, may be
the merits or demerits of the convict system, it never
entered, that we are aware, into the heads of the most
sanguine philanthropists to invest criminals -undergeing
their sentence with the privileges of citizenship. Concede
this, and we expect by-and-bye to have criminal jurors,
mayors, magistrates, and members of parliament.

articles.title: SING OF PRUSSIA AND THE GOVERNMENT.
articles.text:
THE SING OF PRUSSIA AND THE
GOVERNMENT.

A deputation of Conservatives from Halle recently had
an audience of the King of Prussia, and presented an
address to his Majesty, which contained the following
passage
In the course which the majority of the present
House of Representatives have pursued for some months,
and particularly, in the recent revolutions respecting the
military baget, we see only a mournful error, to yield
to which .would infallibly rob our dear country, the
government of -which God has placed in your hands, of
the power and importance which the exertions of two
centuries have acquired for it, and, instead of subjects of
Olt hereditary, beloved king, would make us servants of
democratic leaders Of the people.'
After a short speech by the leader of the deputation,
his, Majesty replied asfollows
'Tell those on 'whose part you come that it is very
gratifying to ray heart to hear such sentiments ex
pressed. Similar marks of approval have-already readied
me front different quarters of the country, and yet many
more have been announced to me. Encroachments of
the kind indicated have already been many times made;
but on-the reorganisation question a rupture has taken
place. After long consideration; I have resolved on the
reerganisation of the army, in order without immoderate
sacrifice, to increase the strength in arms of Prussia,
as required by the present state of the world,
and in order to lighten the service of the old Prussian
militiamen. lam convinced that your exertions for
the welfare of the country and the people-ace absolutely
necessary, and will be enduring. lam quite well
understood, but what I aim at is not approved of. My
-measures a.t-a opposed by others quite different. As
before, I hold true to my programme of 1848, and am
firmly resolved to remain faithful tothe Constitution so
long as it is not torn out of my hands. I shall, how-
ever, oppose encroachments with all the means at my
disposal, -and in so doing I rely on the support of my
Lithful subjects.'
The spokesman of the deputation said, in conclusion,
''May God support your Majesty with true strength in
this unavoidable struggle ! ' On which the King
Yes, n ithout God we can really do nothing.
From-Him all help must come. But men will not now
humble themselves before God, and only rely on their
own strength. This is the reason of so much mischief.'

THE GRATE or CITARLES Lan.—ln the churchyard
of Edmonton the 'inquiring traveller may, after consider-
able search, find the grave of Chmies and Mary Lamb.
The churchyard is large, and has an air of neglect and
desolation, and one of the most neglected parts of it is
the grave of the man whose memory gives the whole
scene an interest. The grave is a little way back from
a side path, and it is overgrown with nettles and long
grass, while over it towers a hideous erection of the
fluted order of village architecture, designed to perpetu-
ate the fame of a certain Gideon Rippon;of Eagle-house.
On the tombstone, between the dates recording that
Charles Lamb died December 27, 1834, aged 59, and
that Mary Anne Lamb died May 20, 1847, aged 80 years,
are inserted twelve of the very worst verses that the
ingenuity of friends could have ' struck out. In the
beautiful and touching lines in' which Wordsworth
sketched the character. and the history of his friend he
tells us that he meant the earlier portion of the piece to
be placed on Lamb's tombstone, but that other arrange-
ments had been made. The visitor to Edmonton may
see what was the effusion that was preferred to Words-
worth's. It begins by declaring that Lamb's meek and
harmless mirth no more. shtll gladden our domestic
hearth.' It goes on to assure the deceased that he is not
all lost, end that his writings shall win many an English
bosom pleased to see that old and happier vein revived
in thee.' Everything is in a sort of rude harmony—the
nettles, the shrine of Gideon Rippon, and the doggrel.
We go out to see the grave of one of the most charming
and original English writers of the 19th century, and we
find a bank of weeds and a supereminent mass of stone
or stum i p n honour of a bank clerk, and a set of verses
for which the schoolboy of Lord Macaulay's Essays
would have been 'deservedly flogged.—Saturday Review.
SUNDAY 0 EMIVAN OE IN TRE FEDI:Tun .Anmv.—
The following is the Sunday regime authorised to be
observed in the Federal army :—The suspension of all
work—the avoidance of all unnecessary movements—
attendance on Divine worship, and the promotion by
officers and men of the utmost deeoram and quiet,
unless an atta-elt-from the enemy or some other extreme
military necessity shall compel the contrary. The
motives presented in these orders are—The necessity of
one day's rest in seven for men and animals; the fact
that discipline, to be permanent, must be based on
moral grounds;' the recognition of our sacred duty to
observe the holy day of the God of Maley and of Battles;'
and the dependence of the army on the benign favour
of the Creator while fighting in a holy cause.'

We read in the United Service Gazette A rumour
has reached us to the effect that disturbances, some-
what similar to those which some time since gained so
unenviable a notoriety for Woolwich, have recently
broken out amongst the cadets at Sandhurst. A great
mystery is, as usual, sought to be preserved, both as to
the causes and the results of this reported emeute, but we
understandthat a court of inquiry commenced its sittings
on Saturday last.'
The German Journal of Frankfort states that during
the last stay of the King of Prussia at Baden, his
Majesty's cash-box was stolen one evening in the room
which Chancellor Bock occupied on the ground-floor of
the hotel. The fact was discovered by a footman, who,
on returning home, saw the window of the room open,
and gave the alarm. As it became apparent that the
thief could not have left the hotel, a strict search was
made throughout the establishment, and the box was at
length found in the garden under a bush. The•thief had
evidently tried hard to break it open, but had not suc-
ceeded for want of the proper tools, with which a pro-
fessional thief is generally provided. The perpetrator of
the robbery has not yet been discovered.
THE Auennisnernic OF Yong.—The following ad-
dress is now in course of signature by the clergy
throughout the arehdeaconry of York We, the
undersigned clergy of the archdeaconry of York, are
unwilling that your Grace should quit the diocese With-
out some expression of our regret at the loss of one,
whose wisdom, kindness, and self-denial we have
largely experienced and gratefully acknowledged. We
trust, however, that the change, which we ourselves
lament, will conduce to the general welfare of the
church. We rejoice that, by your elevation under
God's good providence, to the Primacy of all England,
our national church will receive the benefit of the
mature experience, acquired during an active episcopate
ef twenty-four years in the -northern province. We
pray that the blessing of God may ever rest upon you;
that His grace may guide you in the discharge of the
high functions of that office to which you are now called
—that you may ban enjoy health et body and vigour
of mind—and that you may be the honoured instrument
of promoting, what we are assured is the dearest wish
of your heart, the glory of God and the eternal good of
men,
