articles.title: Jl(t ifitt—Nthe
articles.text:
Jl(t ifitt—Nthe

SATURDAY, OCTOBER 18, 1862.

SIT vIMARY

The Prussian Government have decided to
dismiss their Chamber of Deputies, and spend
for the season a budget adopted by the King
and Peers, on the understanding that they are
two branches of the legislature, the Chamber of
Deputies a third—and that on a disputed ques-
tion between three parties in the constitution,
two form a majority and are better than one.
This doctrine forms no part of the constitu-
tion, but the king has closed the session, and
is to work on his own responsibility. The
dispute relates exclusively to money, the cause
of much mischief; and the king's conduct is
doubtless uncon,titutional.

The French Emperor has accepted the resig-
nation of M. Thouvenel, and MM. Fould and
Persigny are likely to follow, or have followed,
the example of the Foreign Secretary into
retirement. 'The change is supposed to be
adverse to Italy, and favourable to the Pope.
M. Drouyn de Lhuys, who has accepted the
foreign port oho, is not favourable to Italian
independence and unity. He is more conser-
vative, perhaps more convenient, than his
predecessor M. Thouvenel, but for some reason
satisfactory to the Emperor, Be Lhuys is in,
and Thouvenel is out. Napoleon
,has not

abandoned Rome, and he will remain -at Rome
not for the interest of the Pope, but for the
weakening of Italy, and the aggrandisement
of his own government. On that account, per-
haps, the Lord Mayor of London was made
acquainted, with the desire even of our Govern-
ent, that the Roman question should not be
raiscussed in the Guildhall..

Consols in London, and Rentes in Paris,l
fell on the announcement of the change in the I
French ministry. Capitalists dislike this re- !
volution. It may provoke further movements
in Italy: and therefore Italian Five per Cents
fell, and Turkish Consols a;so fell. Italy andi
Turkey are both menaced by the alteration,
or the capitalists believe so.
Capitalists are stupid. No change is effect-
ed. '1 hey or their instructors talk of the
party of the Emperor, and the party of the
Empress, as if the Emperor were latitudina-
rian, and the Empress orthodox Roman.
France does not contain two parties. Napo-
leon is the only party having power. All
other parties are nominal—some of them only
shadows of great names.
Intelligence from China casts some doubts
on the future price of silks and teas. The
Taeping Wangites being attacked by the
Imperalists, threaten to stop the supplies of
silk and tea. Our officers in China have
organised expeditions to the interior, and the
mercantile journalists hope for orders from
home to stop these marauding personages
on the road to ruin trade. They hope in vain.
As nothing has been said by the people against
the proceedings of our officials in the Flowery
land, they will proceed to intervene until the ,
land be no longer worthy of its name.
The diplomatic relations with the Japanesel
empire have caused already several murders,
and have gone so far as fortified resi-
dences to the British and French ambassadors,
which are being prepared for their reception,
along with a guard of British and French
soldiers. The guard is to be weak in numbers,
but they will only be a vanguard. Hereafter
they will be followed by reinforcements. The
aristocracy or oligarchy of Japan are, pro-
bably, not wrong in considering their indepen-
dence jeopardised.
The States, North and South are supposed
to be displeased with the French intervention
in Mexico. The North speaks, but the South
is sil6nt. The North threatens, on the des-
truction of the revolution in the South, to
destroy the French in Mexico, and the British
elsewhere on the Continent, and establish a
republic one and indivisible from Panama to
the Polar Sea. Britain is to be punished for
not acknowledging the independence of the
South, and not sympathising with the North,
by the "united enemies," after they have
agreed on their new terms.
In the meantime President Lincoln is des-
cribed in the South as a fiend, but the fiend's
friends expect help from the South in their
future projects; while in the North candi-
dates for office describe themselves as for de-
vastation before dismemberment—death before
disunion, and talk as people do in Dahomey of
killing men, women, and children, to maintain
a political union.
Mere is fighting in Kentucky, without any
clear statement of gain or loss, and fighting
has occurred on the Mississippi rather to the
damage of the Federals. On the Potomac rests
two armies, tired of their recent slaughter,
and preparing early graves to some more
thousands among them, but of any real pro-
gress towards peace, there is none.
The Government of Peru borrowed some
money in London a few months ago. Now
we learn that the representatives of the Peru-
vians quarrel with the terms. They even talk
of refusing the money. For the first time in
monetary history; a South American State
thinks of refusing money.
An account of the King of Dahomey's doings
in a recent case of slaughtering has been pub-
lished by an eye witness. The King "sacri-
ficed " a large number of human beings, in
consequence of an earthquake, which origina-
ted he said in the grumbling of his fathers
spirit against the cessation of old killing cus-
toms. This black Calignla was not much
farther wrong in his science than some of the
professors in Cambridge, while he is an
apology for their errors.
The citizens of Bombay have collected
£15,000 for the relief of the Lancashire
operatives : the Chamber of Commerce at
Singapore have remitted nearly £1,200. The
collections for the same object in New South
Wales were said to be nearly £15,000 at the
,dates of the last mail.

Cotton continued to be shipped from Bom-
bay in large quantities. Australia, from Mel-
bourne round all the western coast, had been
exposed to a month of floods and heavy rain.
The shipments of gold had been again exten-
sive. South Australia has voted S-5,000 for
emigration.
The mails from the West Indies bring good
news generally of the crops, and notices of an
extended and extending cotton cultivation.
The North American Colonies have apparently
decided on a union of all the groupe, which
would bring together a population of over
31, perhaps nearly 4 millions.
The international railway has been recom-
mended by delegates from the three greater
colonies, and the British Government propose,
we believe, to guarantee the responsibility of
the colonies for three millions sterling, which
will be required in its construction.
A terrible accident has occurred on the
Edinburgh and Glasgow Railway, by the col-
lision of two passenger trains proceeding
from opposite directions, at a point on the
road then under repair, and where only one
line was available.

Seventeen deaths have occurred from the
collision, and more than one hundred persons
have been injnrei, nearly thirty of them in a
very serious manner. The deaths and injuries
are obviously traceable to the parsimony of
the company, who had only one person
engaged as pointsman. Their loss of
carriages, engines, and tenders, is said
to be from .E 5,000 to £6,000, and the addi-
tional loss in damages to injured persons and
the relatives of the slain. may, it is said.
reach £40,000 to £50,000; yet the outlay and
the risk from carelessness have not induced
companies to employ the necessary precautions
against the slaughter of their passengers.

THE ~ BEE-HIVE " AND TRADES'
POLITICS.

TWELVEMONTHS ago We commenced the
publication of the BEE-HIVE, with a statemen'
of the opinions that it was intended to pro-
mote. As an Organ of the Trades' Societies,
we necessarily intimated our purpose of advo:-
cating the rights of labour; but that is
general phrase assumed by different parties,
and ill-defined. In our case, other journals
defined it as the right to go idle, and strike
work. Their conductors professed to believe,
for they could not really suppose, that we
would advise our readers to impoverish them-
selves. The operation would not be for OUP
advantage; .and during the past year we have

,t
.o-

endeavoured rather to soften than to produce
difficulties between the employed classes and
their employers. This course consists with
the best interests of society, and with the in-
terests of our journal. We need readers who
can pay for a paper, and idle men cannot long
afford that little luxury.
_ _ _ _ _

We advocate a reduction in the hours of
labour, that men may have some time for at-
tention to the chief objects of existence. The
condition of many thousand persons among
the labouring classes, witnesseth the necessity
of urgent measures on this subject. The de-
mand for short time to clerks and shopkeepers,
so good and reasonable in itself, is also an
argument for short time to other men who
labour equally hard, and have the same neces-
sities for hours to attend to their families, or
to improve their minds, that undoubtedly
press on clerks and warehousemen; We are
not now to argue this question, in reference to
any class, but as a general principle we assert
that mankind were not born to work for ever,
and that all reductions which can be wisely
made in the hours of toil, are gains to the
cause of intelligence, morality, religion, do-
mestic and social order. So we support all
means of reducing these hours that can
be effectual without also reducing the amount
of work.

Strikes are always evils, although they may
be, as they often , have been, necessary evils.
Some parties say that they are always defeated,
but no greater error, and none more opposed
to facts, could be promulgated. Many of
them, perhaps a great majority of them, hav4
been successful in the achievement of their
object, and that has been generally the preven-
tion of some proposed invasion of pre-existing
regulations. Strikes are proceedings in the
nature of industrial hostilities, and the power
of levying them may have been much more
useful than its absolute exercise, in preventing
schemes which would without that power have
ere now greatly abridged wages, and extended
the daily period of work.
Having asserted the right, and the benefits
which have accrued from the right, in the ac-
complishment of some objects and the preven-
tion of evil purposes, we hesitate not to give
an emphatic preference to industrial tribunals.
We allege that all disputes between the em-
ployed and the employers might be peaceably
and satisfactorily adjusted by the intervention
of official tribunals, and their decision would
certainly have an influence on all parties of a
character both influential and "wholesome."
We seek the establishment of some such plan,
butsit is always delayed, opposed, or postponed,
by the friends of competition.
It is possible to carry competition into
oppression, and thus render it the cause of
immense evil. "Labour is a commodity."
This is the dogma of a sect. But labour is
not a commodity, or to be regarded as a com-
modity, except in a greatly restricted sense.
Labour is connected with the labourer, who is
entitled to all the consideration of a human
being, with great interests to be lost or
won. Competition may be pressed against
labour to destroy or peril these interests,
and then it becomes an evil and a cause
of much sin. Labour is no more a commodity
than the labourer is a chattel. The dogma, like
many others, is a mistake. It rests at the root
of slavery and the slave system; because
labour is really the labourer's life, or the means
of extending and maintaining life, and if a
man's entire time be consumed by the means
of living he cannot advance the great objects
and purposes of life.
We believe that some limit must be placed
on competition, and for that reason we are un-
able to follow one school of political economy
through all its extreme views respecting la-
bour and its productions, but the school begins
to turn back, unable to carry its own notions
out to the extreme point without suffering
from its own opinions when put into practice.
The people of this country are not com-
pelled to engage in any urgent competition for
wages or work. Their territories produce all
the commodities that they require; compre-
hending one fourth or one third part of the
world, not restricted to any particular des-
cription of climate or of soil, but embracing all
descriptions of both in an abundance ample to
support ten times the present population, and if
these colonial resources were properly elicited
and employed, neither labour nor capital could
want employment in the British empire for
several centuries to come.

Their neglect in a single department has
been followed by the existing calamity to la-
bour in the cotton districts, and in a brief
period this stroke must be felt by the capital-
ists engaged in that trade. Common foresight
should have prevented the existing misery.
Our manufacturers needed not to depend for
cotton on one quarter of the world. The plant
grows with great facility in many countries.
Our West Indian islands can produce two
crops annually, and the growers can have no
dread of frosts; while we possess more cotton
growing soil lying waste than any other two
or three nations.

The present catastrophe is merely a conse-
quence of bad government and bad manage-
ment. As the Manchester school declared
that a government should not interfere even
to provide for the employment of its subjects;
a necessity was more obviously placed upon
its members to manage that great trade of
theirs so as to prevent or provide against
the calamity which has occurred. They have
neglected to show by the excellence of their
practice, the excellence of their theory-, and
others now fall back on the old opinion, that a
government may greatly and wisely encourage
all means to employ its own people, and elicit
the resources of its own territories, without
actual trading. The 'absolute and cold neglect
of that and many other measures essential to
social prosperity leaves us little hope for the
future from the experience of the past, except
in great political changes.

articles.title: ORGANIC REFORM
articles.text:
ORGANIC REFORM

MEANS restoration not revolution. It should
be described as conservative and not destruc—
tive. It is only a retreat upon the wisdom of
our ancestors. The Saxon Parliament was
based on a wide suffrage once; we need its re-
establishment on a wide suffrage again. The
Commons House of Parliament has outgrown
the origin of its name, and is not much less
monetary and patrician than the Peers. Like
justice, or the London Tavern, it is open to
any person who may be elected and has money
to parthe cost. Qualification by opinion, or
even by property, has ceasee-to. be nominally
essential, but the qualification of mOney is still
absolutely necessary. The monetary power
alone is represented, aud intelligence is care-
fully ignored. f:t counts for no more than
physical strength ; and*mind," and "matter,"
are treated in the same manner, unless the
" matter " be money.
Autumn is drawing towards its end, and
the autumnal meetings of constituencies and
their members are nearly also at an end,
,butithey have produced nothing whatever re-
specting reform—GARIBA.LDI has been often

mentioned. Italy has been discussed. France
has been blamed. The hostilities of the two
sets of States have been deplored. But little
or nothing has been said respecting reform;
except when some member, bolder than his
fellows, expressed his gratitude that we were
not in the position of the States.

The oppo-nents of reform have made capital
out of the States. As if another war had
never wrecked a fair province until this wast-
ing of Virginia, we are told to be thankful for
deliverance from ourselves, our sins, and temp-
tations, our love of killing and being killed,
our lust of power, our search for victory. These
politicans talk and write as if even now Cain
was killing Abel on the banks of the Potomac,
or as if they heard for the first time the impu-
dent answer to a solemn question, "Am I my
brother's keeper ?"
Hypocrisy in this matter feeds on a mis-
take. Some friends of reform quoted the
States as examples; it was an errcr, but
more than it deserved is made of the error.
We regret the bloodshed there since the spring
time of 1861; but blood has been, shed in
torrents elsewhere, by aristocracies and kings,
constitutional and unconstitutional, and the
example of the States makes for or against
reform in our island.

The sanatory and social reforms essential to
the well-being of our State. will not be speedily
accomplished without organic reform in the
Legislature. Each measure, however small
in promise of good to come; has to be
torn from the fangs of opponents. No
legislation went so rapidly through the last
session of Parliament as the error regarding
poachers. This system of hard-fighting for
every inch of ground is costly, and it would
not be necessary with a more extended repre-
sentation. Errors would be committed, as
they are committed now, but they would be
more rapidly correded. Objections are of
course pleaded against reform, but they only
originate, if they be reasonable and sound, in
the inadequacy of the present system to do
the requisite work. Each colourable objection
is an argument against standing still, for all of
them exist from circumstances inflicted or neg-
lected by the Government.
We know not how any half measures are to
be defended. When we advocate some re-
stricted scheme it is only an assertion that
those beyond the line are unqualified people.
In that course we assert that if a few more
persons should be let in, a great many other
persons should be kept out.
Reform must stand on a manhood suffrage.
Manhood itself may be fixed at twenty-one,
eighteen, or twenty-five. The line is an expe-
diency, not involving principle. If it be equi-
tably struck it cannot fall far wrong; and our
business is to see that the franchise rests some-
how—on the man not on his property. The
people have played with this subject: deluded
with promises they have hoped and waited, and
they have not wrought. But until they
assert and carry a manhood suffrage, on
equality of representation, protected by some
mode of independent voting, generations
will come and go, and misery will be at home
in the land, and all efforts at moral and poli-
tical improvements will be met, as they have
been met, by the progress of evils that they
were meant to control; and even now and
then agreat starvation will be met by a subscrip• •
tion munificent and inadequate for its pur-
pose. Because we cannot hope that great
measures of intellectual and moral improve-
ment can be carried without it, we are to seek
hereafter as we have sought before, a complete
organic reform.

articles.title: COIL MINERS' STRIKES.
articles.text:
COIL MINERS' STRIKES.

Another coal strib ? when are we to have done
with them ? our readers may well ask, and the his-
tory of the one now on in Lancashire, and the other
in Yorkshire, may perhaps give us a clue to the cause
and the remedy. The coil trade is peculiar in cer-
tain respects, and' in its phenomena we see in the
' oldest and barest forms, the working of selfisht,ess,
and of arrangements most interesting to the geniune
political economist. With the progress of demand,
partly attendant, and partly causing the rise of our
manufacturing system, the coal trade has had to
vary considerably, both in its mode of operation in
working, and in the ways and scale of wages, and
no where has capital been more attentive to its own
interests, or more successful in obtaining wealth.
Previously to the mining act of 1853, the capitalists
had labour completely under their control, and how
that control was exercised, let the reports of the
commissioners prove. Women, girls, and children,
working horse work in -mines, nearly naked, at all
hours, was a revelatipn so shocking to the common
humanity of the nation, that he law stepped in and
stopped it, contrapy to all " free trade principles,"
but to the very great advantage of all concerned.
This, and other arrangements,. modified both work-

ing and wages; and yet, to ibis day, the scale of pay
in the colliery districts is less fixed, and less amen-
able to a common standard, than perhaps any other
employment known of. The old theory of wages
depended upon measure, and the men were paid for
tubs and corves by number. In this way, however,
the course of each party "doing the best for them-
selves," led, as usual, to an immense amount of
trickery and cheating. The men packed the corves
and the masters "docked the tubs. At length the
masters, to check fraud on the part of the men,
began to establish pay by weight; but they still
sold by measure. In this selling measure, by guess,
of course mistakes might easily be made, and the
writer who for many years received three corves for
a ton of coal, found, on weighing, their was never
more than 11 cwt. instead of 21. When men have
unchecked their own interest to look to, it is easy to
say which way the guess will run. In this case the
guess ran against the customer, and too little was
given. In the case of weighing from the men, as
the employer appoints the weighman, we may guess
that the opposite inistake is likely to be made. In
order to check this tendency, the miners had a clause
inserted in the weighing clause, to the effect, that
the men might, at their own cost, appoint a person
to check the weights, in order to obtain fair play;
and to which the employers added, as a rider, that
he must be a person ordinarily employed upon the
premises. This was done to cut out "demagogues ;"
and how this is worked we will afterwards tell. In
the Barnsley district, where the colliers have ken
notoriously " chisseled " • weight, if the men
appoint a weigliman, the ::•
,turn him off, and
then they can refuse his e at the pit. And
thus " honourable " de the act. The
result is, at the same pit W ustorners had short
weight sold to them, and itlite same prices, the
men on checking obtained directly twenty per cent
increase of wage ! But of course that was owing to
the little mistakes of the weighman—indeed he ,
said so—for the masters were " all honourable men."l
It should be understood, in this way, a man who
began some thirty years ago a simple workman,
and who became manager, and then, by the death of
the capitalist employer, fell into mastership—died
a year or to ago worth sixty or seventy thousand
pounds ! How he got to ride in his two horsed
carriage, and to have his shooting manors in Scot•
land, is not difficult to guess. But as coal is sold
by weight, and may be checked—and as the men
check the4Weighing—it is found out that coal does
not now pay. True, coal ha! risen near 100 per
cent, during the last ten years, and wages perhaps
25, but still it does not pay so well as it did a few

years ago. And so we have an attempt to reduce
wages. Of course when all other modes of grinding
fail, this can always be fallen back upon. In the
case instanced—tried on not an hundred miles from
merry Wakefield—(by the \vay a much less merry
place than when Goldsmith's vicar lived) the reduc-
tion is proposed in a new form. The men are paid
for getting coal 13d. per score all round, large and
' small alike, but as large coal is worth 50 per cent.
more than small, the scale is altered to 15d. per
score large, and 9d. for small. This is done to
induce more labour to get the coal large. This
, can be done ; but the work is so much harder, and
! takes longer time, that the men say it will make a
!difference of from 15 to 30 per cent. reduction to
their wages. At Wigan a certain nobleman's
!steward halved the seal.; of rise and fall ; but the
men affirm still it is so considerable a reduction in
effect that they will not accept the terms. In th:
other case the men refused the terms, and as the
! master would not give way, and refused to talk with
, their deputation, they left the pit, to the number o
!s!tme 150 ; and are so out on what is called a
strike. But it is clearly not, a strike of the men—
it is the master who has struck against them.
Another popular error may be also corrected by
this strike. The men had no union. No " dema-
gogue" urged them on "to attack a tyrant." They
had no " illiterate stump," " living out of their
hard earned wages, and who, to maintain his leech-
sucking hold upon their blood and marrow, stirred
them up to dhcontent and rebellion." In both
cases, i.e., Lancashire and Yorkshire, the employers
have unions—and in neither case had the men any
union at all. The employers may, however, soon
contrive ne, for the men flock together at once like
sheep when a strange dog encroaches upon their
pasture. Only, as in this case, the men strike,
and then form a union. Funds are to subscribe
when they should be subscribed. All experienced
in actual detail know that working men have no
abstract love for unions, and no liking to pay to
demagogue or defender. It is necessity, sheer
down right pressing, and no mistake as to pres-
514172, that compels them to unite and pay for self-
defence and for class interest. And without such
unity, they know too well, at whatever cost to
maintain, it would cost them far more to quietly
submit to all the capitalist would dictate. In this
case a subscription of 2d. per week would have
ch; eked the possibility of a ,oss of shillings a week
per man. The fact is, the operatives are in fault
for not foreseeing the evil day of reduction—a.4ay
which would rarely come, if ample funds were;pre-
pared beforehand to meet the contingency. of. a
strike. In the meantime, we place these,. facts
before our readers, and bid them ask themselves,
with the pressure of capital to contend :against,
whether it is not better to unite, and ,fiay.for
defeitee, than to rest contented to be crushed.,,,'
AGRICULTURAL LA BO U
TO THE EDITOR OF THE " REE- HlVe'

that evince a little interest in the agricultural
labourers, be encouraged to do better by credit for
good designs. If their members, and the land-
owners especially among them, could only be per-
suaded to supply cottages with a small allotment or
ground attached to each of them, they would take
the right course to cut down poor rates. All the
cottages of Buckinghamshire, and other shires, might
have a 1-irge kitchen garden attached to each of
them. It would occupy pleasantly and profitably
an idle day or a leisure hour; and increase the
comfort of famires and the resources of the country,
which I suppose depend upon the money that
families can make. Agiicultural cottages might
have lots of small fruit clustering round them, and
the young children trained to be neat and trim by
an hour's weeding in plots full of vegetables, twice
or thrice a week, aud the result woold be as good
as " rent free" to the family, and a great deal
better too, for it would be "rent paid pleasantly
from odds and ends. I observed by the newspapers
of last summer, that the two Houses of Parliament
were greatly concerned for poachers and their
punishment. From whence rise poachers and
poaching? Idleness and want make them. If
every cottage had half an acre—at least a half acre
of ground attached—to be employed as a kitchen
garden for the productioa and sale of such vege-
tables as could be profitably raised in the 1 icality,
each cottager's wife would have a great help given
to the sinsli amount of money she must now con-
trive to do with; and each cottage would have a
poaching barometer planted rotted it; for the
garden carefully cultivated would be an unmistake-
able certificate that no poaching was done there.

EVELYN LEE.

articles.title: LATEST INTELLIGENCE.
articles.text:
LATEST INTELLIGENCE.

THE GARIBALDI CITY MEETING.

SIR,—I see by the papers that Mr. Disraeli
has been taken to task by a Mr. Walters for giving
or supefintending the giving of small sums to farm
labourers who have lived a long time without
being very had, or doing anything to trouble the
police or the Poor Law Guardians. Negatives or
that description deserve encouragement, and this
Mr.. Walters, whoever he may be, should be
ashamed of himself for quarrelling with gentlemc
who having a cro, n or two to spare bestow them
on these curious 'antiques. In our days- of railway
travelling, it must refresh a good man's wind to
meet one of the old school, who never did travel,
but kept his place, pleased with the bacon and beer
or hi?. own parish. Men of that contented spirit
must be so scarce that they could make something
, good by going into a menagerie for exhibition with

TRADES' INTELLIGENCE.

ESTABLISHMENT OF 'THE EA.ST LANCA-
SHIRE CEN ['RAI OPERATIVES' RELIEF
COM NIITTEE.'

On Saturday afternoon, a public meeting was .held
in the Oddfelloxvs' Hall, Padiham, to establish The
East Lancashire Central Operatives' Relief Committee.'
The hall was crowded, the audience mainly consisting
of heads of families. There was also a goodly sprink-
ling of respectably attired females. Mr. John Howaith
was called to the chair. After alluding to the wide
spread and deeply rooted distress consequent upon the
cotton famine, he described the meansof relief as being
inadequate to the physical wants of a population who
had been compelled to become unwilling idlers.
Relief Committees and Boards of Guardians combined
did not give enough to appease the hunger of the
people, and they hoped to supply the deficiency by the
establishment of another fund which should suz-,plo-
ment other modes of relief.
The Rev. E. A. Verity, rector of Habergham, was
most cordially received. He said the object of his
appearing before them that [afternoon was to inaugu-
rate the establishment of an important fund, to be
raised on behalf of the distressed operatives of East
Lancashire, to explain as far as possible the objects
and aims of the committee, and to show the necessity,
for its existence. Its head quarters would be in Padi-
ham, and it would bear the title of The East Lanci-
shire Central Operatives' Relief Committee.' (He.ar,
hear.) It had already branches at Elabergham anu
Burnley. Those branches were represented there that
night, and they hoped to extend their operations and
to create other branch committees, as its funds in-
creased, in the adjoining towns of Colne, Accrington,
Church, Enfield, Bacup, Harwood, Over Darwen, and
Blackburn. In the district they proposed to help there
was a population of 200,000, 69,000 of whom were out
Of employment, and 26,000 were working short time.
The weekly wages last year was about £45,000. The
relief administered was only £5,640, viz., £4,000 given
by the Poor Law Guardians and £i,64oby the various
local relief committees. (Hear, hear.) He main-
tained that there was plenty of room for others to step
in and aid the existing efforts put forth to arrest the
appalling tide of indigency. (Hear, hear, and ap-
plause.) Their object was not to supplant or in any
way obstruct the action of those bodies already formed
for the relief of the poor; but, on the other hand, to
supplement those efforts, and with the funds at their
disposal to extend relief where the resources of others
might be found to fall short. (Fiear, hear.)
The Central Operatives' Committee were a respect.
able body of working men, holding all shades
of political and religious opinions. They were influ-
enced solely by feelings of benevolence. (Hear.)
From all other relief committees the working man was
carefully excluded (with the exception of the Salford
Provident Working Man's Association), as though his
presence was unworthy, or, as Sir J. P. K. Shuttle-
worth said, insignificant.' (Laughter and Hear,
hear.') Earls, baronets, lords, and merchants, gentle-
men, and manufacturers were to be found, but not
working men. Why was it? Of all classes they
believed the factory operatives best qualified for
the duties of distribution, whether in respect to condi-
tion intelligence, or feeling. (Hear, hear.) In the
firseplace, the position of the workman enabled him
personally to know and intelligently to understand
the, nature and extent of the operatives' destitution.
(Applause.) In the second place, the operatives were
not animated by any considerations of interest, as em-
ployers of labour generally were, in estimating the
amount of relief; and in the third place, the working
man was better fitted to act upon relief committees which
had for their object the interest of the poor, because he
had a warmer heart and deeper fellow-feeling towards the
destitute, inasmuch as he better comprehended the
trials, crosses' and difficulties of a poor man's life.
(Applause.) It was his further conviction that if,
at the commencement of the crisis, the present Boards
of Guardians had been supplanted, and working men
of respectability and character had been elected in
their place, there would have been no fear of adequate
relief being given, and no need of private charity from
any source. (Rear, hear.) He proceeded to give
several instances of the inefficiency of the existing
relief committee. For instance, they had sent as
much as £l,OOO to Rochdale and Blackburn, towns
which, from their wealth and importance, ought never
to have solicited aid at all; far Rochdale could con-
tribute £50,000 and Blackburn £lOO,OOO, if millowners
were disposed to d) so. How different was that state
of things from Bacup, Rawtenstall, and the adjacent
valleys, where co-operation, the spirit of independence
among working classes was screaming for help. To
those places, where independent support was asked
for, only a few hundred pounds had been sent. (Hear,
hear, and applause.) Thus the flower of industrious
manhood was suffered to droop unaided and perish in
pauperism, through the want of that practical element
whichlhad been included in the East Lancashire
Central Committee, namely, the operative element.
VI He was speaking advisedly when he openly and plainly
stated that it was the will of their gracious Queen—
that it was the wish of the whole kingdom—that Lan-
cashire men should retain their homes, their house-
hold farniture, their social character and position, and
be maintained by the law of the land in health and
comfort until better times should come. (Loud clap-
ping of hands.) There was too much strictness ex
ercised in many instances amounting to cruelty. The
other day he heard that the sum of two pence was de-
ducted by a relieving,' officer out of the weekly allowance
of a poor operative, because he had received that small
sum for holding a gentleman's horse for a few
minutes.' (Cries of Shame, shame,' and derisive
cheering.) Another poor woman had had is. 6d. de-
ducted, because she had earned that sum at a sewing
school. (Cries of Shame?) Those were acts which
indicated an obtusity of intellect on the part of these
committees, confounding as they must be—the factory
operative with the ordinary tramp. Those were the
principles of the E tst Lancashire Central. Their
motto was that the most efficient means of relieving
the poor was through a committee of working men,
and not through employers. (Cheers.) They did
not affirm that employers had not the ability, dis-
position, and spirit to dispense relief, but they ob-
jected to their interests which were opposed. to
their dispositions, and they, all knew the failing of
human nature, which was to lean to the dictates ot the
pocket—(Hear, hear)—and not of the heart. A more
important and far more interesting feature in the cha-
racter of the East Lancashire Central was that it
proposed to draw its funds not from the upper or
the middle classes of society, but from the working
men. It appealed to the working classes of England,
Ireland, and Scotland; to Englishmen abroal as well
as at home. To benevolent societies, such as the Odd-
fellows' Druids, Foresters Gardeners, Mechanics, &c.,
and to trade societies, such as the engineers, colliers,
silk weavers, potters, glass blowers, nailmakers, Shef-
field trades, and wool cumbers. From all those and a
thousand others it was proposed to draw their re-
sources. Already a handsome sum had arrived, which
would be divided and dispensed the following week at
Padiham, Habergham, and Burnley, where committees
were already formed, and they hoped to real se such a
Stun as would cheer the hearts and comfort the homes
of many a distressed family in that town. The rev.
gentleman concluded by stating that a weekly state-
ment should be made of all receipts and disbursements.
The resolution for the establishment of the association
was carried unanimously, and the central committee
and officers were at once appointed. Mr. Wilkinson
was elected as treasurer, by si horn subscriptions will
be received. The committee will meet daily at Speak-
buildings, Burnley-road, Padiham.

articles.title: OPERATIVE TAILORS.
articles.text:
OPERATIVE TAILORS.

On Thursday night -
a meeting of journeymen tailors
was held in Phoenix Hall, Edinburgh, Mr. Paterson
presiding. The meeting was called for the purpose of a
report
hearing by the Trade Union Committee on
the present rate
Of wages in Edinburgh, and recom-
mending the men generally to support the Society in
their attempts to induce the masters to recognise an
uniform scale of prices. The Society at present num-
bers 504 members, and has a slim of £204 on hand,
but they,
,do not feel themselves authorised in taking
such measures without larger support. After consider-
able discussion, the meeting pledged itself to support
the Society in their endeavour
to draw up a scales of
prices and obtain the sanction of the masters. The
hall was well filled.
On Tuesday, a tailor of the name of John Fallon,
was brought before the Leeds magistrates on a charge
of intimidation and assault. The case arose out of a.
recent dispute between Messrs. J*. Wales Smith and
Son, tailors, and their workmen. They to the number
of :43 had turned out on strike. The defendant had
assaulted and threatened a workman named Williams,
and he had to answer a second charge brought by a
man named Carroll. The prisoner was sentenced to
two months' imprisonment with hard labour. Notice
f appeal was given.

MIDDLESEX SESSIONS.

THE CASE OF STEPHEN EDWARD MRANRY.

On the application of Mr. Dickie, Stephen Edward
Meaney, convicted at the last session, was placed in
the dock before Mr. Bodkin, the assistantjudge.
The Assistant Judge said he had been consulted on
this case by Mr. Payne, and having given it some
consideration he had determined to submit a case upon
it to the Court of Criminal Appeal. He did not wish
to detain the prisoner in custody until the question was
decided, and therefore would allow him to be released
on his entering into his own recognizances in the sum
of £BO, and to find two substantial sureties in the sum
of £4O each, for his appearance at the session after the
next held here, to receive judgment if called upon,
after the question had been submitted to a court of
appeal.
As it was required that the prisoner should give
twenty-four hours' notice of the bail he proposed, he
was removed from the dock to the cell below.

POLICE INTELLIGENCE.

GUILDHALL.

INJURY TO A CAB.—John Hodges, 44, describing
himself as a cook at the London Coffee-house, Ludgate-
hill, was charged before Mr. Alderman Allen with
wilfully cutting the lining of a Hansom cab. Joseph
Hervey, a cab-driver, said that he was engaged by the
defendant last evening to carry him from the other
side of Notting-hill-gate to Ludgate-hill; not anything
was said about the fare. On passing through the gate
he gave a florin for the toll, and desired him (com-
plainant) to keep the change of is. 9d. This was
done, and on reaching St. Paul's defendant alighted
and said Good night,' and was walking away, when
9d. more was demanded of him. The claim being
disputed they proceeded to the station-house, and on
leaving it they discovered that the squab and other
portions of the cab lining had been cut in a most mis-
chievous manner. The damage done amounted to 50s.
The prisoner was ordered to pay that amount, or suffer
one month's imprisonment.
BO W -STREET.

ANTIQUARIES AT FAULT.--James Smith and Wlfl.
Aiken, dressed as labourers, were charged with ob-
taining money on false pretences from Mr. Holland, a
broker, in Portugal-street. On several occasions
prosecutor had purchased from the defendants various
articles which they said they had picked up while at
work at Hungerford Market upon the new railway
terminus. There were two little images of saints and
a medal, for which he gave 35.. and for two other
images be gave lie. 6d. He afterwards sent them to
the British Museum, where he was told they were
forgeries.—The defendants said all they told the com-
plainant was, that they had got the articles from some
of the men at work in Hungerford Market, but they
never said they were at work themselves.—Smith
observed that the complainant no doubt expected to
get £3O or £4O by the articles, and if he could have
made anything by the bargain, nothing would have
been heard of the case.—Mr. Corrie thought he could
not make it a criminal offence, and the case must be
dismissed.

THE UNPROTECTED FKILILE' AND

TILE C.AB-WAN.

On Monday, at Westminster Police-court, Mrs.
Piers, a lady apparently 70 years of age, who was
stated to be staying at the Great Western Motel, was
summoned for 61. cab fare.
Henry Charles Kemenenhoe, the cab driver, said he
carried the lady from the Great Western to 13, Craven-
street, Strand, and thence to King's road, Chelsea,
after a deviation on the route at her request. Directly
after she left the house in Craven-street he pulled up
at her request and took a message back to the house,
in doing which he picked up a portemonnaie cm the
pavement, and taking it to the lady in the cab she
owned it, and said she would handsomely reward him
for his honesty. When she discharged him she gave
him 2s. 6d. for his fare and is. for his honesty. He
put the latter to the former, and then found that she
still owed him 6d., as his fare was 31. for distance
and is. for time, but she refused to give him any
more.
The lady, who sat in the prisoner's dock by accident,
went through the details of the j mrney in a rich clear
voice, differing with the complainant only regarding
the amount of time occupied, and stating that she
gave him his full fare, although he had falsely
stated otherwise. She described his finding and
bringing her her portemonnaie, as he himself had
stated it.
Mr. Dayman : The cabman appears to have made
out a legal claim.
The Lady: 1 have been in London some time, and
I've had. a great deal to do with these cabmen. At
first I hired one by time, and I honestly told him so,
when he drove me into a gutter, and crawled
on at the pace of three miles an hour. I asked him to
go faster, when he told me he wasn't bound to go
more than four miles an hour by Act of Parliament,
and had the impudence to say he was doing all that.
I have sat behind four horses half my life, and I know
'what pace is. I tried another, and he was as great a
crawler; he did not do mere than two miles an hour,
so I left him and got another, but I was no better off.
lam no girl -A* 17. I understand these cabmen, 80 I
determined for the future not to say a word about time
when I got in, but pay according to it afterwards.
Mr. Dayman : The driver makes his distance to
exceed five miles. - . -

The Lady: I have nothing to do with distance.
Distance is nothing to me. I don't travel in cabs by
distance.
Mr. Dayman : If you do not engage him by time he
may charge the distance he carries you.
The Lady,: I beg your pardon, he can do no such
thing. I know better.
Mr. Dayman : Then I am wrong.
The Lady: Yes, you are. I have my wits about
me. I know what lam doing. You are quite wrong.
You wn see a letter in the papers in about a fort-
night's time, stating how lam used. You will find it
signed, An Unprotected Female;' not that I want
any protection. I can take care of myself.
Mr. Dayman read the clause in the Act of Parlia-
ment showing that it was at the option of the driver
to charge by time or distance, unless expressly engaged
by the former before starting, and inquired whether
'she had entered into any such engagement.

Tne Lady: Not I, indeed!
Mr. Dayman : If you dispute the distance you can
have it measured.
The Lady: A fine notion, indeed, for me to sit here
while half London is being measured!
Mr. Dayman : It is not necessary you should remain
here while it is measured. Will you have it mea-
sured ?
The Lady: Not I, indeed. I have nothing to do
with distances. I have paid him all his fare and gave
him a little present besides. He could not have stop-
ped the time, he says, and his time of starting is

wrong.
Mr. D tyman : He has made out his case.
The Lady. I don't care what he says. I know I
am right. Axe you Mr. Dayman? Pray answer me.
Mr. Dayman: Why do yoa ask?
The Lady: I met you at Mr. Landell's some years
ago.
Mr. Dayman: Indeed you are mistaken.
The Lady I don't think I can be, the name is so
familiar to me. You must be the Mr. Dayman.
Mr. Dayman : But rE,ally I am not.
The complainant said he was a very poor man with
a family, and as he had wasted much time over this
complaint he hoped the magistrate would give him
full costs.
Mr. Dayman ordered the lady to pay the 6d. and ss.
costs.
The lady became very indignant at the decision,
but a friend who was with her paid the required
amount.

CTIRISTIAN SOCIETY OF OPERATIVE SILK WEAVERS.
—On Monday evening, October 13, an oration was
delivered in aid of the funds of the above society at
Commercial-road Chapel, by Mr. Allen Carr, on the
subject of Hearts and Homes.' The Rev. T. Goadby,
8.A., the minister of the chapel, presided. In his
opening remarks the chairman, on mentioning the
claims this society had upon the notice of the benevolent,
enumerated the particular agencies it sustained for
doing good, and gave expression to his sympathy with
its objects.
DEERFOOT DEFEATED.—On Monday afternoon a ten-
mile race took place on the Newmarket road Ground,
Norwich, between Brighton, the Norwich milkboy,'
and Deerfoot, the &meet Indian. The prize was a
cup of the value of £3O; and the match attracted a
considerable attendance. After a well sustained ma-
tt*, Brighton gained a decided advantage towards the
'cltse, and won by some fifty yards. The ten miles
were run in 64 minutes 30 seconds.

articles.title: CO-OPERATIVE INTELLI-
articles.text:
CO-OPERATIVE INTELLI-

GENCE.

REFUSAL OF RELIEF TO SHAREHOLDERS IN Co-OPE-
RATIVE SOCIETIES. —As the poor law guardians will not
relieve any person in the cotton localities who bolds
any share or shares in any manufacturing or other
company, nor give them any relief at the soup kitchen,
a meeting of shareholders in the Bacup society was
called on Monday last, to devise some means whereby
food may be obtained, as it is impossible to sell the
shares at present, and the scrips are of little use to the
inner man. The following resolution was passed
'That a committee be appointed out of the different
companies, who shall borrow money at five per cent.,
the shareholders to borrow from them at six per cent.,
and give their scrips for security.'
A COMPANY SUING ONE OF ITS OWN MEMBERS. —At
the county court, on l'hutsday, the Huddersfield Dis-
trict Manufacturing Company brought an action
against John Beevors, one of its own members, to re-
cover -£8 10s. 71. in respect of arrears of call upon
shares; but the plaintiffs were norsuited, after a
lengthy argumentation, on its being shown that legal
notice of the calls had not been served upon the de-
fendant.
BARNSLEY BRITISH CO- OPERATIVE SOCIETY.— The
second quarterly meeting of the above society was
held in the New Connection School-room, Market-
street, Barnsley, on Tuesday evening last, when Mr.
Carless presided. The balance-sheet was read by Mr.
G. Lawton, secretary. The report stated that during
the past quarter a profit of £27 9s id. had been
realised, from which interest at 5 per cent. per annum
and 10 per cent. on fixed stock, would be deducted.
A dividend of one shilling in the pound on members'
purchases was decided on. leaving £lO 14s. Ild, for
contingent purposes. Mr. Kay moved and Mr. Wood
seconded the adoption of the report, which was carried.
Votes of thanks to the chairman and the auditor, who
is about to leave, concluded the meeting.
DENHOLME. —The members of this branch of the
Queenshead Industrial Society, held a public tea party
and soiree in the Foresters' Hall, Denholme, on Satur-
day evening, when about 270 sat down to tea, after
which the cloth svas removed, and an entertainment
given. The platform was occupied by the Rev. J. F.
W. Eyre, the Rev. J. B. Grant, Messrs. J. Farnell,
R. Greenwood, of Queenshead, and the members of
the Denholme Philharmonic Society. Mr. John Bates,
of Queenshead, was in the chair, and in opening the
meeting expressed the pleasure he felt in seeing those
two rev. gentlemen, Mr. Eyre and Mr. Grant, amongst
them. Mr. Grant and Mr. Eyre each delivered excel-
lent and encouraging addresses. Other speeches fol-
lowed by Mr. Farnell and Mr. Greenwood. The
humorous delivery of the latter was duly appreciated.
Mrs. Akroyd and Mr. Steven Bottomley, each sung a
number of songs in good style; and the Philharmonic
Society performed at intervals some of their choicest
overtures. The hall was densely crowded. Towards
the close, a collection was made to assist the distressed
operatives in Lancashire, which realised £1 14s. id.
WARL-Ey.—The Warley branch of the Sswerby
Bridge Industrial Society held their annual tea meet-
ing in the large room of the May Pole Inn, on Satur-
day, the 4th inst., when upwards of 60 sat down.
After the cloth was withdrawn, Mr. Wm. Bowers was
called to the chair, who, in his opening remarks, por-
trayed in a very lucid manner the benefits to be
derived from co-operation, which met with a hearty
response. The next toast or sentiment given by the
chairman was 'Success to the Warley branch of the
Sowerby Bridge Industrial Society,' which was very
ably responded to by the secretary, Mr. Joseph Green-
wood, an old and much respected friend in the cause
of co-operation. The next toasts or sentiments given
were Success to the Sowerby Bridge Industrial
Society and the Sowerby Bridge United District Flour
Society, which were very ably responded to by Messrs.
J. Sutcliffe and Henry Broadbent, directors of the
above boards. The Warley amateur glee singers
were in attendance, and sung at intervals several
glees, due,tts, &e., which won for them repeated
encores.
FELLING CO- OBERATIVE SOCIETY.—The second annual
soiree of this society was held on Saturday evening in
the Infant School, at the Felling Chemical Works.
About 200 took tea, and in the evening a meeting was
held, Mr. Edward Smith, the treasurer of the society,
in the chair. The attendance was large, and all
appeared to take great interest in the success of their
flourishing establishment. A letter from Mr. Jos.
Cowen, jun., expressing his regret at being unable to
attend, was read. Mr. Redhead, the secretary, read
the annual report. At the commencement of the year
there were 68 shareholders, and during the year 29 had
been admitted, making a total of 97, but 12 having
withdrawn, 85 members remained, being an increase of
17 on the preceding year. The committee trusted that
more of the inhabitants of the district would avail
, themselves of the means offered for their advantage.
The treasurer's report showed for goods sold to mem-
bers during the year, 42,285. 6s. 4d.; to non-members,
£655 4s. 2d; total, £2.940 103. 6d. The expenditure
, for goods amounted to £2,616 7s. 11d., and after paying
• expenses, a balance of a 4s. sd. remained in band.
, The profits were £212 9s. 9d., and a dividend of
is. 11d, in the pound had been paid. During the
L evening Messrs. G. Gammage, M. Sheen, Jas. Weir,
, Jas. Ridley, Chas. Young, J. Jennings, W. Wade,
Archibald Wilson, and H. Hepburn took part in the
meeting, and suggestions were thrown out that a
• clothing establishment might be opened in connection
with the provision store.

WEST CRAMLINGTON CO- OPERATIVE STORE. The
quarterly meeting of the above society was held on
Saturday evening. Mr. M. Lowther, who was called
to the chair, briefly stated the business of the meeting,
and called on the secretary, Mr, Joseph Bell, to read
the report, which showed that the receipts for goods
for the quarter had been £1,271 19s being an in-
crease of £2OO over the preceding quarter. The
capital of the society had increased upwards of £lOO
after the payment of interest on all paid-up shares at
.5 per cent. per annum, and £3 for depreciation of
fixed stock and other expenses, a clear profit of
£95 13s. Vid. was left to be divided on members' pur-
chases, at 2s. Id. in the pound. The report also
showed that there had been thirty new members en-
rolled during the quarter, while three had withdrawn.
The premises of the society are now being raised
another storey higher, and the work is fast approach-
ing to completion, the result of which will materially
facilitate the business of the store. The transactions
of the committee gave the utmost satisfaction. The
proceedings terminated with a vote of thanks to the
chairman.
LEITH CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.—The third quarterly
meeting of the Leith Co-operative Society was held in
the Cordwainers' Hall, on Tuesday evening the 7th
Inst. The report showed that £1,207 18s. had been
drawn during the past quarter for goods sold, on which
a clear profit of £l9 6s. si-d. had been realised. A
dividend of is. id. per pound to shareholders, and
60. to non-shareholders, was declared upon purchases
for the past three quarters—the sales during the first
quarter being £769 Bs. 6d ; second quarter, £1,027
2s. 6d.; thidquarter, £1,207 18s.; total, £3,004 95.;
profit on total, £95 118. 21d. This society having
resolved to sell their bread at a price that would just
cover the expenses, have voluntarily relinquished a
profit of at least £67 3s. id., which would have given
a sum of £152 14s. 31. avaiahle for dividend. The
average sale of bread has been 1,521 41b. loaves weekly
—and a total of 27,434 since the commencement. The
committee has evcry reason to believe that the society
is gaining ground in public estimation.
DUNSTON CO. OPERATIVE STORE.-0/1 Saturday the
quarterly meeting of the members of this store was
held in the long room of Mr. John Fulthorp's, Black-
smith's Arms. The chair was taken by Mr. William
Foster, when the Secretary read the report, which was
unanimously adopted and confirmed. The society
now numbers 104 members, and has a capital of £340.
The sales at the store the present quarter have
exceeded those of the last by upwards of £99. Twelve
new member. have been enrolled during the quarter.
A. new store is about to be built, the old one being far
too small. After paying 5 per cent. on paid-up shares
and is. 9d. in the pound, there is left a balance of
£1 Os. 6J. for deprecation of fixed stock. After a
cordial vote of' thanks to Mr. Fulthorp and the officers
and shopman of the store, the company separated.
GATESHEAD INDUSTRIAL CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY_ —On
retsehrel
ay d eilerrti. nkr
Wednesday evening, October 8, the members held
tlacheoiruio fthrn, zat
in the Nelson-street
X. Fletcher in the chair.
From the balance sheet read by the secretary (Mr.
srfio
Wm. Lyall), it appeared that the £lOO. borrowed at
the commencement of the society, had been repaid.
' Sales for the quarter £877 12s. 3d., being an increase
on the previous quarter—the profit on which, after
paying all expenses, enabled the committee to reduce
the fixed stock account £4 2s. 10d., and declare a divi-
dend of is. 61 in the pound on members' purchases.
The members were informed that the rules of the
society would require some revision in. conformity with
the act passed last session, and that the matter would
be brought under their notice at an early period. After
arranging for a social tea and soiree, to be held at the
end of the year, and the usual votes of thanks to trea-
surer, committee, auditors, and chairman, the meeting
broke up highly pleased with the evening's proceed-
ings.

FRIENDLY OPERATIVE CARPENTERS AND JOINERS'
Socirry or GREAT BRITAIN.—The 36th annual report
of this society has been published. It appears that
the number of lodges is 72, distributed throughout the
country, principally in the north and north-western
districts, comprising 3,786 members. The amount
paid in strikes during the year has been £984 Bs. 6d.

articles.title: FRIENDLY SOCIETIES.
articles.text:
FRIENDLY SOCIETIES.

Under this head we desire to record all movements
connected with Freemasonry, Forestry, Oddfellow-
ship, Druidism, Old Friends, &c., and shall feel
obliged by Secretaries or Alembers of Courts and
Lodges furnishing us with any information. A
gentleman from our office will attend any meeting
or dinner of the above, where publicity is thought
desirable, on receiving a card or circular of invita-
tion.]

articles.title: FREEMASONS.
articles.text:
FREEMASONS.

The Provincial Grand Lodge for the North and
East-ridings of Yorkshire, was held at the Humber
Lodge, in Osborne-street, on Wednesday afternoon.
The Right Hon. the Earl of Zetland, Host Worshipful
Grand Master, who was prevented attending, was ably
represented by the R. W. Brother George Marwood,
Deputy-prov. G.M. There was a large attendance .of
influential masons from every part of the province.
['he lodge was opened by the Worshipful Brother
Coatswoith, master of the Humber Lodge, and P.G.S.D.
Several matters were discussed respecting the great
progress of masonry in the province, and projects
entered into to extend the benevolent purposes of the
craft. After the Provincial Grand Lodge business
was transacted the lodge was closed by Brother Coats-
worth and the officers of the Humber Lodge. A grand
banquet was held in the evening, at the Royal Station
Hotel, which was attended by a larger number of
brethren than for many years past. The whole pro
ceedings passed off with the greatest harmony and
satisfaction, and too much credit cannot be given to
the W.M. of the Humber Lodge, and also to Mr.
Holliday, who provided the banquet.

ODDFELLOWS.—(MANCHnSTER UNITY.)
The Order of Independent Oddfellows (Manchester
Unity) are getting tip a fund in aid of the operatives
of Lancashire and Cheshire, who have been plunged
into distress by the cotton famine. We are glad to
hear that the appeal has already been responded to,
and that as much as £6OO has found its way to the
hands of Mr. Henry Ratcliffe, the secretary at Man-
chester. The same Order of Odd Fellows raised
£2,000 for the famine in Ireland, and £2,500 for the
Crimean fund; but in the present case a large num-
ber of members, it must be borne in mind, are recipients
of, rather than contributors to, the relief required.
The Odd Fellows will probably do well if they raise
£l,OOO.
IMPORTANT TO SECILETARIES.-Mr. E. Blount, the
secretary of the Sir William Wallace Lodge of Odd
Fello vvs, held at the Royal Tent tavern, near Golden-
square, was summoned, at the Marlborough-street
Police Court on Monday, for neglecting to. pre-
sent to Mr. Tidd Pratt, the registrar, the annual
report and general financial statement, as required by
the Friendly Societies Act.—Mr. Tidd Pratt's clerk
attended to press the charge against the defendant,
and said the cases of neglect on the part of the secre-
taries of companies were so frequent, that it was
necessary to take steps for preventing an infringement
of the law.—The defendant was fined 20s. and costs.
—Other cases of a similar nature were brought forward
against the secretaries of companies, and they were
also fined in 20s. and costs.

FORESTERS.

NEWCASTLE PRESEN-T-AT-iO—N-.-011 Monday evening, at
the usual fortnightly meeting of Court Northumber-
land, No. 3,831, held at the house of Bro. Hugh
Lambert, Foresters' Arms, Wellington-street, New-
castle, Bro. William Coward, D.S., was presented by
the members of the above Court with a handsome silver
medal. The presentation was made by Bro. R. R. L.
Murray, C.R., and was suitably responded to by Bro.
Coward.

AN AGENT OP THE ROYAL LIVER SOCIETY IN
TROUBLE.—At the Guildhall, Kidderminister, Con-
stantine Smith was charged with converting to his own
use the sum of £2 10s. 91, belonging to the above
society, the chief offices of which are at Liverpool.
The defendant, it appeared, wal appointed the Kidder-
minster agent to the society about two years ago, and
up to June last had sent in the accustomed returns.
Some weeks having elapsed without the defendant
rendering any statement, he was discharged. A balance
of a 108. oth being left in dispute between defendant
and the society, the latter was called on by one of the
agents, and he paid over £3, refusing to pay any more.
Tho defendant claimed 6s. a week as salary from the
20th June to the 27th of August, and had tendered the
balance to the society. The bench ordered the
defendant to pay the amount he was summoned for,
£2 10s. 9d., and the costs, or, in default, to go to prison
for one month.

articles.title: DISTRESS IN LANCASHIRE.- ST. PANC.R./IS MEETING.
articles.text:
THE DISTRESS IN LANCASHIRE.-
ST. PANC.R./IS MEETING.

A public meeting of the inhabitants of St. Pancras
in aid of the funds for the relief of the distress in the
cotton districts, was held on Monday evening in the St.
Pancras Vestry-hall, King's-road, the Rev. Canon
Champneys, the vicar, in the chair, supported by Mr.
Harvey Lewis, ALP. for Marylebone, the parochial
clergy, and the leading members of the St. Pancras
veAry.
The Chairman said few heavier troubles had fallen
upon this country than that ulider which some por-
tions of our manufacturing districts 'were now labour-
ing. It was universally acknowledged that the cotton
operativee were now suffering the most severe priva-
tions from no fault of their own, and therefore they
had the strongest possible claims upon the sympathy
and aid of their fellow-countrymen- The conduct of
the cotton operatives under their sufferings was
beyond all praise,—a conduct in itself demanding the
greatest admiration of the whole civilized world. The
Ichairman then referred to several statistical facts
connected with those unions in which the distress pre-
vailed. He said that in these unions last year, in the
first week in October, 43,508 persons were receiving
relief, while in the same week of the present year the
number was 163,492, being an excess of nearly 120,000.
The amount paid in October list year was £2,590,
while in October of this year it was £9,674, being an
increase of over £7,000. It was the duty of all to
assist in relieving this distress, and he felt sure the
inhabitants of St. Pancras would not be behind other '
districts in this respect.
Mr. Plaws, the vestry clerk, then read the report
of the committee which had been formed by the in-
habitants some weeks since. The sum received by the
committee up to the present time had been £313.
Mr. Clayton moved the first resolution as folio we
That, in the opinion of this meeting, the distress of
the cotton artisans, arising as it does from causes
entirely beyond their control, should be regarded as a
national calamity, which it is the duty of all good
citizens to aid. in mitigating; and that the manly
fortitude with which the sufferers have borne their
privations gives them an aditional claim upon our
sympathy and assistance.' He felt that it was in the
power of every man to do something, and that some-
thing should be done at once. It had been used as an
argument by some for not subscribing that the cotton
lords had not done their duty. That might be so, and
assuming that it was so it was yet no argument to
excuse others from doing their duty. (Hear.)
Colonel Wilkinson seconded the resolution. He
thought there never had arisen in this country a more
urgent necessity for the benovolence and sympathy of
Englishmen, and he felt certain every man in England
would do his duty.
Mr. Merriman, in supporting the resolution, con-
tended that the manufacturers as a body had done

their duty.
Mr. Brian, a house-painter, wished to move a rider
to the resolution to the following effect:—' That this
meeting is further of opinion that the application of
the labour test is cruel and unjust.'
No person seconding the proposed rider, it fell to
the ground, and the resolution having been put from
the chair, was carried unanimously.
Mr Harvey Lewis, M.P., moved the next resolu-
tion, thanking the vestry of St. Pancras for initiating
the movement in this parish for the relief of the dis-
tress in the cottoni • eta. He thought the English
tpr
character stood g ly out in the conduct of the
Lancashire opera —conduct of which he, as an
Englishman, felt ite proud. There had been no
riot, no disorder, no unnecessary agitation ; but their
sufferings had been borne with dignity and patience.
1 The resolution having been agreed to, several other
gentlemen addressed the meeting, and a vote of thanks
to the chairman concluded the proceedings.

BOOKBINDERS' PROVIDENT ASYLU3I SOCIETY.—The
24th annual meeting of the members of this society
will, we understand, be held. on Monday evening next
at the London Mechanics' Institution, for the election
of officers and discussion of several proposed alterations
in the rules, and the committee trust that a good at-
tendance will take place. In the earlier part of the
day an election will take place of two inmates to the
asylum.

THE AMALGAMATED ASSOCIATION OF HOUSE-PAINTERS.
—We are informed that several of the members of
No. 5 lodge paid a friendly visit to the members of
No. 2 at their meeting on Saturday evening last,
which is, we understand, to be returned to No. 5 on
their next meeting night. Such a course, if adopted by
other lodges where practicable, would go far to pro-
mote that sympathy and esteem so essential to the
principles of association.

articles.title: CORRESPONDENCE.
articles.text:
CORRESPONDENCE.

Chß LEGISLATION.

TO THE EDITOR OF THE BEEHIVE.
Sra,—The calm and moderate tonein which the dele-
gates of the London cabmen conduct their deliberations
leads one to hope that they belong to that very limited
class of persons who can and will look at both sides of
a question, and that they will not resent suggestions
made by an employer (not owner) of cabs, who heartily
sympathises with all attempts of operatives to plead
their own cause; but feels, as the delegates themselves
i.eem to feel, that everything should not be attempted
at once, where the situation has, as in the present case,
become complicated.
1. Mr. Smith's clause proposing free trade in cabs,
though ultimately negatived, touched a very important
principle ; one which may possibly appear again should
the projected Cab Company succeed. No doubt con-
fusion would arise as things now are, but it should be
remembered that omnibuses have ere this (and may
now) run on the great lines of traffic with various fare
in operation at the same time; but the public have
shown themselves able to defeat immediately any at-
tempt at excessive charges, and the conveyance trade is
proved to be most readily influenced by the ordinary
laws of supply and demand.
2. I doubt Mr. Smith's clause as to licences being
attainable. Their distribution and suspension must
be with one central authority, which probably receives
reports from magistrates; the final decision, however,
resting entirely with itself.
• 3. Nor, with all sympathy for the feeling which
suggests it, do I think the objection to the badge
valid. The good sense and candour of delegates who
freely allow that there are very disreputable men in
the trade, will, I think, allow also that the badge
gives the public some desirable security against
their misconduct; and that it is only in itself irk-
some so long as it suggests the idea of an unpopular
calling. Make the calling popular and respected, and
the mark will loose its sting.
4. On the relations of owners and drivers I have
no right to speak; but I cannot see why a master
should be able to recover from
,a driver by one pro-
cess, and from me, if I don't" pay him for hire of
horses and carriages, by another. It is the owner's
business to find out with whom they are dealing, and
trust them or not accordingly.
5. What constitutes plying for hire?' In some
provincial towns a notice is displayed or not on a
cab, according as it is plying' or not. Could not
this be introduced in London? When the notice is
up, the driver should be bound to take any hirer
(reasonable loads and distances being, I presume,
provided for in other clauses) ; and people would be
really glad to know at a glance if a cab is going
home,' a plea which is, I hope, even now often al-
lowed. The notice would just prevent it being made
falsely when a fare did not look tempting.'
6. I have always thought the existing law about
agreements unjust. Railways are treated better in
being exemptea from all obligation to land us at their
stations at the times published in their bills.
7. The adoption of Mr. Griffin's amendment on Mr.
Miles' motion for the settlement of disputes is as wise
as it is creditable to the moderation of the committee.
After thus conceding that, We will be taken to the
police-office, but will be satisfied with our fare's name
and address,'—l do hope neither magistrate nor public'
will spare any one who refuses to give them.
8. The Luggage' law clearly requires adjustmtn.t.
From the existing rule about a third person, I infer that
two persons are considered a sufficient load for ordinary
fares. Let, then, all outside luggage be paid for when
twa or more persons are conveyed.' I don't think
cabmen mind taking me and a portmanteau, for instance,
(Mr. Wakelin's clause would make the latter pay
extra), and perhaps two packages might be deemed
equivalent to a third person, and all above two be
charged for. So the proverbial 'Ladies' little all'
would pay its proper share.
9. Legalising a is. demand fc.r the first hiring, will
most properly establish as binding what I think even
now is a very general practice. I should be glad to be
saved the struggle between sense of law and right
which ends in giving a well-earned bob for a short
turn in a cab. No carriage goes out of a yard in the
country under 2s. 61, and no cab ought to go off, and
perhaps lose a good place on a stand for 6d. only.
10. The four miles radius. I conceive that back
fare is earned not so much by the distance traversed as
by the distance from probable subsequent hiring at
which a cab is dismissed. Ido not see that the
present radius extends anywhere beyond really popu •
bus districts, where a fare might very likely be picked
up without much loss of time, and the measurement of
the four miles by road would introduce much complica-
tion. _ _ _

Lastly, I cannot help expressing regret at the loud
outcry raised against Lieut. Paschale's new regu-
lations. The Delegates would, I believe, be themselves
as glad as anyone to know that all drivers
could read and write, and the argument 'read-
_ _

ing and writing won't drive a Cab,' is merely
that which has, happily in vain, been urged
against acquiring attainments of various kinds, as
guarantees for educational and general competence, in
candidates for the public service. It may be said that
cab-driving is a private trade; but as in the matter of
licences Government acts for the public, may not the
public look to it for further guarantees?
I sincerely hope these remarks, if you think them
worth private or public notice, will be received in the
spirit in which they are made, that spirit of fair-deal-
ing which should animate any one who, like
Your obedient servant,
WISHES TO KNOW HIS FARE AND PAY IT.'
London, Oct., 2, 1862.

articles.title: DISTRESS IN LANCASHIRE.
articles.text:
DISTRESS IN LANCASHIRE.

TO THE EDITOR OF THE BEEHIVE.

Sin—l am sorry to see such a very meagre list
of subscriptions for the ' Lancashire distress' in your
paper every week. At a time like the present, when
our wealthy countrymen are subscribing so very libe
rilly on this, as they have done on other recent occa-
sions, to alleviate the sufferings of 0.,e distressed, at
which I rejoice, for I think it is one of the most cheer-
ing' signs of the times' that the working classes are
steadily progressing in the estimation of those socially
above them,—then, I say, is this the time for working
men to hang back? Why, Sir, you ought to be able
to fill a whole column every week with the subscriptions
of shops and factories in London and its vicinity. I
believe there is sympathy ; but we want to see the fruits
of it in a substantial form. If it requires self-denial, a
little extra forbearance can surely be endured, at such a
time, and for such a cause. I think it only requires some
one to speak of it in earl establishment; therefore, let
every reader of this at once begin to talk about .t with
his fellow workmen, and the thing is done; and British
workmen will not only maintain their character for
independence, but for a kind and feeling heart.
I think it Would very much increase our interest in
the cause if the Padiham Committee' would occasionally
give us some account of their proceedings.
W. F.

articles.title: BEEHIVE SHARE CLUB.
articles.text:
BEEHIVE SHARE CLUB.

TO THE EDITOR OF THE BEEHIVE.

Stu,—A few of the members of the St. Helen's Opera-
tive Painter's and Plumber's Society having for some
time been subscribers to your BEEHIVE newspaper, hare
commenced a Beehive Share Club on a small scale,
and have pledged themselves to support and extend the
same by every means in their power. As your paper
supplies a deficiency which has long b3en felt, that
is, a working man's paper, whose columns are always
open to them, and by which they are enabled to bring
before the public their claims to their rights and
privileges, and exposing any act of oppression to
which they may be liable; for combining together for
the protection of themselves and their fellow work-
men; in endeavouring to ameliorate the evils atten-
dant on their trade, and the advancement of the rights
and privileges of labour; and for the general education
and elevation of the labouring classes. Believing that
you have these objects in view, we consider it our
duty to support you in successfully cairying out the
same. I enclose postage stamps for two shares. Wish-
ing you every success your paper r well merits, and
hoping that ere long every working man will become
either shareholders or subscribers to the BEEHIVE
newspaper,
