remain yours truly,
JAMES BEATON, Secretary.

AIRDRIL—MINERs' UNioNs.—The agitation for the
formation of unions recently originated in the Airdrie
district appears to have spread eastward. On Saturday
last a meeting of coal and ironstone miners, was held at
Armadale, for theturpose of taking into consideration
the propriety of their uniting themselves into a societ/
similar to those formed in the west. After a numlis
of addresses had been delivered, a motion to this eff -
was carried unanimously, an association formed,
.and
a number of names enrolled. In Airdrie, the exertions
making by the men to.,..organise themselves into a
union have not been rellaxed, notwithstanding the con-
cession of the required advance in wages by the coal
and iron masters. A series of rules and regulations '
has been drawn up, and will be discussed and in all
probability adopted at an early meeting. Grievous
complaints are made by the men of the defective ven-
tilation and arrangement of a number of the pits, and
they are determined to use every effort to procure a
more thorough and searching investigation into the
1 justice of those complaints than they have hitherto
been able to secure.

articles.title: MARLBOROUGH-STREET.
articles.text:
MARLBOROUGH-STREET.

THE HYDE-PARK Riors.—Pietro Ansani, the Italian,
charged with stabbing the young man Wardell and
another person on Sunday, the sth instant, in the riot
in Hyde-park, was again brought before Mr. Tyrwhitt.
Inspector Draper said that neither of the wounded per-
sons were able to appear to-day. Mr. Tyrwhitt said
he should remand the prisoner for another week, refus-
ing bail. John Mahony, who was remanded on a
charge of assault in the riot, was next brought up. The
evidence taken on the last occasion having been read
over by the chief clerk, a young man said he was
knocked down by a party, of which the prisoner was
one, but he could not say positively the prisoner knocked
him down. The case being imperfect, Mr. Tyrwhitt
said he should remand the prisoner for another week.
Prisoner begged that that might not be done. Mr.
Tyrwhitt said he should certainly remand him. The
prisoner had had his day, and now came the reckon-
ing.
STRANGE FREAK or A CABMA.N.—Thomas King, of
25, Harley-mews, a cab driver, badge 8,704, was
charged before Mr. Knox with stealing a horse and
cab, of the value of £4O, the property of Mr. Samuel P.
Nash, an extensive cabowner, of Edward-street,
Regent's-park. Henry Buckle, a cab driver, badge
2,523, said : On the previous evening he left his cab
and horse on the rank in Great Portland-street, and
went into a public-house. On coming out he missed
the horse and cab, and went into Oxford-street in
search of them, when he saw the prisoner driving three
persons. He ran after him and got on the box, when
the prisoner said I can't take you; I am engaged.'
He told the prisoner that perhaps he would give
him a ride, but he objected, and told him
(witness) to get down. He, however, kept on the box
till he saw a policeman, and then pulled up the horse
and gave the prisoner in charge for stealing the
horse and cab.—Mr. Knox said he did not think the
prisoner meant to steal the horse and cab, but that his
object was to take them to earn a few shillings. He
should deal with the case as one of unlawful possession,
and committed the prisoner for two months, with hard
labour.

articles.title: CLE RKENIVELL.
articles.text:
CLE RKENIVELL.

THE CABMAN'S ATTORNEY-GENERAL.—John Lock, a
cab•master in the Gray's-inn-road, was summoned
before Air. D'Eyncourt, for unlawfully detaining from
a cabman of the name of Lovel, but who is known as
the 'Cab nan's Attorney General,' his license.—The
complainant got into the witness-box with an Act of
Parliament in his hand, and fluently detailed how he
had been dismissed from his employment through
being unable to make up, when suddenly asked, the
sum which be had to pay each day for the use of a
horse and cab. He had since frequently applied for
his licence, and been refused. The defence was that
the licence had not been asked for; but the magistrate
held the charge proved, and ordered the complainant,
as costs and compensation, the sum of 255., and that
the licence should be given back to him.—The com-
plainant left the court in triumph, the magistrate
paying him the compliment that he would have made
a good lawyer.

articles.title: THAMES.
articles.text:
THAMES.

TAKING A COOLER.—Henry Praeey, a tall young
man, who described himself as a labourer, was brought
before Mr. Selfe, charged with attempting to commit
suicide.—Mr. John Brown, a manure dealer, of No.
38, Longfellow-road, Bow, stated that at nine o'clock
in the morning he saw the prisoner on the bank of the
Regent's canal, near the iron railway bridge, in the
parish of Bethnal green, and he saw him deliberately
throw himself into the canal. The prisoner went down
and came up again, and he shoved a piece of board to-
wards him, to which he clung and was saved.—The
prisoner, on being asked why he jumped into the
canal, replied carelessly: To have a cooler, sin—Mr.
Sell: With your clothes on ?—The prisoner : Yes,
with my clothes on.—Mr. Self: What do you mean
by it ?—The prisoner: I meant this, to have a cooler,
and had one.—Mr. Self: You have been drinking to
excess, I fear.—The prisoner: I have been drinking
heavily the last few weeks.—Mr. Selfe : What are
you ? The prisoner: A labourer.—Mr. Selfe : You
would have been drowned if that good man Brown had
not saved you. I shall remand you for a week to the
Clerkenwell House of Detention.

DEATH FROM FIRE.-Mr. Bedford held an inquest
on Saturday at St. George's Hospital, on the body of
Ann Streetley, aged 58, lately residing at 6, Lower
George street, who expired in that hospital, from burns
caused by her clothes taking fire, according to her own
statement, through falling asleep and upsetting the
candle on her dress. No one saw the occurrence. The
house surgeon said deceased was admitted on Tuesday
morning about half-past one o'clock; she was exten-
sively burned about the face, arms, Trek, body, and
legs. She was then intoxicated, awl very talkative.
She died the same morning at a quarter to three
o'clock. A verdict of 'Accidental death' was re-
turned.

articles.title: PERTIN_ENT QUESTION.
articles.text:
PERTIN_ENT QUESTION.

(From the London Review.)
With all the Southern proclivities' of Mr. Gladstone,
we are happy to observe that he does not permit himself
to become the apologist of slavery. Mr. Gladstone
seems to entertain the opinion very prevalent with some
people who seek thereby to justify their favours to wards
the secessionist movement,—viz., that in the establish-
ment of the independence of the South lies the best
hope for the extinction of slavery. We do not purpose
to meet this opinion with any elaborate argument. We
will apply to it a short, but, as seems to us a decisive
test. It is contained in the following :—Do the .Southern
statesmen who are fighting for seGession believe that
independence will achieve the extinction of slavery ?
Does Jefferson Davis or Mr. Gladstone know best what
is intended to be and what is likely to be the result of
Southern success? If the Union afforded, as Mr. Glad-
stone thinks, the best security for slave property, why
are the slave proprietors so determined to get rid of the
Union P If secession is to bring about emancipation,
why are the slave owners secessionists? In his next
after-dinner oration we hope Mr. Gladstone will attempt
all Ulmer to this inquiry.

articles.text:
COLLISION ON T.ffE SOUTH-TVESTEI?_N

RAILWAY.

On the 10th instant an accident, which, as regards
loss of property, was attended with serious consequences,
occurred near the Guilford station. It appears that at
about twenty minutes past eleven o'clock, as the goods
train which leaves Alton at 9.35 was approaching the
station, the engine driver observed the danger signal
set, and immediately shut off the steam, reversed the
engine, and used every means in his power to slacken
the speed; but as the train had just arrived at the in-
cline, which is at this place one in one hundred, and
which °den& for about two miles and a quarter, his
efforts were of little avail, and the train went rushing on.
The guard also applied the breaks, but a heavy storm
which had just fallen rendered their application almost
useless; the consequence was, that the train went at a
rapid pace downthe incline, at the foot of which it came
into collision with the pick up' goods train of the
South-Eastern Railway, consisting of about thirty-
four waggons, which was performing its ordinary
shunting at the time. The engine-driver of the South
Eastern Company's train hearing the whistle of the
approaching train, and being fully aware of the
inevitable danger, with great self-possession imme-
diately ran a-head, taking with him about half the
train which had been previously detached, and thus no
doubt prevented a double collision, for which he de-
serves the greatest credit. Of the remaining waggons
belonging to tho South-Eastern Company, seven were
completely smashed and rendered unfit for use includ-
ing the guard's break-van, which fortunately was
empty. Of the South. Western train, which contained
about thirty waggons, laden chiefly with market
goods, four were overturned and greatly damaged,
whilst several others were shattered to a thousand
pieces, the massive iron work being bent and broken
like BO many straws. The tender, which being before
the engine, struck the guard's break, was much
damaged, the water tank being driven completely out
of its frame. The wheels of several waggons were
broken oft and the trucks themselves were piled up
one upon another nearly to the height of the railway
bridge. A huge block of freestone, measuring four
or five feet in thickness, was also broken in pieces,
and the damage done will amount to a very large
sum. Finding that a collision was unavoidable,
the -engine-driver on the South-Western line jumped
#otn the engine, and called upon the stoker to do the
same. The former escaped comparatively uninjured,
but the latter sustained a serious injury to the knee,
arm, and other parts of the body. The guard of this
train also jumped from his van, and escaped unhurt.
Mr. Dyson, the station-master at Guildford, was ap-
prised of the occurrence, and was immediately on the
spot with a strong body of men, who were set to work
clearing away the shattered remains of the carriages
and other debris with which the line was strewn.
Owing to the praiseworthy exertions of the men, under
the superintendence of Mr. Dyson, the line was cleared
for traffic at about six on Saturday morning. No
blame appears to be attached to any person, the driver
of the South-Western engine, Walter Lloyd, having
used every means in his power to prevent the accident.
He has been in the employ of the London and South
Western Railway Company for many years, and has
always borne a high character for the caution in-
variably e-xercised by him in the discharge of his duty.
Mr. Ross, surgeon, was in prompt attendance upon
George Stone, the fireman, and the man is progressing
favourably,

articles.title: NEW- CHANCERY dCIS.
articles.text:
NEW- CHANCERY dCIS.

Three Chancery Acts were passed in the late session,
two of which will come into operation at the com-
mencement of the forthcoming Michaelmas Term, and
the third .on the let of January next. Two of the
statutes-4 The Land Transfer Act,' and The Declara-
tion of Title Act'—may be regarded as important Chan-
cery reforms; and the other, 'The Chancery Regula-
tion Act,' has reference to questions of law and fact.
The first act was passed on the 17th July last (25 and
26 Viet. c. 42), and is entituled An Act to regulate the
procedure of the High Court of Chancery, and the
Court of Chancery of the County Palatine of Lan-
caster.' It recites that the Court of Chancery has
power in certain cases to refuse or postpone the re-
medies within its jurisdiction until questions of law
and facton which the title to such remedies depend have
been determined or ascertained in one of the courts of
common law, and that it is expedient that the power
should no longer exist; and the practice of the
Court of Chancery of the County Palatine of Lancaster
having been assimilated, it is necessary that the future
procedure of the two courts should be alike. There-
fore it is. enacted that the courts are to determine
every question of law and fact incident to the relief
sought; but where questions may be more conve-
niently tried at the assizes or at the sittings in London
or Middlesex, issues may be directed, The provisions
of the 21 and 22 Viet., c. 21, are to apply to the Courts
of Chancery. The Court of Chancery may sit, with
the assistance of a common law judge. The act is to
take effect from and aft the let November next.
The second act in order was passed on the 29th July
(25 and 2G Viet. c. 53), and is entituled An Act to
facilitate the proof of title to, and the consequence of,
real estates.' The third act was passed on the 29th
July (25th and 26th Viet., c. 66), and is entituled
Act for obtaining a declaration of title.' The object
of this statute is to enable persons having interests in
land to obtain in certain cases a judicial declaration of
their title, so as to enable them to make an indefeasible
title to persons claiming under them, as purchasers for
a valuable consideration. Rules and orders are to be
made to carry out the act, which is to take effect or.
the let January next.

THE NEW PRIMATE AND TUE ATHANASIAN CREED.
—A correspondent of the Cambridge Independent writes:
The friends of church reforms and liturgical revision
will be surprised, perhaps, to know that they have
plausible reason for expecting some sympathy in one,
direction at least of their efforts, from the new Arch-
bishop of Canterbury. Several years ago Dr. Longley's
sister married a gentleman who was a dissenter, and at
heterodox sect. A correspondence, which was after-
wards published, ensued between the brothers-in-law,
and though the controversy ended in each retaining his
own opinion, it afforded an admirable specimen of the
temper in which such controversy should be carried en,
and in no-degree lessened the regard which both parties
felt for each other. The lady died two years ago in the
profession of the opinions of the sect she had joined. I
mention the matter, in order to quote a sentence used by
Dr. Longley in the course of the controversy, It is true
that at that time he was only a simple clergyman, and
had no dreams even of archbishoprics, but it is possible
he may not even now shrink from the avowal.
"Nothing," he says, "that I have advanced on the
subject of the Athanasian creed is, as I conceive, ki the
least degree inconsistent with my joining in the senti•
ment of Tillotson, and wishing it removed from our
church service. If I were called upon to give my vote
upon the subject, it would be for its omission." '
CONFEDERATE STATES • CURRENCY.—In 1860 the
currency of the Southern States of America consisted of
160,000,000 dollars, half in bank notes and half in
specie. After the fall of Fort Sumter gold began to
disappear, and the banks increased their issues, which
now amount to 100,000,000 dollars. On the 9th of
March, 1861, the first Confederate Treasury notes were
issued, amounting to 2,021,000. dollars. On the 17th of
the next month there was an issue of interest notes, of
which 22,790,900 dols. have been emitted. On the 16th
of May Treasury notes amounting to 17,347,955 dollars,
and on the 19th of Augnst, notes to the amount of
167,764;615 dollars were issued. During the above
period also 846,000 dollars- worth of one and two dollar
notes were issued. Thus at the present time 210,779,560
dollars worth of Confederate notes are in circulation,
and paper money to the amount of 310,000,000 dollars.
The circulation of the Confederate States is double its
normal dimensions, and is depreciated to one-half of its
nominal value.

XURDER OF GENE.RAL NELSON.

Loufsvf LE, KY Sept. 29.
The Galt House, at about eight o'clock this meriting,
was the scene of a terrible affair, in consequence of a
difficulty between Brigadier• General Jefferson C. Davis
and Major-General .Neison.
It appears that there has been a difficulty between the
parties for some time.

- General Nelson was standing in the office of the Galt
House when Gen. Davis approached him and spok e to
him. Gen. Nelson refused to listen to him and used
some insulting lancruage. Gen. Davis immediately
borrowed a pistol and followed Gen. Nelson who was
going up-stairs to his room, and while on the stairs
Gen. Davis shot him. The ball entered the heart el
Gen. Nelson, who walked to his room and was laid
on a mattress, where he in a few minutes afterwards
expired. _

There are many conflicting accounts of the shooting
of General Nelson by General Davis. About a week
ago Nelson placed Davis in command of the Home
Guard forces of the city. At night Davis reported to
Nelson the number of men working on the intrenchments
and enrolled for service. Nelson cursed him for not
having more. Davis replied that he was a general offi-
cer, and demanded the treatment of a gentleman. Nel-
son, in an insulting manner, ordered him to report at
Cincinnati, and told him he would order the Provosc-
Marshal to eject him from the city.
This morning Governor Morton of Indiana and Gene-
ral Nelson were standing near the desk in the Galt
House, when General Davis approacd, and requested
Governor Morton to witness a conversation between
himself and General Nelson. He demanded of Nelson
an apology for the rude treatment he had received last
week. Nelson being a little deaf asked him to speak
louder. Davis again demanded an apology.
Nelson denounced him and slapped him on the face.
Davis stepped back, clenched his fist, and again de-
manded an apology. Nelson again slapped him in the
face, and again denounced him as a coward. Davis
turned away, procured a pistol from a friend, and fol-
lowed Nelson, who was going up-stairs. Davis told
Nelson to defend himself, immediately thereon firing.
The ball penetrated his left breast, and General Nel-
son died in about twenty minutes.

PMILADELPHIA, Monday, Sept. 29.
A special dispatch to a morning paper, of this city,
says that General Nelson called General Davis 'a
cowardly son of a bitch,' when General Davis fired at
him and killed him.

articles.title: H BEE-HIVE. SATURDAY, OC [OBER 18, 1862
articles.text:
H BEE-HIVE. SATURDAY, OC [OBER 18, 1862

THE ETRCUTION OF THE ROA
SAHIB.

A Cawnpore correspondent of the Times of India gives
a few details of the execution of the miscreant Rao
Sahib, who, after a lengthened trial, was proved to have
taken an active part in the cold-blooded atrocities per-
petrated on defenceless women and children at Cawnpore,
at the outbreak of the late terrible mutiny in India.
Writing under date of August 22, he says: The Rao
Sahib was brought out, heavily ironed, in front of the
gaol, a few minutes before six yesterday morning to un-
dergo the extreme penalty of the law for the crimes
charged and proved against him. There were not more
than a dozen Europeans present, but the natives turned
out in great force and I dare say there were at least
four thousand standing about a hundred yards, and in
form of a half moon from the gallows. A number of
the better class of native ladies were also present to
witness the proceedings. Precisely at six the bamboo
props were knocked from beneath a small platform on
which the prisoner, with a look on his relentless cruel
face which betokened the greatest amount of inherent
cowardice, was standing, or rather reclining, suspended
by the neck, in the arms of two Mahtees, when, at a
nod from the collector, away dangled all that was mortal
of one of the chief instigators of many a foul deed done
to helpless women and little innocent prattling children.
Ile remained suspended about half-an-hour, and was
then eased (not cut) down into the arms of his mother's
friends, and by them put, not very gently, on the ground
tinder the scaffold. I forgot to tell you that they (the
Mahtees) put a thing on his head to represent a black
cap, but to my vision it looked like a bag that had once
been white. It answered the purpose, however, and
saved appearances. Before ascending the final step he
addressed the collector, asking permission for his mother
to be put in possession of his remains. This I..ast request
was refused, and I think very properly. The doctor
attended upon him to the last, and finally ordered a
European inspector to remove the corpse from the ground
and take it away to the banks of holy Gunge, and,
within a few hundred yards of the very ghat where the
Cawnpore fugitives were shot down, there to be stripped
by the same men who waited on him at the gallows,
after which he was burned and his askes thrown into
the river.'

articles.title: DISASTROUS SLIP Al! A QUARRY.
articles.text:
DISASTROUS SLIP Al! A QUARRY.

A few days ago an alarming accident occurred at the
Easdale Slate Quarries, in Argyleshire, belonging to the
Marquis of Breadalbane, and immense damage to pro-
perty is the consequence. One of the most extensive
of the quarries is situated on a small island of about half
a-mile in circumference, and is exposed to a very wild
and tempestuous sea. The rubbish taken out of the
quarry has been generally filled into waggons and thrown
over the side. This, however, of itself is not a very
secure bulwark, and from the nature of the debris it
does not consolidate, and the natural boundary between
the sea and the quarry being slate rock, was easily to a
great extent lost sight of. A piece of the boundary
rock fell in, impelled by the great force of water
from without. There was no breach, however,
made, but only a large tunnel or perforation twenty
or thirty feet below the surface. The extensive
steam apparatus used for drawing up the slates,
consisting of pumps, crams, cranks, pumping gear,
with inclined plane and railroad for taking up the slates,
and a great portion of other valuable machinery, were
precipitated into the quarry, which was nearly 300 feet
deep. The quarry was soon filled with water, but
luckily there was no loss of life, no one being at work
at the time. Means are now being taken to reach the
point where the perforation in the rock has been made,
and having built a strong wall at the point, to keep out
the inroad of the sea. The water already in the quarry
will then be pumped out—an operation which will
require months to be completed. The expense will be
very great, indeed, such as that it was at one time
doubted whether the recovery of the slates and sunk
property would repay the cost, but the quarry is a
valuable working. About eighty families were thrown
out of employment by this catastrophe, but they have
been provided with work at the other quarries belonging
to his lordship. From 20,000 to 30,000 slates were
made there per day, for which there is an increasing
demand, and the value of the slates at the bottom is
estimated at £15,000.

NOVEL CArrunn or FOXEB.—A. Bideford correspond-
ent writes:---' The Braunds of Bucks, or the foxes and
fish-hooks, properly delineated, would make an amus-
ing comedy. Not long ago, James Braund, a fisherman
residing at Bucks, in the parish of Parkham, North
Devon, having baited a hook with a hug's maw, " tilled"
it on the beach to catch gull, or any other sea-bird. He
buried the greater part of the maw, which concealed
the treacherous hook, in the shingle. When he came
to look after his hook, and to see what he had caught,
he was not a little surprised to find a fox dancing
and capering about at the end of its tether. He
deemed it the surest way to secure his prize to shoot
it, and soon got his gun and bagged the vixen.
Last <Tuesday Mr. Braund had 'another :and 'almost
equally strange fox adventure. His fishing nets
had been spread to dry, and, as is the custom, the
dog-fish had been shook out, but it is supposed that
one of these must have been under the net, and
attracted a fox out on a forage. At all events, Captain
Braund found a fine old dog fox rolled up in the net. It
is thought that in,his efforts to draw out the fish he drew
up the loose net and entangled himself, and the more he
struggled to free himself the more inextricably he be-
came entangled. On seeing the nature of the prisoner,
"Here's a greyhound, Lucifer," said Braund, and then
looking at the fox, added. " Thee'rt not content with
faesting. on. Lady Elwes' hares and rabbits ths.se eight
or ten years, but have been scouring the baieh for visch ;
I'll cook thy goose for tha now." Whereon, as Braund
afterwards said, "the cratur looked so vashous that I
vetched my gun and soun settled his vishingpei?ensities."
It was what is called in the locality a greyhound dog
fox, of mature age, weighing 1241 b., and a regular
beauty in symmetry and appearance. Mr. Brtund has
presented the animal to a Bideford printer, who
intends to have it preserved and set up.'
SERIOUS AFFAIR.—A BOY KILLED.—We regret to
hear that a melancholy and fatal accident has happened
in Glenmorriston. A few days ago, two boys of the
ages of about eight and eleven years, whose names we
have not ascertained, had quarrelled, and set to battle
with their fists. The younger of the boys, it appears,
was getting the better of the other, when an older
companion stepped in, and seizing the 1 id, gave him a
kick in the spine c. ith so much severity that the lad had
to be carried home, and died five days thereafter, it is
believea from the effects of the kick. The authorities
are-engaged in an invest/gation of this painful case.
HOPS.—The:fallowing is an extract of a 'letter re-
ceived from Saaz, dated Oct. 7, 1862 :—` The quantity
of hops grown in Bohemia and Bavaria, derived from
reliable soure, s :—Bavaria has rather more than half a
crop, and Bohemia less than half a crop. The prices of
Bavarian varied from £6 to £8 per cwt.; Auscha, £7 to
£9 per cwt.; Bohemian, £lO to £l2 per cwt.; lately
there has been an advance of £2 per cwt., which is well
maintained. Should any English demand arise prices
will go higher.'

articles.title: BYDE PARE .Y ETEV G.
articles.text:
THE BYDE PARE .Y ETEV G.

I The violent storms of rain on Sunday acted more
I effectually than almost .ny body of police could have d to
in preventing a meeting, and therefore a riot, in II de
' park. We do not think, however, that we do any in-
justice to the character of many roughs who assembled
near where the mound stood last week when we say that
it was more than likely that but for the rain some stupid
breach of the peace would have occurred. The police
notice had been posted everywhere, warning the public
that no meeting of any kind would be allowed, but never-
theless, about 2 o'clock small groups of idlers began to
collect on the scene of the previous Sunday's disturbance.
At first these were apparently very respectable per-
sons, members of the large and foolish class who on these
occasions of anticipated disturbance come to look on and
see what is doing. They would doubtless have repudi-
ated as insulting any charge of connexion or sympathy
with the rowdies on both sides who enacted such silly
blackg,uardism on the previous occasion; yet, strange
as it may appear to these people, it is nevertheless true
that even their being on the spot is, to a certain extent,
aiding and abetting the purposes of intending rioters,
who derive encouragement from the mere presence of
respectable people, and find half their game done to hand
by a crowd of this kind. The police can deal readily
enough with the disorderly members of a mob; it is the
very silly, brit quiet and respectable lookers-on who
hamper their movements, and among whom the most
turbulent of the roughs often manage to effect their
escape. At 2 o'clock there were probably 500 or GOO
loungers of this class, all waiting to see' if anything
would happen. A few police, probably not more than
30 or 40, were on the ground in twos and threes, and
about a dozen superintendents and inspectors of various
divisions. A very strong body of police numbering
nearly 800 men, under the command of Captain Harris,
were in the immediate neighbourhood, but none were
seen, as it had been determined not to bring them on the
ground as long as there was no disposition either to hold
a meeting or make a disturbance. Soon after 3 the
crowd began to be reinforced by many small parties who
came from different directions, and who were all of the
class known by the comprehensive term of roughs,'
just such people who make the bulk of the crowds at
fires and executions. With these were the usual troops
of metropolitan gamins,' who pelted each other, hunted
poor stray dogs till they almost drove them mad, and who
otherwise did their utmost to create confusion and even
riot; altogether the aspect of the whole crowd agured
badly for peace being long maintained, when just before
4 o'clock the rain set in with drenching vehemence and at
once dispersed and sent away all those of the lookers-on
who had the least pretensions to respectability. The
rougher elements of the crowd, too, were broken up and
driven to shelter under the trees, where, partly for the
shelter itself and partly, no doubt, to see what next would
happen, they remained for some time watching the misty
clouds of rain huddling drearily across the park, and
making the thin, brown, leafy covering of the trees
thinner with every gust. Everything and everybody
looked wet and miserable, and the groups under shelter
soon.grew smaller and smaller by degrees, till at last
even the handful of police were in a majority, and the
scene of the indended demonstration had no more people
on its surface than the Serpentine, and for much the
same reason. So ended the Hyde Park meetings,. for
none will even be attempted next Sunday. The chip of
Sunday will be too much for the fast dying-out feeling.

articles.title: COND.EMYED MURDERESS.
articles.text:
THE COND.EMYED MURDERESS.

Notwithstanding the near approach of the day en
which the wretched woman Catherine Taylor will have
to expiate with her life the fearful crime of which she
was found guilty upon such conclusive evidence, she
still appears to exhibit the same carelessness and com-
posure that she did immediatqy after and during- the
trial, and she does not appear at all discouraged at the
near approach of death. It seems that she has not a
single relation or friend to take the least interest in her.
It appears that the wretched woman still continues to
assert her entire innocence of the crime for which she
is to suffer, and she persists in declaring that
Mrs. Soames, her alleged victim, died a natural
death; and she also declares that there is no foun-
dation for the statement that she had caused the
death of several other persons—a faGt that was so
forcibly alluded to by the learned Judge who tried the
prisoner, when he passed sentence upon her. It has
already been stated that Mr. Neale, her solicitor, has
sent a memorial to the Home Secretary, urging in her
behalf the insufficiency of the evidence upon legal and
technical grounds, to justify her conviction, and it
appears that the prisoner has, herself, drawn up a
statement, which was sent to the Home Office in
reference to her case, in which she also appeals for
mercy; and she asserts her innocence of the crime of
which she has been convicted. The precise character
of this statement by the prisoner cannot, of course, be
made public, but it is understood that she enters into a
lengthened history of all the circumstances connected
with the death of the unhappy woman, Mrs. Soames,
and declares, most earnestly, that all the symptoms she
exhibited were the result el natural disease, and that
she never adskinistered to her poison of any description.

articles.title: EX-QUEEN OF NAPLES
articles.text:
THE EX-QUEEN OF NAPLES

TAKI.VG THE VEIL.

A dispatch from Ausburg, dated Oct. 10, contains the
following:—

' Queen' Marie of Naples has just been escorted to the
Ursuline Convent by her brother Prince Louis. This
retreat chosen by the wife of Francis 11. is definitive.
She renounce;' the world.

An explanation of the above paragraph throws a doubt
upon the 'definitive' character of the renunciation of
the world spoken of. The youthful Queen of Naples
has had a quarrel with her husband; but as the catholic
church does not allow amarried woman to become a nun
without her husband's consent, the latter will probably
have a word to say on the subject.
The Ausburg Gazette retracts its statement that the
retirement of this royal lady to a convent was a 'definitive
renunciation of the world.' It seems that she has only
gone to St. Ursula temporarily to assuage the troubles
of her soul.'

QUAKERS IN VIRGINIA. -It is remarkable that ;
settlement of Quakers, near Mount Vernon, have con-
tinued unmolested during the entire war, though alter-
nately included within National and rebel lines. Thei.
semi-weekly meetings have been regularly continued
sometimes a rebel picket pacing in front of the building
and perhaps a Union sentinel having the same beat th.
next week. They have remained undisturbed both ii
property and person.
The Earl of Derby and the Earl of Clarendon paid ;
visit to Liverpool on the 14th, and were received by tht
Mayor, who conducted them to the chief places of loco
interest; Lord Clarendon, who is not so familiar a
Lord Derby with Liverpool affairs, being greatl
interested. Amongst other places visited and closel)
inspected was the site of the proposed Government dock
yard and naval arsenal at Tranmere Pool, Cheshire
which has been suggested by Mr. Laird, M.P.
An extraordinary case of alleged conspiracy to murder
is reported at Aughnacloy, in the county of Tyrone.
which hitherto has been free from the taint of agra-:
rian crime. It is stated that Mr. Johnson, of Ivy Hill,
county Monaghan, a magistrate and extensive land-
holder, having property in Tyrone, incurred the hos-
tility of some tenants in consequence of legal proceed.
ing,s which he was obliged to take, and that, to be re-
venged, three men named M'Kenna, together with Win.
Corbett, a publican hired a man named Kelly to
assassinate him. The price to be paid for the murder
was £1 in hand, and £2O as soon as the work was
completed. Arrangements were to be made to secure
the escape of the assassin from the hands of justice.
Kelly, however, divulged the p104.i, or pretended plot, for
some doubt is thrown upon his story, and all the persons
whom he seeks to implicate have been arrested.
A boy 13 years old made a narrow escape when the lona
went down lately. Being of an adventurous disposition,
the boy resolved to cast in his lot with the Southerners,
or at all events to take the best means in his power to
see the war, and, accordingly, in tl- e hurry of the lona's
departure he slipped on board, and smuggled himself out
of sight in the afterhold, with the intention of revealing
himself when the vessel got fairly out to sea. He lay
with patience for a long tire, until the terrible crash
caused by the collision with the Chanticleer revealed to
him the fact that something had occurred quite out of the
ordinary course of sea life. Rapidly ascending from hit
hiding place he scoured along the deck, and was lucky
enough to get hold of the bowsprit chains of the Chanti-
cleer, by means of which he was ultimately saved.

WHAT Is A SHEBEEN ?—The Liverpool Albion,
noticing the Parliamentary measures of last session,
says :---‘ The acts applying exclusively to Scotland com-
prise some enactments that appear rather incompre
bensible, if not inclining to the comic in their import, to
Southern apprehension. Per instance one of them (25
and 26 Vic., cap. 35, sec. 19) ordains "if any person be
found drunk or &inking in a sbebeen he may be taken
into cusaody, and detained in any station-house or other
convenient place." We have looked through our law
dictionaries, in vain, to find what a shebeen is, and
r• main as much in the dark as we are on the mysteries oi
the cave of Trophonious, or the famed oracle of
Delphos. There is nothing wrong, we believe,
for in another-part of the Act a very tender and con-
servative care is evinced towards tipsy people. Section
23 provides that any person "found in a state of intoxi-
cation, and incapable of taking care of himself, and not
under the care of some suitable person, may be taken in
charge by any officer of police.'"

articles.title: CA R I ,INAL TP7sE ff.42lT AND THE
articles.text:
CA R I ,INAL TP7sE ff.42lT AND THE

HYDE PARK RIOTS.

In all the Roman Catholic chapels, under the autho-
rity of Cardinal Wiseman, a pastoral was read on Sun-
day, in which the recent riots in Hyde-park were
strongly condemned, and any renewal of them strictly
forbidden. The Cardinal says:—
'My dear children, if any of you hoar my words who
took a share in those riotous proceedings on either of the
last Sundays, and still more, who intend to renew those
wicked scenes, I beg, I entreat, I conjure you, as your
father in Christ, nay, solemuly enjoin you as your
bishop, not even to go into the park to-day, or any
future day where there may be the least danger of con-
flict or collision. You will not for a moment suspect
me of sympathy with those assemblies which have led
to these distressing occurrences, and which I trust will
be prevented by the good sense of the pes)ple and the
watchfulness of our public authorities. Such senseless
meetings become scandalous where, under a political
pretence, the religion of others is insulted, and cries
provocative of resentment and violence are uttered.
But, dear children, if others choose to act wickedly as
well as foolishly, this is no reason why you should do
so. Leave tern to their own folly, and be not the cause
of greater evils ensuing from it.
Children of St. Patrick ! . . . . In your pa-
tience you have, indeed, hitherto possessed your souls.
In your impatience w ill you lose them now? Because
a fraction of the population of this one city are pleased
• to profane the holiness of God's day of rest by senseless
outcries egainst our Holy Father, Christ's Vicar on
Earth, will you allow yourselves to excite an equal or
greater profanation by deeds of violence, and even of
bloodshed, and possible murder? God forbid! I be-
lieve in and hope for better things from you; not only
can you do no good by such a course to the cause which
you support, but you injure it most grievously—the
cause of your dear Pontiff in the course of justice, of
truth, of virtue, of religion, of God himself. Now
bludgeons and blows and tumult are not the means by
which such a cause is to be enforced or defended.
Nothing would offend our Sovereign Pontiff's tender
heart more than to hear that you, his most cherished
Irish children, have attempted to support his sacred
cause with such violence. He himself his offered meek-
ness and sweetness to the vaunts and vulgar abuse, as
well as to the threats of his enemies, arrested by God's
hand when advancing against his capital. Imitate his
conduct, act on the same noble principles, and leave his
cause to God.

And you, moth.ns and daughters, on whom falls the
heaviest penalty when the men of your families fall into
crime and suffer its punishment, do you cling to the
arms of your dear ones if they attempt to rush from
home to join in further disturbances—hang on their
necks and weep and entreat and caress them into
Catholic sentiments of meekness and gentleness. Steal
or tear away their weapons of lawless violence from
their hands, and put the rosary or the sacred medal of
Mary immaculate in their place. No Irishman's heart
will resist the united pleadings of religion and domestic
affections. Join these together, my dear daughters in
Christ, and for once command those whom you habi-
tually, affectionately obey.'

articles.title: DISTRESS IN LANCASIIIRE.
articles.text:
THE DISTRESS IN LANCASIIIRE.

There are now at least 85 different local relief com-
mittees, if not more, in so many towns, villages, and
districts in Lancashire and Cheshire, to whom the Lord
Mayor's Committee have sent grants of money in aid—
to many of them again and again—and who have,
therefore, come to rely to a great extent on this source
of extraneous assistance in feeding the famishing people.
The sum they have remitted in this way, as the almoners
of the public bounty, amounts now, in round numbers,
to upwards of £40,400, averaging from £2,000 to
£4,000 a week for months past.
BLACKBURN.—The returns of out-relief for the union,
as presented to the Board of Guardians at their weekly
meeting on Saturday, show a large increase of destitu-
tion during the past week. It seems that no less than
18,161 persons had been relieved with £954 17s. 4d.,
against 17,144 persons relieved with £876 2s. 11d, in
the preceding Iveek, and 2,552 persons relieved with
i £136 6s. Bd. n the corresponding week of 1861.
WIGAN.—The reports of the relieving officers to the
Wigan Board of Guardians on Friday showed that dur-
ing the week just ended 4,079 persons had been relieved
with £263 17s. id., an increase on the week of 246
persons and of £22 11s. 4d. in the cost. As compared
with last year, the increase was in the number of persons
1,846, and in the cost £137 us. The number in the
workhouse was 465, an increase of 90, and 50 vagrants
had been relieved. This makes the total number of
persons aided during the week 14,775, the additions to
the returns of guardians and relief committee having
been no less than 500 during the week.
STOCKPORT.—The number of persons relieved by the
various committees has risen from 11,605 last week to
13,472 this, showing an increase of 1,767. In addition
to the above there are 7,201 persons receiving parochial
relief in the town, raising the entire number of persons
who are receiving assistance to 20,673.
PRESTON.—The number of recipients on the books of
the Charitable Relief Committee is 28,583. The dis-
tribution of kind during the week has been 83,0281 b. of
bread, 12,033 quarts of soup, and 3,900 quarts of
coffee; the total cost being £62o.—nearly double what
it was three months ago. The committee' in view ofb
the necessities of the winter, have taken a large build-
ing, formerly occupied as a foundry, in Crooked-lane,
in which to store wearing apparel, bedding, &c., the
rooms on the groußd floor being converted into an addi-
tional soup kitchen.
BURNLEY.—A meeting of the Relief Committee of this
borough was held on Thursday last, presided over by the
mayor. The committee appointed to consider the in-
creased rate of relief recommended that it be increased
to is. 6d. per head, instead of is. 9d., as previously sug-
gested. This was put in the form of a motion, and
unanimously agreed to.
BURY.—From returns of the state of employment
which have just been collected by the superintendent of
police, it appears that in this borough, containing
37,564 inhabitants, the total number of hands employed
in factories is 12,174, of whom 6,685 are on short time,
3,004 on full time, and 2,485 altogether out of employ-
ment. To meet this distress a new poor-rate has been
laid for the township of Bury at 2s. in the pound, which
it is estimated will produce £7,139, and one for Elton,
which will produce £1,827. About 3,000 persons are
receiving parochial relief within the borough, and 729
families have been relieved by the relief committee.

FATAL BOAT ACCIDENT.—On Sunday two gentlemen
residing in Liverpool, Messrs. Campbell and Baker,
went out from Hoylake in one of their own boats for a
cruise. A gust of wind arising, the boat was capsized;
and though both gentlemen attempted to swim to shore
they were prevented by the heavy sea which was
running at the time, and perished. A boatman who was
with them had a narrow escape, and was only saved by
the timely assistance of the Hoylake lifeboat.
FIRST-FRUITS Or, PRESIDENT LINCOLN'S SLAVE
PROCLAMATION.—The first case of emancipation under
President Lincoln's Proclamation is thus alluded to in
the letter of a New York correspondent, dated Cincin-
natti, Sept. 24 :—' Three negro "boys" were brought
before Lieutenant-Colonel Sipes, military governor of
the two towns of Covington and Newport, yesterday
morning, about ten o'•clock. (The President's proclama-
tion was only published here in yesterday morning's
papers.) They were closely examined by Colonel Sipes,
and testified that they had escaped from Kirby
Smith's army where they were employed as servants.
When asked if their masters were in the rebel army,
they replied that their "young mas'rs" were. When
asked where they were going, they said they "didn't
know"--they "jest run." Colonel Sipes remarked that,
under the President's new proclamation, his duty was
plain; and to-day they were provided with "freepapers"
in due form, and Went into the world the "first-born" of
the new order of things.'
THE DANISH PitiNcess.--Some London correspondents
of some country papers have picked up somewhere a
notion. that the Princess Alexandra, daughter of Duke
Christian of Glucksburg, and future Princess of Wales,
is, by a str Inge error, regarded as a Danish Princess. We
are to understand that she is root and branch a German.
The truth is, that the only clouding of her distinct suc-
cession from the line of Sovereigns which has occupied
the throne of Denmark for the last four centuries consists
in the fact that her father, Duke Christian, descends
through his grandmother and mother, instead of through
his grandfather and father, from King Frederick
V. Of Frederick's sops! Christian and another Freierick,
the elder became Christian Vll.—but his daughter Louise
married a Landgrave of Hesse, and it was a daughter of
hers, married to a Duke of Glucksburg, whose son
i
Christian, named n 1853 successor to the throne of Den-
mark, is the f:ther. of the Princess Alexandra. Through
her mother the Princess descends quite as directly from
Use Danish line, Prince Christian being married to the
granddaughter of that Frederick who was son of King
Frederick V. and brother of King Christian VII. Con-
nected thus both by the father's and mother's side with
the Royal House of Denmark, and daughter also of the
next King of the Dane!, we have as much right to call
this young lady a Danish Princess as we have to say that
her future husband is an English Prince.—Examiner.
SIGNS OF WINTER. —On the North Yorkshire hills,
on Sunday, snow and rain fell nearly all day, with cold,
boisterous north-east winds. The weather in the north
has been very unsettled since Friday, and it is much to
be regretted that a large breadth of the harvest—oats
..thiefly—is yet unsecured in the exposed positions, and
sonic crops are still to cut.
.During the Week very little
progress has been made with the harvest; what has
beeii stacked has been in very damp condition, and fac-
tors are wearied with offers of out-of-conditioned new
vain.

A VISIT TO THE NEW IRON-CLAD

articles.title: SHIP YARDS.
articles.text:
SHIP YARDS.

(From the New York Tribune of Sept. 30.)
Our naval reporter yesterday visited the yards in which
iron-clad ships ape building for the Government. In them
all tne utmost energy and industry were visible. The
following is a rough estimate of the number of hands
employed in the different places named :
Delameter works
Greenpoint 2,000 men.
Jersey City
Dry Dock (Whitney's ship) 5OO men.
Mr. Webb's

Total 5,200 men.

,
Besides these, in nearly all first-elass foundries and
smitheries contracts have been obtained, thus necessita-
ting the employment of more hands. In the Navy-
yard there are nearly 4,000 men, and, working on the
wooden vessels in course of construction hereabout,
there must be at least 5,000; so that it would hardly
exaggerate the fact to state that nearly 20,000 men are
now employed in the vicinity of New York, whose
wages the Navy Department will pay ultimately.
The Weehawken will probably be the next iron-clad
vessel launched. She is building at Colwell's foundry
in Jersey City. Plankino• has already begun and the
deck floor is being laid. °On the upper part of the hull
the first iron plates were laid yesterday. They form,
with the wooden portion of the bulwarks, a defence
quite as wide, and far stronger, than the generality of
stone walls,' so common in the suburbs. The lower
part of the hull is being planed and prepared for the
mail. It is expected that by the Ist proximo the Wee-
hawken will be afloat.

In the same yard with this vessel, the Comanche,
intended for California, is being built. She is all iron.
Work on her is advancing rapidly.
Greenpoint is like a human beehive. Ears are worth-
less when mane you get inside the bounds of the Con-
tinental Works. The Montauk, Kaatskill, and Passaic,
of the nine Monitor fleet, and the Onondaga and
Puritan, of special fleet, are in hand. The Passaic,
launched and engined,' is preparing rapidly for sea.
The Montauk and Kaatskill will be afloat in a month.
They are very much like their sister ships. The Puritan
is the Great Eastern of the lot, being nearly as large as
the three combined. She is only in frame. The Onon-
daga is further advanced. She is all iron, and will have
two turrets. The Morgan Iron Works are getting up
her machinery.
The Dictator is going up at the Delameter Iron
Works. Her ribs are ship shaped, and the several parts
of the monster begin to look recognisable.
Mr. Whitney's iron ship is more advanced than any
save the Weehawken. The Moodna is the name given
to her by Mr. Welles. The hull is finished, and a good
portion of the armour on. The entire shell' of the
vessel is complete, and, if it were of wood, would be in
launching condition. The turrets are two in number,
and are nearly ready. Before the expiration of October
the Moodna will be ready for floating out.
Mr. Webb's ram has just been commenced. She will
be 7,000 tons burden. All other ships on the iron sys-
tem will be mere catamarans to her. At present she
looks too unlike anything to be described. In two
months she vk ill be a great ram, able to go to sea, and
accommodate a larger ship's company than the Niagara.
Her name has not been mentioned yet, but people think
it ought to be Washington, as we have no man-of-war
of that name.

SIGHT AND SIZE OP THE EYE.—In the higher order
of creation, where the eye assumes that general character
with which we are familiar, it will be found that the
degree of sight depends very much upon the size of the
organ and upon its lustre. In the mole, where the eye
is small, the creature has but imperfect sight; and if ever
it gets out of its burrow it is lost, and there is no great
difficulty in taking it alive. The eye of the weasel is
not large, but shines very bright, and unless you come
upon it suddenly (when it is in pursuit of its prey), so
rapid are its movements, from the keenness of its sight,
that you mu,t be an expert marksman ever to hit it with
your shot. Again, the eye of the cow and the
though large, are without much lustre, and their sight is
inferior to that of the dog and cat, in which creatures
great brilliancy often exists.

tinue in its present shape until the Ist of January next,
the number of slaves which will on that day be virtually

will be as follows :

THE NEW MUNICIPAL GUARDS OP NAPLES.-011r
new Municipal Guards are the admired of all beholders,
and make a very spruce appearance. They wear a dark
blue coat, with gilt bands round the neck and sleeves;
gilt buttons with the cross of Savoy on them; white
belt, and a long sword with a blue tassel. The trousers
are gray, with a blue stripe at the side, while the whole
of this highly decorated personage is surmounted by a
blue casquette, with gold straps round it. As to the
personale of these men, they look well, and have a very
manly appearance. As you willeinfer, they have almost
it military organisation; they are lodged in the Hospital
of the Sacramento, have four carlini (Is. 6d.) a day, and
are provided with every requisite, en with linen.
Their ditties, or a part of them, are prescribed by the
regulations which the municipality have laid down for
maintaining decency in the city, and though these reeula-
dons do not embrace half the evils of which we 'iaave
reason to complain, still they strike at the more glaring,
and, if carried out, will make Naples, comparatively
speaking, a paradise.—Letter from Naples.
A BEAUTY OF BOItNEO.---Mr. Spencer St. John thus
describes the daughter of one of the Datus of Borneo :
She was the loveliest girl in Borneo. I have never
seen a naiive surpass her in figure, or equal her gentle,
expressive countenance. She appeared but sixteen
years of age' and as she stood near, leaning against the
door-post in the most graceful attitude, we had a perfect
view of all her perfections. He dress was slight
indeed, consisting of nothing but a short petticoat
reaching from her waist to a little above her knees.
Her skin was of the light clear brawn, which is almost
the perfection of colour in a sunny clime; and, as she
was just returning from bathing, her hair' unbound, fell
in great luxuriance over her shoulders. Her eyes were
black, not flashing, but rather contemplative, and her
features were regular —even her nose was straight. So
intent was she in watching our movements, and wonder-
ing at our novel mode of eating with spoons and knives
and forks, that she unconsciously remained in her
• graceful attitude for some time; but, suddenly recol-
lecting that she was not appearing to the best advan-
tage in her light costume, she moved away slowly to
her room, and presently came forth dressed in a silk
jacket and a new petticoat, with bead necklaces and
gold ornaments. In our eyes she did not look so inte-
resting as before.'
SINGULAR REGOVERY OF £350 LEFT IN A RAILWAY
CARRIAGE.—On the 11th Mr. Chubb, cashier at the Soho
Foundry, left Birmingham by the 11.35 p.m. train,
having previously obtained the necessary cash for the
payment of wages from the bank. The money was
placed in two small bags, which were carried in a black
leather travelling bag. When Mr. Chubb got out of
the railway carriage at the Smethwick station, he, it
would appear, forgot all about the cash for the moment,
and the train proceeded on to Dudley. Here Banks,
the head porter, in the performance of his duty, looked
into all the carriages, and in one of the first-class found a
black leather travelling bag. This he took to the station-
master, who, on finding that the bag had not been
fastened, examined its contents, and found that it con-
tained £350 in sovereigns and half-sovereigns. Shortly
afterwards inquiries were made for a bag containing
money, and on an explanation being given of its con-
tents, it was at once sent to the Soho Foundry Com-
pany. The gentleman who left the money in the
carriage wished to reward the porter Danks for his
honesty, and, we believe, tendered him a sovereign,
intimating, however, that this was simply his own
reward, and was not to be regarded as such a liberal
donation as he thought the man ought to have.
• THE RECOGNITION OF THE SOUTHERN CONFEDE-
RACY.—In consequence of a notice by Mr. M'Fie, one
of the members of the Liverpool Chamber of Commerce'
to the effect that he would bring forward a requisition
to call a special meeting of the chamber, to consider
the recognition by her Majesty's government of ,the
Southern Confederacy, the meeting of the council of
that body was unusually well attended on Monday, and
considerable interest was manifested in the matter on
'Change and elsewhere. After some routine and unin-
teresting business had been gone through, the chairman
(Mr. Chill* announced that Mr. M'Fie had altered his
determination, and would not bring forward the requi-
sition. This result was received with much satisfaction,
and the council expressed theanselves satisfied with th
present policy of the government, believing that as the
government had steered them right up to the present
time, they would continue to do so. Mr. Baruchson,
one of the members who had formed one of a deputa-
tion to the congress of the International Social Science
Association, at Brussels, said the majority of associa-
tions were in favour of maintaining a strict silence ma
this subject.

During the past week 29 wrecks were reported, making
a total for the present year of 1,322.
Garibaldi intends, it is said, to have himself removed in
a few days from Varignano to an hotel at La Spezzia, in
which his son Menotti has already taken up his residence.
Father Panteleo, Garibaldi's chaplain, who was arrested
at Naples, has been set as liberty.
The Superior Court of California has decided that the
poll tax of 2i dollars per mmth on every Chinaman in the
state is in accordance with the constitution.
The pioneer of a fleet of immense iron-clad ships is now
building at Jersey, for the protection of Pacific coast.
Major Samuel Blackell, formerly Lientenant-Governor
of Dominica, has been appointed Governor of Sierra Leone.
The expenditure of the Confederate Government, up to
the Ist of August last, is declared by the Secessionist
journals to be about 70 millions sterling.
Miss Burdett Coutts has been making personal inquiry
into the distress of the cotton districts. Miss Coutts is
accompanied by a friend, Mrs. Brown.
Shortly after the 10th of November the Queen will
arrive at Windsor Castle, where her Majesty will remain
until after the expiration of the twelve months from the
death of the Prince Consort, and will probably spend the
Christmas at the Castle.
A few days ago Prince Charles, brother to the King of
Prussia, visited Windsor Castle and the royal farms and
gardens at Frogmore.
We understand that Mr. Ingram, of the royal gardens
at Frogmore, carried away four prizes for fruit and vege-
tables, at the late Grand International Horticultural Show
at South Kensington.
Mr. Henry Harley, of Windsor, is engaged by the de-
scendants of the poet Walter to put into thorough repair
the beautiful marble tomb in the churchyard of Beacons-
field to the memory of that poet.
A young German student arrived in town last week from
Heidelberg, on a visit to some English friends. He was
asked what he was most anxious to see after the Great
Exhibition. ‘Blondin in the pulpit and Spurgeon on the
tight-rope,' was his reply.
Immense quantities of herrings have been caught on the
coast of Down. The fishermen have got ready all their
old boats, mended all their nets, and they are very busy in
laying in a store of wholesome fish for winter. Herrings
are sold for a farthing each.
The Mayor of Bradford, following the example of the
Lord Mayor of London, has refused to convene a public
meeting for the purpose of expressing sympathy with
Garibaldi, and protesting against the French occupation of
Rome.

The police of Vienna, considering that political and im-
moral songs are bung by itinerant singers in the streets,
has given orders for all such persons to be subjected to a
strict surveillance. In future, no verses will be allowed to
be sung unless they have been previously submitted to the
direction of the press.
The following statement of the relative proportions of
the war and merchant navies of Europe is given in a new
work, entitled Puissance Comparee Divers Etats de
l'Europe ' One thousand tons of the merchant navy
are protected, on the average by 3.17 guns in Portugal,
2.70 in Denmark, 2.15 in Holland, 2.10 in Austria, 2 in
France, 1.40 in England, 1-25 in Spain, 0.99 in Prussia,
and 0.58 in Greece.'

The celebrated mosaic table in the Roman Court, which
has been so much admired, has been purchased by the
King of Italy, on tilt for £2,000.
It has been said a brevet would take place on the coming
of age of the Prince of Wales. We believe there is no
authority for the assertion.
_ _

It is ;aid the colonelcy of the 32nd Foot will be given to
Lord Melville, who will be transferred from the 100th.
What's in a name ? ' was very curiously illustrated the
other day at an agricultural association dinner, at which
Lord Berners, author of the new Game Preservation Act,
presided. One of the toasts was actually proposed by a
Mr. Pochin, who should at once have been proceeded
against according to law.
_ . _ _

-In the city of --igew York 6,000 persons are employed fis
the printing trade. They use up every year 5,000,000
dollars' worth of paper, ink, &c., and produce 11,000,000
dollars' worth of books. The capital employed is esti-
mated at 8,500,000 dollars.
Amongst the shipments made at Chicago during the
week ending the 20th ult., were the following, viz. :-
61,330 bArrels of flour; 394,674 bushels of wheat ;
1,524,678 bushels of corn; 120,512 bushels of oats ;
13,050 bushels of rye; 179,27011a5. of seeds; 28,0001b5. of
meat; 1,728,0281b5. of lard; 39,9051b5. of tallow; and
17,637 live hogs.
_ _

_
Garibaldi is—on the relief list of a benefit society. He is
the president of a little society at Belgiojosa, in Lombardy,
and, as an invalided member unable to gain his living,'
is entitled by the rules to 24 francs, which he received a
week or two ago. The general was amused and delighted,
it is said, by the remittance, and sent off his formal receipt
by the following post.
The contract for putting up the chains of the late Hun-
gerford-bridge and completing the suspension-bridge at
Clifton has been taken, and the works are expected to be
commenced in about three weeks. In anticipation of this
long unfinished structure being at length completed, Sir
Greville Smyth, of Ashton Court, had sold 125 acres of
land for the purpose of building villas on the Somerset_
shire side of the Avon.

It is a pity that the company which has just now made
its bow to supply us with £lOO,OOO worth of cabs had not
thought of their spec.' at the commencement of this sea-
son; but better late than never,' and perhaps the evil of
being under the present greedy tribe of cab proprietors
was not made manifest before, and the company is the
result of a season cf as arrant extortion as ever was prac-
tised in London. The plan of this company embraces the
Continental principle of supply.
London will be riddled by pneumatic pipes shortly,
as well as underground railways. The first pipe for blow-
ing along letters at the rate of fourteen miles an hOur is
laid on between the North Western Railway termi-
nus and the district post-office of that locality.
It will be at work within a mouth, and will
then be continued to the General Post Office, doubt-
less spreading with rapidity all over London. As a lady,
crinoline and all, was once experimentally sent through
the pipe, it points out what the invention is likely some
day to be applied to. At any rate, railway officials can be
shot through as according to St. Martin's4e-Grand
notions, they are of little consequence.
At a meeting of the Aberlour Rifle Corps, on Saturday
night, for the nomination of officers, the corps uninamously
chose Lieutenant Slack as their captain and Ensign Hurry
as lieutenant. This is a good combination; there is little
likelihood of the commanding officer being 'slack' in his
attention to his duties and to the interests of the corps,
when he has a personified hurry' constantly at his heels.'
The ebpulation of Michigan has grown in twenty years
from 212,000 to 751,000; the value of real estate from 38
million dollars to 263 million; the wheat and other grain
grown, from 7 million bushels to 25 million; the wool
produced, from 153,000 lbs. to 4 million lbs. ; the number
of sheep and cattle reared, from 300,000 to 1,700.000; and
the quantity of hay grown, from 130,000 tons to '761,000
tons.

Details of great interest are expected concerning the
interior of our Australian possessions from Mr. Lomberg,
who has safely crossed the continent. It is thought that
the whole district passed over by the traveller is fertile in
the extreme, and will open up a field of enterprise for the
settler when the fever of gold-mining is over, or it has
settled into a more healthy business, and presents less of
the character of a lot: cry.
The following epitaph, written by Walter Savage
Landor, has been placed upon the grave of Mr. G. p. R.
James, at Venice :--‘ George Payne Rainsford Jame:,
British Consul-General in the Adriatic, died at Venice,
aged 60, on the 9th of June, 1860. His merits as a writer
are known wherever the English language is, and as a
man they rest in the hearts of many. A few friends have
erected this humble and perishable naonment.'
The rich railway speculator, Salamanca, is to have the
husband
of
at entertainingsalaman ca,s the Queen of Spain and her
palace. For this pur-
pose he has sent for all the magnificent furniture from
his mansion at Caravanchal, and this is being transported
across the snow-clad summits of the Sierra Morena at
immense cost. He will entertain his
Sovereign more
sumptuously than Wolsey feasted bluff Harry at Hampton
Court, or Leicester banqueted Queen Bess at Kenilworth.
An odd feature in this Royal progress is the gifts of car-
riages and horses which have poured in upon the Queen.
At Cadiz the municipality presented a sumptuous carriage,
horses, and harness to the Queen; at ldeville a similar gift
was made by Baron Bammaija ; and Senor Calderon hag
Prepared a like costly gift for his sovereign to enter
Granada. The Royal stales, all spacious as they are, will
scarce suffice to contain these equipages.

A correspondent gives us a remarkable instance of the
power of surperstition in some quarters of the Highlands.
During the fishing season, as we are informed, a person
is in the habit of going about amongst the Highlanders,
who picks upa good livelihood by pretending to secure tO
the believers in his conjuring powers a liberal supply of
herrings. He also pretends to have certain influences over
the produce of the cow. The peregrinations of this
character are by no means limited. Lochbrown, Poolewe,
and Gairloch form a small part of his field of operations.
His business is said to extend from Wick all round to
Greenock, which he visits at certain seasons of the year,
besprinkled commencing at the south and going along the coast north:.

A curious announcement has appeared in the Dublin
journals. It professes to come from an officer of the
Indian army, at present resident in England, who is
desirous of obtaining the agency of an Irish estate. He is
of business habits, and has the highest testimonials from
general and other officers with whom he has served; but
these are not the grounds upon which he rests his fitness
for the office. Ile coolly winds up the list of his qualifica-
tions by stating that he does not mind being shot at!
There is an offensive spirit of bravado in this declaration,
when the fate of Braddell, M. Thiebault, and other recent
victims of assassination is recollected. This officer may be
courageous enough, but he lacks the equally necessary
?).
attribute of discretion. Had M. nuebault, had more
discretion and less bravery he rag t have been alive now.
Mr. F. T. Buckland gives a curious account, in a weekly
periodical, of a French
giant, M. Joseph Brice, who is
now exhibiting himself in the metropolis. He is so ta.l
that when he called on Mr. Buckland, at the Albany-street
Barracks, the troop horses shied and snorted .at him,
though they are pretty well; accustomed to tall men.'
Lifegutrdsmen of the highest statue can walk under his
outstretched arm and not touch it by some inches, and
when his arms are extended his stretch measures AO less
than 951 inches. M. Brice is 'ajoli garcon '—a very
nice' giant indeed—possessed of the best of good tempers,
and quite the reverse of the disagreeable, quarrelsome
raonsterf that giants are generally supposed to be. Hid
exact hzight is said to Ise 7 feet 6 inches.

LATER FROM AMERICA.

NEW Yonx., Oar. 3, Evening.—The address of the
loyal governors to President Lincoln has been pub-
lished. They pledge their support to the President,
declare that the work of restoring the Union shall
not fail, and urge raising a reserve force of 109,000
men for twelve months. They approve the President's
emancipation proclamation, and think that the policy
now inaugurated will give speedy triumph to the
Federal arms. Heavy skirmishißg has taken place
between General Buell's advance guard and the Con-
federates. Buell's army is drawn up in a line of battle at
Bardstown, 21 miles from Louisville. An engagement is i
expected. A resolution has been introduced n the Con-
federate Congress that President Lincoln's emancipation
proclamation is a gross violation of the usages of war, and
should be held up to the execration of mankind, and
counteracted by such severe retaliatory measures as in
the judgment of President Davis may be calculated to
secure its withdrawal or arrest its execution. Several
members favoured hoisting the black flag, and declar.
ing every citizen in the Southern Confederacy a soldier
authorised to kill every man found on Confederate soil
in arms against the government. The resolutions were
referred to the Judiciary Committee.

NE W Yoxx,Oct. 4, -Morning.—The Richmond En-
parer tays that President Lincoln's proclamation will
simply drive the negroes to their destruction. They
are cheerful and happy now,. but Lincoln plots their
death, for their insurrection is their swift destruction.
Released from authority the negro is a savage, and
the same ignorance which drives him to destruction
stimulates him to excess. The same journal says :
'Our military operations are henceforward to assume
a grave character. Lincoln's new problem destroys
all terms between us, and the next campaign will
'be a tremendous one, both for the character
and the magnitude of the hostilities.' The New
York World of to-day thinks that the pro-
clamation will add to the horrors of the war, and
make it twice as difficult to conquer the South, and
events will prove the proclamation to be the greatest
mistake of the war. The Southern journals say that
M'Clellan's army is on the south side of the Potomac,
and advancing by way of Harper's Ferry, and Shep-
herdstown. An engagement is impending. The Con-
federate General Lee has made preparations to meet
the enemy. The Richmond Whig has information that
the entire Confederate loss at the battle of Manassas was
5,000, and in all engagements in Maryland from 5,000 to
7,000. General Beauregard has assumed the command
of the Confederate army in South Carolinaand Georgia.
President Lincoln has passed several days in visiting
Harper's Ferry and the Antietam battle-field, and re
viewing the troops. General Bader has ordered all
persons refusing to take the oath of allegiance to have
their names registered as enemies of the United
States. Those taking the oath will be recommended
for pardon. The Federal General Morgan, who wa:
with his forces lately at Cumberland Gap, has reached
the Ohio river, opposite Portsmouth. After Novembei
the Ist next no foreign invoices will be received fox
entry at the New York custom-house unless eertifict,
to by consul's certificate at the place of shipmen,
abroad.

articles.title: ANOTHER RAILWAY ACCIDENT.
articles.text:
ANOTHER RAILWAY ACCIDENT.

On the 13th the mail train on the London,Chatham.
and Dover Railway, which leaves the Victoria station
at 8 p.m., met with an accident, the cause of which at
present cannot be ascertained, between Sittingbourm
and Teynham, and about quarter of a mile from the
latter place. It appears that the train in ,question
passed through Sittingbourne at 9.29 p.m. letting oft
steam, contrary to the usual custom with mail or
express trains passing through the smaller stations,
and when it reached a spot about two miles from Sitting-
bourne it ran off the metals, the engine tearing up part of
the up-line, then apparently bounding back to its own
line, and finally rushing across the line, the tender
with it, barricading the road. Theeecond-class carriage,
which was next the tender, was thrown off the rails.
the other carriages being more or less upset. The
engine-driver, named Wm. Reed, was thrown out, and
was found with the fire-box of the engine Testing on
his breast. The body was dreadfully mutilated, the
poorfellow's right leg being broken below the knee
his scalp nearly torn off, and, it is believed, his chest
crushed. The left hand and arm was also burnt fear-
fully, the skin pealing from them like parchment The
stoker, in a manner that seems miraculous, escaped
with a contusion of the spine, and the scraping of the
skin off the left hand. Five or six of the passengers
received slight contusions, but beyond this, as far as
could be gathered, we are happy to state nothing of a
serious nature occurred. Drs. Rae and Fisher' of
Sittingbourne, were speedily on the spot. They had
those who were injured sent on to Sittinghourney•one
of the gentlemen remaining to see the driver ex-
tricated. On information of the accident being received
at Sittingbourne and Faversham junctions, gangs of
workmen, porters, &c., were immediately dispatched
to the spot, accompanied by their respective station
masters, Messrs. Barnard and Breeze. It would seem
that a goods train was passing the mail train et the
time of the accident, and, in fact, had only cleared the
down train by about three yards, when the latter ran
off the metals. Had the goods train been but half a
minute later, the loss of life would probably have been
fearful. Fortunately, also, there was no embankment
just there, or the train must inevitably have been east
down. The sight presented by the line at the place of
the accident was surprising. For nearly 100 yards
the line was torn up. Part of the funnel of the engine
Was embedded in the earth, the other part being thrown
about ten yards further on while the dome' was pre-
cipitated some twenty yards on the other, or down side
of the line. The body of Reed was not extricated until
about three hours after the occurrence, and was then
conveyed on a trolley' to Sittingbourne to await an
inquest.
Deceased leaves a wife and several children-

At four o'clock on Tuesday -afternoon Mr. Hills, the
district coroner, opened an inquiry into the cause of
the accident, at the Fountain Hotel, Sittingbourne.
The Coroner, after the jury had been sworn, stated
that it was not his intention to take evidence at great
length on that occasion, as he intended adjourning the
inquiry to enable all the facts connected with the acci-
dent to be laid before the jury. It would be better for
the jury to visit the spot where the accident happened,
Which would probably enable- them to arrive at the
cause of the accident. _ _ _

• The jury, accompanied by the coroner and the offi-
cials i
ls of the company, then proceeded n omnibuses
and cabs to the scene of the accident, and spent some
time in inspecting the line at the spot. The huge
engine still lay where it fell over, but the tender and
all the carriages but one had been removed. The
dowir line of 'rail had also been relaid to enable the
traffic to be carried over the line. Superintendent
Green, of the Kent county police, who visited the spot
immediately after the accident, pointed out to the jury
the spot at which the engine first left the line, which
he clearly observed by the appearance of the rails and
permanent way. The line, however, having been
since repaired, there was nothing in the appearance of
the metals to assist
the accident. _ the jury in defining. the cause of

ift-e-r spending about an hour in the examination of
the line, engine, and broken carriages, the jury
returned to Sittingbourne, and the inquest was then
adjourned.

THE VINTAGE.--Accounts from the celebrated vine-
Yards of Nuits, in the Cote d' Or, of the Bth inst., state
that the vintage is quite concluded, and the wine-growers
are now able to judge of the quality as well as of the
quantity of the produce. The quality of the wine is
said to be good and the quantity equal to that of a good
ordinary year, and the vines of inferior quality will pro-
duce more than a good ordinary crop. The vine-dressers
at first feared that the quality would be inferior, but,
the vintage having been delayed as long as possible, fine
Weather set in, and the grapes became perfectly ripe.
Although the vintage in Burgundy is not one of the very
best
The it may be classPd among the good ordinary years.
, vintage is nearly 'concluded in the Bortlelais and
""ughout the South of France, but the result is not
everywhere satisfactory. In many places the oidium
and a scorching sun has caused much. damage, which
must affect both the quantity and quality of the wine.
The vine dressers who applied sulphur to the vines have
escaped loss, Wijije others are forced to use extraordinary
measures to -
preserve their wine from decomposition.

articles.text:
THE BEE-HIVE, SATURDA V, eCTOBER 18, 1862.

THE COMMISSIONERS OF THE IN-
TERNATIONAL EXHIBITION.

TO THE EDITOR.

Sir,—Her Majesty's Commissioners met to-day for
the first time since the publicntion of Earl Granville's
letter from Gotha, of the 4th instant, and since the
receipt of the annexed letter from the Hon. Frederic
Cadogan.
They direct me to request that you will be so good as
to publish Mr. Cadogan's letter, and that you will
further allow. them to avail themselves of this oppor-
tunity of statmg in your columns, in the most emphatic
terms, that at the time when the refreshment contract
was let to Messrs. Veillard and Martin Gueppet, neither
they themselves nor the Executive of the Exhibition
had any knowledge whatever of the existence of a deed
of agreement between the contractors and Mr. Cadogan.
They did not, of course, suppose that Mr. Cadogan's
constant services were given to the refreshment con-
tractors gratuitously; but it was not till some time after
the opening of the Exhibition—six months after the con-
tract was signed—that the existence of a formal agree-
ment became known to them. The details of that agree-
ment are unknown to them even at the present mo-
ment.

DEAR SIR WENTWORTII3—I regret very much to find
that there exists in the minds of some persons an impres-
sion that the paragraph in my letter to the Times, of the
24th September, where I say the existence of this
agreement was well known not only to the Executive,'
&e., is calculated to infer that her Majesty's Com-
misioners were cognisant of the existence of this agree-
ment at the time that M. Veillard's tender was accepted,
an impression totally at variance with. the true facts of
the case.

My words were intended to show that there was
nothing concealed in my arrangement with M. Veillard,
and that, from the granting of the contract to M. Veil-
late, my position toward him was a matter of common
notoriety. _

Very sincerely yours,
FREI", 'CAD 0 G AN.
