PURSUIT AND CAPTURE OF A

RULVAJJTAY _H USB A 21, D.

A rather funny case has just transpired at Liverpool.
It originated near Carlisle, and ended, so far as present
appearances are concerned, in the detective office of
Liverpool. A few days since, a man named Joseph
Storey, a well-to-do farmer, residing in the neighbour-
hood of Carlisle, left his home with one of his female
domestics, taking with him about .£7OO, and leaving
behind those other inconvenient articles to him—a wife
and four children. From some information which the
deserted wife received, she started off to Liverpool,
accompanied with a stout female friend. On their
arrival there they put themselves in communication. with
_ _

a detective offiCe; of that place, and afterwards pro-
ceeded to a coffee-house, in Islington, where they found
the runaway husband and his paramour. The scene
here can be better imagined than described. The gay
Lothario was thunderstruck, while his frail fair one at
once made ' tracks,' not before, however, she •Deceived
a parting recognition from Mrs. Storey's stout
female friend. The old delinquent now became quite
penitent, and made the most religious vows -as to his
future good conduct. The tears of repentance rolled
down the old sinner's cheeks while he asked forgiveness
of his injured spouse. This was all very well until his
wife cried out, 'Where is your money This brought
Mr. Storey to his senses, and with a look of dismay he
answered, Eh, she has gone and taken a' with her.'
The husband without the money was indeed poor com-
fort, and Mrs. Storey thought so. She at once bundled
him out in search of a police-officer, while she herself,
and her friend kept on the look-out for Meg. R;enturdly
the services of Detective Carlisle were secured, and very
soon Meg was discovered in.a lodging-house. Without
an attempt at concealment, the girl delivered up to the
detective nearly all the money which old Storey had
given her to take care of. The amount was about £6OO
in notes and gold. The money was handed over to Mrs.
Storey, who left at once for Carlisle, the •old gentle-
man preferring to stay behind for a few days. When
last seen he was in the condition which people gen.rally
find themselves in who keep their spirits up by pouring
spirits down.

articles.title: D.ESPE.RATE BOBBERY BY GAROTTERS.
articles.text:
D.ESPE.RATE BOBBERY BY
GAROTTERS.

On'Sunday morning, about one o'clock, Joseph Chee-
tham, who resides at No. 4 Milner. square, Islington,
for the purpose of taking care of the house of his em-
ployers, Messrs. Dove Brothers, was aroused from his
sleep by a violent noise at the door. Having partly
dressed himself, he went •downstairs to see what was
wanted; but the moment he opened the door a man,
who had evidently been waiting under the porch, sprang
upon and pinioned his arms, thereby depriving him of
all power of resistance, while at the same time a second
man, who had also been waiting near the lamp-post,
rushed forward And struck him repeatedly in the face,
breaking two of his teeth; he then seized him by the
throat with one hand, and thrust the other hand into
his mouth. Whilst in this position one of the garotters
matched from his waistcoat pocket a gold guard chain,
and also a gold Albert chain.; they next tried his
pockets, which fortunately were empty. After grasping
him in this brutal fashion until he became nearly in-
sensible, they released him and decamped with their
booty through the square. Cheetham states that he
severely bit the hand that was thrust into his mouth.
Two gentlemen, residing in the square, hearing his
groans, went to his assistance, and found the poor fellow
in the state above described, and his face covered with
blood. He is still suffering greatly from the effects of
this desperate attack—his mouth and throat being very
much swollen, bruised, and discoloured. It does not
.speak much for the vigilance of the police in this district,
that no constable made his appearance near the spot for
three-quarters of an hour after the occurrence.

The good effects of the emancipation of the serfs, in
an economical point of view,' says the Nord, begins to
be already felt in Russia. At the fair at Nigni, the com-
mercial barometer of the empire, the sale of objects for
the use of the popular classes was very considerable,
being an evident sign of prosperity and improvement
among the emancipated serfs. Also, the taxes have been
all paid up, a thing never known before.'
Loss OF THE LOILD ROYSTON' STEAMER.—A tele-
graphic dispatch has been received at Bordeaux, an-
nouncing the total destruction at sea by fire of the
English steamer Lord Royston, Captain Huett. The
Lord Royston was on her passage from Bordeaux to
London when the accident occurred. The crew, who
were forced to abandon the vessel, were picked up at
sea by the French galliot Gazelle, and safely landed at
La Tremblade.

A FURIOUS BURGLAR.—At the Hull sessions, just
held before Samuel Warren, five prisoners, Earned
Henry Gill, David Newmarch, John Broadbent, Robert
Watkin, and George Plaxton, were charged with being
concerned in breaking into the dwelling-house of Mr.
John Jubb, and stealing eleven silver tea-spoons, one
table-spoon, one silver cream jug, two salt-spoons, two
silver pencil-cases, one silver watch, a number of articles
of wearing apparel, and .L 1 .11 money. The jury found
all the prisoners guilty, and the recorder sentenced each
of them to six years' penal servitude. Immediately
upon hearing the sentence, the prisoner Broadbent, who
is a very powerful fellow, commenced to attack the pri-
soner Watkin, who had told he jury that Broadbent was
one of the chief of the burglars. Broadbent struck him
violently on the nose and face, and a severe struggle
ensued between them. The turnkeys endeavoured to
secure Broadbent, but he was so infuriated, and kicked
and yelled to such an extent, that it was not until he
had been knocked down with a blow from one of the
men that he was secured. He cried out that he would
kill Watkin, and die like a soldier,' rather than suffer
six years' imprisonment he handcuffs were ultimately
placed upon him, and he was secured in the cell. Watkin
evidently suffered a great deal from the treatment which
he received from Broadbent. Intease excitement prevailed
in the court during the affray.

articles.title: T.HE POP.E AND THE IRISH BISHOPS.
articles.text:
T.HE POP.E AND THE IRISH BISHOPS.

The Lord Primate and several of the bishops of the
province of Ulster, having been unable to attend the
canonization of the Japanese martyrs in Rome (says the
Ulster Observer), sent to his Holiness an address, to
which they have received the following reply :
Venerable Brethren, Health and Apostolical at Benedic-
tion—Your exalted and conspicuous fidelity, love and
respect towards ourselves and the cht.ir of Peter breathe
forth in every line of the letter which you sent to us on
the 22nd day of the month of August last. For whe
you could not, in accordance with your wishes, be pre-
sent with us on the occasion of the canonization of
many saints, solemnized by us on the Bth day of June
last, you fully declare in this letter that you fervently
adhere to everything that our venerable brethren, the
bishops of the catholic world, present in Rome on the
Feast cf. Pentecost, in the celebrated address which they
presented to us, openly and publicly declared, and even
proudly gloried in. Animated by the same sentiments, you
too bitterly bewail our sorrows, and forcibly condemn
and abhor the wicked and manifold conspiracies, the
impious aßcl sacrilegious attacks by which the enemies
of God wad man, following the ways of iniquity, wage
an unholy war against the catholic church, the apos-
tolic see, and our own person, and by which, discarding
all laws, human and divine, they seek to subvert our
civil authority, and deprive us of the principalities of
our See. These exalted sentiments have brought no
small consolation to us in the midst of our bitter
trials—sentiments which, desetving of the highest
praise, clearly and openly demonstrate how much
you, venerable brethren, have at heart the cause
of the catholic church, of the apostolic see, and of
truth and justice. Wherefore, we are confident
that you, relying on the Divine assistance, and
sustained by your piety and episcopal zeal, will not
relax your exertions, and that, particularly in this
sad and trying crisis, you will, with renewed alac-
crity and courage, fight the good fight, diligently con.
sult for the wed-being of your flocks, expose and refute
the dangerous fallacies and errors of designing men, and
courageously repel their unholy onslaughts. Continue
then, in conjunction with your clergy and faithful
people, to pour forth, without intermission, your fervent
prayers to God, that He may arise and judge His cause,
and support us by His effectual assistance; that He may
sustain His church, and, in the might of His omnipo-
tence, humble her enemies and the enemies of the Holy
See, and bring them from the ways of perdition to the
path of justice and salvation. Finally, we wish you to
be assured of the special affection with which we regard
you ; and of this let the apostolic benediction be a certain
pledge, which, from the bottom of our hearts, we now
impart to you yourselves, venerable brethren, and to all
the clergy, and faithful laity committed to your care.
Given at Rome, at St. Peter's, on the 4th day of Sept.,
in the year 1862, being the seventeeth of our ponti-
ficate. Pits, P.P., 11.

articles.title: ATTEMPTED FRATRICIDE.
articles.text:
ATTEMPTED FRATRICIDE.

On the 12th, at the Bow-street Police-court, John
Joseph Parker, described as a grocer's shopman, was
charged with attempting to murder his brother, Matthew
Parker, by discharging a pistol at him.
Matthew Parker.: I live at 57, Museum-street. I have
no profession. I live on my own private means. The
prisoner is my brother. He is a grocer's shopman' at
present out of employment. This morning, about half-
past eleven o'clock, I was in George-street, St. Giles's.
I had been collecting my rents, when the prisoner came
up from behind me, and, without saying a word, dis-
charged a pistol in my face. I staggered for a moment,
turned round, and then thinking he might fire again, I
run up George-street into Great Russell-street.
Mr. Henry: Was the pistol loaded ?—Witness: Yes.
I had some of the shots extracted afterwards. I ran
away -without ,either of us saying a word. He followed
me and, as I turned into Great Russell-street, I saw
him l drawing another pistol from his pocket. I then
called to the people to stop him, as I continued to run
on. I ran .as far as Hanway-street. Some of the
people stopped him, and took the pistol from him. I
gave him in custody. 1 went to the hospital, where
two or three shot were taken from my. face. He was
only a few feet from me when he fired.
The prisoner did not put any ,question to his brother,
but observed,' I have frequently asked him to assist me,
being in great distress.'
Peter Shepherd, of Hamilton-street, Camden-town,
pianoforte tuner:: I was at the corner of Bainbridge-
street and George-street this morning, and I saw the
prisoner pass me. He made a rush at the last witness,
and fired a pistol in his face. The prosecutor ran away,
followed by the prisoner, who had another pistol in his
hand. 1 followed. By that time there were two or
three others running. By the time wre got to Itathbone-
place the people had stopped the complainant instead of
the prisoner, as the former was running first. The pri-
soner was pointing the second pistol at his brother
over the shoulder of another man. I took off the cap
for fear the Pistol should go •off, and in doing so I
dropped the cap on the ground. I afterwards went to
the spot and picked it up. It was flattened, having
been trodden on. The prisoner said. he would give
himself up to the police. The prisoner made no other
observation.

The prisoner: I deny that I pointed the second pistol
at my brother. I was stopped too soon for that.
Inspector Honey, of the E division of police.: I was on
duty at the station-house when the prisoner was brought
there on this charge. I read the charge to the prisoner,
who made no observation. The pistol produced was de-
livered to me. It was loaded to the muzzle. I drew the
charge, consisting of gunpowder and three slugs. After-
wards I saw two small shot extracted by the surgeon
from the right check of the prosecutor. The prisoner
said something about having a wife and three children.
That was all he said in my hearing.
John Head, police constable E 89 : About half-past
eleven o'clock this morning I was on duty in Totten-
ham court-road, and saw a crowd in Hanway-street,
where I found the prisoner in custody of a private
constable on duty there. The latter told me that he
was charged with assaulting somebody. He did
not state the nature of the assault. I did not know
that it was firing at his brother with a pistol. The
prisoner said,-' All right, policeman, I will go with you.'
On the way to the station the prisoner said, He has
done me out of some money, and my wife and child are
starving.' At the station-house I searched him, and
found on him a pistol, which I now produce. It was
unloaded, and had an exploded cap on the nipple. It
had apparently been recently discharged. I also found
on him 9d. in money, but nothing else.
Mr. Samuel Jones Gee, house surgeon at University
College Hospital: I was in attendance this morning
when the prosecutor was brought to the hospital. I
found about seven or eight small circular wounds, about
the size of a pea, scattered over his face, especially the
forehead and the right theek. Except two, they were
mere abrasions of the skin. From each of the two
spoken of, I extracted a shot, buried underneath the
skin. I delivered the two shot to Inspector Honey, and
they were just like the two which he produces.
Mr. Henry: Prisoner, you have heard the evidence
in this very serious charge against you; do you wish. to
say anything to the charge? Anything you do say will
be taken down in writing and may be used in evidence
against you.—The prisoner: I have been in very great
distress and destitution, and in very bad health. I have
repeatedly applied to my brother to assist me, and he has
promised to do so, but has never kept his promises. He
made promises before my father on his death-bed. The
property was to be divided amongst us, but he has kept
it all to himself.

The prosecutor said there was no truth in this state-
ment.

Mr. Henry: I did not interrupt him, because a pri-
soner may say anything. But there is really no occasion
to answer it. It is not material to this charge. (To the
prisoner) : You are committed for trial for shooting at your
brother with intent to murder.—The prisoner: Very
well, sir.
He was then removed.

An application was made for the delivery to the pri-
soner's wife of the sum of 9d. found on the prisoner by
the officer.

Mr. Henry ordered it to be given to her.

NARROW ESCAPE FROM A RAILWAY Coutstox.—on
the 11th, as the parliamentary train by the London-and
North Western Railway from London was on its way to
Manchester, it had a narrow escape from destruction at
Longsight. The train was due at Manchester at 5.35
p.m., and as it approached Longsight soon after five
o'clock, the driver saw approaching him a train from Man-
chester, on the same line of rails. He was slackening
speed to stop at Longsight, but found it necessary to
reverse his engine and put on breaks to avoid a collision,
so imminent seemed the danger. The driver of the other
train did the same, and fortunately both trains were
stopped; but the two engines had approached within a
yard of each other before this could be effectually ac-
complished. The train from Manchester was au engine
and two empty cattle trucks, and the driver appears to
have been running up the wrong line to the Longsight
depot, for coke, notwithstanding every effort to stop him
as he passed the Ardwick station. The train from Lon-
don had fortunately been detained at Stockport four
minutes beyond its time, to have extra carriages put on,
or in all probability it would have met the other train
between Longsight and Ardwick, when.both were at high
speed, and the loss of life might have been great,asthere
were 14 carriages nearly full of passengers in the parlia-
mentary train. The conduct of the driver of the cattle
ten, whole said to be from Holyhead, will, no doubt,
undergo inquiry, as the rules of the company are severe
against driving on the wrong line under any circum-
stance&

articles.title: FRIGIITFUL R 4 ILWAY A CCID FN 2'.
articles.text:
FRIGIITFUL R 4 ILWAY A CCID FN 2'.

On Monday night, one of the most disastrous rail-
way accidents that has ever occurred in Scotland took '
place near Winchbu.g, on the E iinburgh end Gla,g( w
Railway, involvin: great loss ot life and serious injury
to a large number of passengers. The accident
occurred to the passenger train leaving Edinburgh for
the north on Monday evening at six o'clock, which
came into collision with the ordinary passenger train
which left Glasgow at fire o'clock, at a short distance
west of Win_chbui gb. It appears that for solve time
past repairs have been making on a portion of the line
between Winchbuig and Linlithgow, and during the
repairs the trains have been running there on a
single line for a short distance. The train which
left Edinburgh for Rath at six o'clock was a
small train, consisting of two third- class and
two first-class carriages with one van and a horse-box.
It reached Ratho, the first stopping station, all right
about a quarter past six o'clock, and proceeded to Lin-
lithgow, its next stopping station where it was due at
thirty-five minutes past six o'clock. Shortly after
passing Winchburg, about half-past six o'clock, and
while it was on the single line of rails, the train came
into collision with the passenger train from Glasgow,
which was an unusually heavy one on account of the
Falkirk Tryst. The scene which followed the collision
is described by the passengers who have escaped as
one of the most distressing and heartrending that
could possibly be conceived. The engines and tenders
of both trains were smashed to pieces, and tilted up on
their ends, the first carriage of the Scottish Central
train from Edinburgh, a third-class, was completely
destroyed, as was also a third-class carriage in front
of the Glasgow train. Piled above the broken debris
of these carriages and the engines and tender were a
large number of the carriages of the Glasgow train,
chiefly third-class, with their numerous passengers.
The cries and groans of the wounded and the dying,
and the shrieks of those terrified passengers who had
escaped with comparatively slight injuries arising from
the concussion' are described as most agonising, and
the horrors of the scene were greatly aggravated by
the darkness of the night and the nature of the ground,
the line running through a deep cutting of rock at the
spot where the accident occurred. 'Owing to the speed
at which both trains were running at the time of the
collision the number of passengers injured from
-the concussion was very large, and their injuries,
both external and internal, were generally of a
very severe character. Up to an early hour on Tues-
day morning no reliable information could be
obtained as to the number of persons killed
and wounded, as at the time the last train
left the scene of the accident, shortly after midnight,
the line continued blocked up with the debris of the
broken carriages piled up in an immense heap, and all
the wounded and killed were not taken to Edinburgh.
The fearful extent of the catastrophe may be imagined,
however, from the fact that by the several trains which
arrived after the accident, eleven dead bodies were taken
to Edinburgh, and twenty-three persons all so severely
injured that they had to be conveyed to the Royal In-
firmary, in addition to a considerable number injured,
who, immediately on their arrival, -were, at their own
request, conveyed in cabs to their places of residence.
Robert Morton, the engine-driver of the Scottish Cen-
tral train, and Cochrane, the stoker, were both killed,
and it is reported that the driver of the Glasgow train
was much hurt about the head. The guard of the
Scottish Central train was at the time of the accident
in the van at the back of the train, and escaped with a
slight contusion on the head.

When the telegraphic message for surgical aid
reached Edinburgh, a special train was immediately
prepared. Proceeding to the special train to Craig-
town-bridge, they found the scene already described—
the engines and tenders all smashed up and standing
half on end, with eight or nine carriages above them,
looking, as it is said, as high as a three-storey house.
Beneath the rubbish, and close to the tender, some
four or five people were lying close together, most of
whom had been crashed orsmothered to death, Among
them, however, was the wife and child of the guard of
the Glasgow train, both of whom were alive when
first discovered. It is reported as having been a
touching sight to see the guard, who had been him-
self injured about the head, and whose face was lite-
rally covered over with blood, exerting himself to the
danger of his life in endeavouring to extricate his wife
and child; and all the passengers within sight anct
hearing were much affected by hearing the child cry
out, 'Oh, father, take me out!' The mother died be-
fore she ePalenl be taken out, but the child, we are glad
to learn, has been .saved. As the dead bodies were ex-
tricated they were placed in a horse-box and guard's
van, and the injured were placed in first-class carriages
and removed in special trains to Edinburgh.
The scene at the Edinburgh station as the trains
arrived with the dead and wounded was most exciting,
the station being crowded with iriends of passengers
full of anxiety as to their fate. Many a touching scene
occurred as friends were recognised among the
wounded, and taken away to their homes or to the
infirmary, according as. their wounds were severe or
otherwise.

As usual on such occasions there were many narrow
escapes. Among these we may mention the case of
Mr. 'Cranston, of the Waverley Hotel, who was in the
front third-class carriage of the Glasgow train., sitting
next the aide on the second last seat. When the colli-
sion occurred the side of the carriage fell away, and Iva
fell or rather slid to the ground on the line, just as the
van and other carriages came down on the tap of the
carriage amongst all the passengers.. He escaped alto-
gether unhurt, without even a scratch, and his escape
is almost miraculous.

A young lady, Mrs. Paterson, of Lasewade, was
struck on the breast, and a brooch which she wore broke
in two. She escaped uninjured, and spent the night in
Cranton's Hotel.

Mr. Lamb, a traveller for Simpson and Co., of Ox-
ford-street, was a passenger in the train, and escaped
with a gash on his brow, and was able to walk to
Cranston's Hotel.

James Baird, the guard in charge of the train from
Glasgow, escaped without a scratch. He states that as
soon as the collision occurred, be jumped off and ran
along the line with his lamp in his hand, to prevent any
other train coming up.
The oause of the accident (says the Scotsman) was
undoubtedly some misunderstanding as to the signal at
the single line, but nothing is positively known as to
who is in fault.

The eleven dead bodies removed to the police office
are laid out in two rooms for identification, and present,
as may be imagined, an appalling spectacle.

The operations in Ireland for the relief of the dis-
tressed cotton spinners of Lancashire are being carried
on with energy. Contributions are daily forwarded to
the central committee in Dublin, and in some of the
provinces local associations are formed for the_purpose
of aiding in this charitable work.

TIIE RECENT FIRE AT THE LIVERPOOL WORKHOUSE.
—At the meeting of the Liverpool select vestry, held
on Tuesday, a long report was read from one of the com-
mittees, exonerating the authorities of the workhouse
from the blame attached to them by the water commit-
tee of the corporation in regard to the water supply foe
the building in case of fire. The report stated that the
authorities had done all that lay in their power to meet
the requirements of the case.
A PRIZE Bum.—A young Irishman wrote last week
from London to his family :-4I am very happy to say
that I have to-day, when luckily all my pockets were
empty, been robbed of every single thing in them. Had
I been robbed to-morrow, after I received my uncle's
legacy, the - pick-pockets would have reaped a rich
harvest. Fortunately I had long ago resolved to take a
cab to-morrow, having been duly warned of the light-
fingered gentry.'
A great horticultural fete, just held at Namur, was
one of the most remarkable ever seen in Belgium. More
than 30,000 specimens of fruits were exhibited, com-
prising 8,000 varieties, and 9,000 plates were required
to hold the immense collection. The finest pears were
exhibited by Belgians, the finest apples by Germans, and
the finest grapes by the French.

A MAGISTRATE CHARGED WITH BRAWLING IN
CHURCH.—A most extraordinary case was heard on
Friday, before the magistrates, at Exeter Castle Mr.
Henry Hooper, a leading man in the ‘;ity, an alderman
and magistrate, was summoned, at the instance of
the Rev. John Ingle, one of the masters of Mount
Radford School, for brawling and using indecent lan-
guage in the church of St. Leonard, in the city. It
appeared from the statements and evidence that a child
of Mr. Ingle died some time ago, and that gentleman
proposed to erect above its grave a memorial wooden
cross. The rector of the parish referred the matter to
churchwardens, of whom Mr. Hooper is one. Mr.
Hooper objected to the erection of the cross and a
parish meeting was called. It was represented to the
meeting that it had no power to act in the matter,
whereupon Mr. Hooper became excited and made use
of abusive language towards Mr. Ingle. The defendant
maintained that the rev, gentleman himself had not
limited his conduct by the most orderly rules of pro-
priety; and ultimately the magistrates dismissed the
case, with the comment that the conduct of both parties
had been disgraceful.
A malignant fever has broken out in Philadelphia.
It is supposed to have been occasioned by some bags of
fruit from the West Indies.

ing to make her change her determination of shutting
herself up in a convent rather than return to her hus-

The ceremony of opening the new building just
erected at West Hill, about half a mile from the city,
for the Winchester Diocesan Training School for
Masters, took place at Winchester, on the 14th.
The ceremony of opening the school was performed
by the Bishop of Winchester. Among those present
were Lord Palmerston, M.P., Lady Palmerston, the
Bishop of Oxford, the Bishop of Salisbury, Sir F. 1.
Baring, M.P., and Lady Arabella Baring, the Dean of
Winchester, Archdeacon lalerton, and a large body of
the clergy and gentry of the neighbourhood.
Prayer having been offered,
The Bishop of Winchester delivered the opening
address.

The remainder of the service was then proceeded
with, and on the conclusion, the building having been
pronounced open, the National Anthem was sung.
Divine service was afterwards performed in the
Cathedral, when an eloquent sermon was preached by
the Bishop of Oxford, from Romans 12th and 7th
verse, He that teacheth on teaching.'
On the conclusion of the service the Mayor and Cor-
poration proceeded to the Chapter House, when the
Recorder presented an address to Lord Palmerston.
Lord Palmerston replied as folio vys :—Mr. Mayor and
Gentlemen, I beg to return to you my most sincere
thanks for the address which you have just been kind
enough to present to me. I can assure you it has given
me great pleasure to be allowed to attend upon so
interesting, and I will say, important an occasion as
that which has brought us all together to-day. I trust
that the proceedings which have taken place to-day may
lead te a useful result and a large development of that
system of education which we have assembled to
commemorate, and I my say to found, because we-
have opened a building in which for the future it is to be
carried on. Jam very sensible of the approval which you
have been kind enough to express of the course which I
have pursued in public life. I need not say that the
approval of neighbours—of those who are close to one's
residence, and who have better and more frequent
opportunities of judging than those perhaps who are at
a greater distance, must be more valuable in proportion as
those who expres it have better opportunities of forming
a judgment. It will be the anxious desire of myself,
and of those colleagues with whom I have the happiness
to act, to endeavour to merit the approval of our fellow-
countrymen; and I trust that, profiting by that indul-
gent consideration which the people of this country
always give to the exertions of those who are engaed
in the public service, we shall be able to retain, as long
as we continue in office, that good opinion which you have
been kind enough to express to-day.
The Mayor and Corporation then retired.

The Poole Herald states that Garibaldi will, 2s soon as
he is able to leave Italy, visit a gentleman in the neigh-
bourhood of Lymington, in Hants.
The American papers state that the French have im-
ported a quantity of telegraph wire and railway stores
into Mexico.

The steamers to arrive this week (besides the Etna,
which arrived on Tuesday) are the Borussia, from New
York on the 14th inst., and the Nova Scotia, from
Quebec, also on the 14th. The next Cunard steamer is
the Scotia, and, as this is the most speedy vessel of the
fleet, her advicf a of the Bth inst. may probably be
telegraphed on Friday afternoon.
A Brest journal mentions the arrival in that port on
board the transport Chandernagor, from St. Nazaire,
of the spur or beak of the Magenta, iron-plated
frigate, to which it is about to be adjusted. Its weight
is about 13,000 kilogrammes (13 tons). The gunboats
Salve, Redoute, Arquebuse, and Poudre were in the
basin, about, it was said, to be taken to pieces. Their
engines had been taken out, and were to be sent to
China, to be placed in other gunboats, there to be
constructed. It was reported that, in consequence of
recent trials made with the iron-plated frigate Nor-
mandie, the cuirass of ships thus protected would con-
sist in a simple plating of sheet steel, much thinner,
and consequently much lighter, than the covering now
employed.
WILD HONEY.—The bush around Adelong, Aus-
tralia, has this summer been remarkably prolific in
honey, the wild bee appearing to increase at a much
faster ratio than his domesticated brother. The num-
ber of hives captured, and the weight of their valuable
contents, are really surprising. We hear of one party
of Americans, well acquainted with the habits of this
little industrious insect, and able to track them like
genuine Kentucky bee-hunters, who are regular clip-
pers at the business, gathering their honey by the
quarter-cask, and from this source indulging to its full
measure their national weakness for sweet morsels.
There are but few homes on the Adelong to which the
labours of the bee have not this season contributed a
welcome addition to their supply of comforts.
The Cork Constitution gives the following curious
story about Hayes, but does not vouch for its authen•
ticity : On Saturday week, in the vicinity of Water-
grass-hill; a man, attracted by the noise of a flock of
turkeys in passing through a plantation in which
something appeared to have frightened them came
upon a renew half-seated against a tree. He was
about 60, stooped in the shoulders, and had a pistol in
his hand. The man was somewhat startled, and
thought it better to speak to him kindly. Inquiring
if he'd like a drink, or if he wanted anything, ha
replied, "No;" that he was sometimes hard up, but
had enough then, and, putting his hand into
his breeches pocket, drew out a parcel of notes
and some silver. The operation disclosed another
pistol, covered by the waistcoat. He inquired his way
ta Youghal, asked if there was a police station in a
direction he pointed to, and, when answered in the
affirmative, said. he mustn't go near that. Soon after
he set off, and if he reached Youghal that day he
timed his movements well, for many of the police, we
understand, were absent—some at Lismore, some at
the sessions at Middleton.'

A BLOODLESS DUEL.—A hostile encounter, luckily
bloodless, took place yesterday, on the French frontier,
between M. Bm-tero, a deputy and editor of the Gazette
del Popolo of Turin, and 31. Bensa, one of the King's
private secrehries, who, as you may remember, was by
common report described as a writer in the Tribuno, the
journal which combated the Ricasoli Ministry, and pro-
moted the rise of the Ratazzi Cabinet. It had lately
been rumoured that M. Bensa had been appointed
Consul-General at Tunis, and his nomination had given
rise to very severe comments on the part of the press,
even of those organs which are most devoted to the
interests of the present Ministers, among which no one
had been more outspoken than the Gazette dcl Popolo.
The consequence was a duel, in which the combatants
exchanged two shots each, without the least injury to
either of them. The appointment of M. Bensa has been
stoutly denied by some of the semi-official organs; it,
however, appeared in the Bulletino Consolare, a Govern-
ment publication at Genoa.—Letter front Turin.
Sia G. BOWYER'S APPROVAL OF IRISH RIOTERS.—
The hon. member for Dundalk claims the cessation
of out-door Garibaldi meetings as a triumph of the
Irish. He writes If the meeting had "gone off
well" it would have been boasted as a triumph of
anti-Papal agitation. It was perfectly natural, then,
that the Irish working men, deeply attached to their
Church and its head, and having plenty of strength
and pluck, should determine to break up the meeting.
That this would be so was obvious, and must have been
well known to the Garibaldians, and to the Home Office
and the police. The meeting was a dangerous one, and
ought to have been prevented. It was not prevented,
and bloodshed ensued. I deeply lament such a result;
but I protest against all the blame being thrown on my
Irish friends. Those who distributed offensive placards
all over London, and got up the meeting to attack the
Pope, knowingly provoked a breach of the. peace. They
were the first aggressors. By assembling in large
numbers in the Park—especially
.on a Sunday—to
agitate against the head a 3 religion professed by a
great body of their fello w-countrymen, they exercised
a legal right in an illegal manner by endangering the
peace. The Irish merely did what everybody knew
that they would do under the circumstances. But I
have no doubt that the admonitions of their Bishop
and their clergy, as well as their own Christian feeling,
will put an end to all animosity, now that the Govern-
ment has shown a firm determination to prevent any-
thing calculated to produce riot and disturbance.'
EMIGRATION TO CANADA.—It may be of some service
to intending emigrants to Canada and New Brunswick
to know that the Emigration Commissioners receive and
remit, free of charge, for the use of newly arrived emi-
grants of the poorer classes, to the Government immigra-
tion agents in Canada and New Brunswick any sum of
money not less than £5 nor more than £2O, from any
one person, which may be paid to them or to their
credit at the Bank of England for the purpose. The
persons transmitting the money must furnish the com-
missioners with the names and ages of the emigrants
for whose benefit the money is deposited, and specify
the manner in which it is to be expended in the colony—
whether wholly in cash or partly in cash and partly in
providing emigrants with provisions and conveyance to
their destination. The commissioners do not engage to
effect purchases of land, or otherwise to invest or retain
the money for the benefit of individuals, but simply to
instruct the Government agents to apply it to the imme-
diate use oi the people after their arrival, either in the
mode directed by the depositor, or, in the absence of
such directions, in the manner which the immigration
agents may deem most advantageous for the emigrants.
Owing to the various rates of exchange, a given sum
will not always produce the same amount of colonial
currency, but the sum to be received in the colony will
in all cases exceed in nominal amount the sum deposited
in this country. This plan can obviously be only made
available in the cases of emigrants proceeding to those
places in British Nt.--", America where there are immi-
gration agents, viz., (), via and PlAlw Brunswick-

JOHN BULL TO GARIBALDI.
My dear Garibaldi, what shall I do,
Beyond what I've done, to satisfy you?
For many a year have I stretched my hands
To shake them with men of all other lands.
My Brothers, I 've said, arise and be free,
Observe what I do, and imitate me.
Lay tyranny prostrate, and priestcraft low,
But bide ye your time ere you strike the blow.
Oh, kick all your despots off and afar
That drag you to die for their fame in war;
Renounce the vain glory that makes you slaves,
And tools that subserve Imperial knaves.
I've called upon France, and holloaed to Spain,
To Germany critd again and again,
I call to the Yankees every day;
They turn a deaf ear to all that I say.
I'm evermore crying, Now, then' my mates,
Do, pray, leave off coating vessels with plates,
From forging new cannon let UR all cease,
And carry on business, trading in peace.
Ferocious abuse and truculent threat
Is all the return I ever had yet,
Except from one Hero, true man alone,
Whose favour, received, these lines are to own.

A QUESTION FOE, CATTLE CLUES.—A farmer in the
neighbourhood of Lyons is said to have discovered an
expeditious method of fattening cattle, which consists
in giving them cod-liver oil. Perhaps the good done
by this substance in plithisis pulmonalis is more appa-
rent than real; but experience will show whether its
administration tends to promote or arrest the consump-
tion of butcher's meat.

articles.title: PURIFICATION OF PARIS.
articles.text:
THE PURIFICATION OF PARIS.

The Paris correspondent of the Times writes word
that:—

'A new system for laying the dust without watering
the carriage .way has been for some time in operatics,
in the Avenue des Champs Elysees. It consists 0,1
sprinkling the road with chloride of lime, which,. b 44
ing remarkable for its power of absorbing moisture,
soon becomes damp, and thereby prevents any dust
from rising even in the hottest day.'
Whether this ,plan will answer or no remains ,for a
drier season than the past to decide; but if it succeeds
in laying the dust, let us hope it will be introduced
throughout Paris. Chloride of lime has, besides the
property of absorbing moisture, that of destroying un-
pleasant odours; and in sprinkling it about the French
capital to lay the dust the scavenger will, as it were
kill two birds with one stone.

CONVERSION OF THE FRENCH. Young France's
Hebrew Guardian, M. Fould, has actually.pulled, the
gay young fellow's accounts almost straight, and is
teaching him to save money. We are delighted with
the balance-sheet just issued, and expect to see edify-
ing results. In private life most of us have had, the
pleasure of beholding such reforms. Some prudent
friend takes hold of young Charley Rattletoni, and
converts him to economy, and how we smile. Charley,
who never had any money in his pocket, except-just
enough to muddle away in paying cabmen too much,
buying cigars when he should have stuck to Cavendish,
and travelling first-class when his betters were going
second, suddenly becomes prudent—looks- at the
change that is given him, wears his second best hat on
a wet :day, and actually walks instead of taking a
Hansom. He gives you mysterious hints about his
stock-broker, pretends to read the share.lists and in
general conveasation tries it on with Bank-parlour
slang, which, as no two people mean the same by any
financial definition, answers very well, and awes the
women. We hope to see young France come out in
similarly respectable fashion, and instead of talking
swagger about shooting in Mexico, volunteering in
Italy, and other expensive diversions, begin to bt
grave, and speak of Postal Savings' Banks, Water-
company Shares, Street Drainage, and such like
desiderata in Paris. Talk of Converting the Jews,
what shall be done unto a Jew who has converted a
Christian nation—and a lot of its debt?

employers have used as a Bourbon tool, and who it
lying in an Italian prison Under a heavy- sentence.
Couldn't he be let out, Italia? You don't keep cages
for such very helpless little rate as that ? Rattazzl, for
the sake of your name, let him go. Translate that
very little Bishop, and give him letters dimissory
Rome. Please let him out. We wouldn't ask it if ha
were other than harmless, but what can be feared from
such a convertite ?'

ROPEMAKERS' Appeal to the Metropolitan
Trades, and Trades of the United Kingdom.
BROTHEIt i OItKING NILN It is with a feeling of reluc-
tance that we, tne London. 0, erative Ropemakers, ven-
ture to draw your attention to our present position,
knowing as we do the great depression of trade in almost
every department of manufacture, and yet we fel
encouraged to lay our case before you, soliciting your
sympathy and aid, by the conviction that we are well
known by the London trades, and to many trades in the
country, for our willingness to assist i thers in times of
difficulty. We will therefore simply state our case to
you, hoping that you will deem it worthy of your kind
consideration.
On the 11th of last June one of our employers offered
reduction of sevenpence
per day, or three and six-
pence per week, from our wages, and we, having a well
organised trade society, could not submit to any reduc-
tion of wages,' recognising as fair workmen should do
that a iair day s work is entitled to a fair day's pay, and
having enjoyed the present rate of wages for the last
seven years, and there being no reasonable plea given
why such reduction should take place.
Having sent demi, ations to the employers to reason
the matter with them, and used every effort to pre-
vent a strike, but finding that the employers were
determined if possible to effect a general reduction of
wages throughout the trade, there was no other course
ieft us but to withoraw the whole of the journeymen
from the firm, viz.—Messrs. J. and H. Baker, Bermond-
sey, This is the eighth week of the strike, and our
'nen are firm and in good spirits, being convinced of the
'ustness ot their claims and ultimate success, for al-
though the firm has resorted to all kinds of misrepre-
sentation to obtain men their shop is still empty. for as
fast as the men come up from the couutry through their
e gents and advertisements in the country local papers,
they (the men) after having the question of dispute
xplained to them, leave their work, and by our assis-
tance leave London again, which creates a large expense
r,ver the actual cost of keeping our own members on
strike. We have expenited over £l5O, a large sum for
only one firm, but then we are fighting for the whole
trade, for some of the other employers have already
given notice to their men, that as soon as Messr. Baker
and Brothers get supplied with men at th t reduction
that they will give no more for their work than the
Messrs Baker's, and if we are compelled to submit to
this reduction we shall lose 11,500 per year in wages
(then leaving a large surplus of men out of work), a sum
you will admit worth struggling for.
Having thus briefly stared our present position we
earnestly appeal to the sympathy of our fellow workmen
in other trades solicitine their assistance to enable us to
defend successfully our right of wages and ti ade against
these grasping employers. In appealing to our fellow
working men, we may say that we have had always a
willing heart and ready hand to assist other trades
placed in similar circnins ances ; indeed, since 1853 there
has not been a question affecting the interest of the
-working classes, or a dispute in any other trade, but
what we have supported and sustained to our utmost
ability. We therefore make this appeal ' with some
.egree of confidene, that you will r,adily respond to.us
in our present diflieultti a. and show to the employing
:lasses that there is a spirit of union and brotherhood
amongst the working men of England, that will enable
them to rally round their fellow but oppressed brother
Workmen.
We beg to remain yours very respectfully, on behalf of
the trade Thomas Hay, Charles Howe, William Matthews,
Charles Terdre, Robert Still, committee; Richard Bur-
ridge, treasurer; Daniel z,mith, seer tary,

to any society to give the informadon that may be re-
quired, or forward any information on the question of
dispute, by applying to
